question_text:
A company collects data for temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure in cities across multiple continents.
The average volume of data that the company collects from each site daily is 500 GB. Each site has a high-speed Internet connection.
The company wants to aggregate the data from all these global sites as quickly as possible in a single Amazon S3 bucket. The solution must minimize operational complexity.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The sites already have fast internet connections, so they can upload directly to a single S3 bucket. S3 Transfer Acceleration sends traffic through a nearby AWS edge location and over the AWS backbone. Multipart uploads transfer parts of large files in parallel. Together, these features speed up uploads with little operational overhead.
Option B: Regional buckets and replication add setup and source object cleanup.
Option C: Shipping Snowball devices takes days, while the sites already have fast connections.
Option D: EC2 instances, EBS volumes, snapshots, and restores add cost and complexity before the data reaches S3.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination S3 bucket. Use multipart uploads to directly upload site data to the destination S3 bucket.
Upload the data from each site to an S3 bucket in the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket. Then remove the data from the origin S3 bucket.
Schedule AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device jobs daily to transfer data from each site to the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy objects to the destination S3 bucket.

Upload the data from each site to an Amazon EC2 instance in the closest Region. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. At regular intervals, take an EBS snapshot and copy it to the Region that contains the destination S3 bucket. Restore the EBS volume in that Region.

question_text:
A company needs the ability to analyze the log files of its proprietary application. The logs are stored in JSON format in an Amazon S3 bucket. Queries will be simple and will run on-demand. A solutions architect needs to perform the analysis with minimal changes to the existing architecture.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The data already exists in S3 and the query is simple and needs-based. Amazon Atena reads objects directly from the S3 buckets, understands the JSON format and charges them in scanned bytes - without clustering, without data loading, and without changing the structure.
Option A: Loading the entire amount of data to Redshift implies the need for an independent data storage, a loading conduit and a cluster that is always in operation.
Option B: Log already exists in S3, moving it to Cloudwatch Logs is structured change and storage costs are higher.
Option D: A glue directory with a temporary EMR cluster can solve the task, but they need to be configured and cost nodes, and a single service is sufficient.

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift to load all the content into one place and run the SQL queries as needed.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the logs. Run SQL queries as needed from the Amazon CloudWatch console.
Use Amazon Athena directly with Amazon S3 to run the queries as needed.
Use AWS Glue to catalog the logs. Use a transient Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to run the SQL queries as needed.

question_text:
A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts for different departments. The management account has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains project reports. The company wants to limit access to this S3 bucket to only users of accounts within the organization in AWS Organizations.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The company needs to allow access to anyone in the organization, without having to rewriting the strategy every time a new account is added. This is precisely the function of the ws: PrinceOrgID Global Conditional Key: The barrel policy assigns the organization ID (o-xxx), and the request is successful only if the subject belongs to an account within the organization. Access is automatically effective when an account is added; access automatically disappears when an account is removed. It is not necessary to list or maintain, so the operating costs are minimal.
Option B:aws: PrinceOrgPaths limits access to specific organizational units (OUs) and requires a list of OU paths and continuous maintenance during organizational reorganization. However, this mandate allows for visits by the entire Organization.
Option C: Monitoring organizational events and updating strategies is a self-researched synchronisation mechanism for the list of accounts: there is a risk of code, delay and error, and a ready-made condition key already exists.
Option D: Adding labels to users means that they must be manually applied and removed in each account. The membership of the organization is automatically checked.

options.text: Add the aws PrincipalOrgID global condition key with a reference to the organization ID to the S3 bucket policy.
Create an organizational unit (OU) for each department. Add the aws:PrincipalOrgPaths global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.
Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor the CreateAccount, InviteAccountToOrganization, LeaveOrganization, and RemoveAccountFromOrganization events. Update the S3 bucket policy accordingly.
Tag each user that needs access to the S3 bucket. Add the aws:PrincipalTag global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.

question_text:
An application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a VPC. The application processes logs that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The EC2 instance needs to access the S3 bucket without connectivity to the internet.
Which solution will provide private network connectivity to Amazon S3?
explanation_en:
Private connections from VPC to S3 are provided by gateway endpoints: the path to the service prefix list is added to the route chart of the subnet, and barrel requests will be transmitted within the AWS network rather than to the Internet. The endpoint itself is not expensive.
Option B: Re-export log streaming to Cloudwatch Logs is a redesign of log processing rather than a web-based solution, and access to S3 still requires a route.
Option C: The example role is granted access, but the route remains unchanged: traffic continues through the Internet without endpoints.
Option D: Private access to S3 through API Gateway is non-existent: the mechanism does not work that way.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint to the S3 bucket.
Stream the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Export the logs to the S3 bucket.
Create an instance profile on Amazon EC2 to allow S3 access.
Create an Amazon API Gateway API with a private link to access the S3 endpoint.

question_text:
A company is hosting a web application on AWS using a single Amazon EC2 instance that stores user-uploaded documents in an Amazon EBS volume. For better scalability and availability, the company duplicated the architecture and created a second EC2 instance and EBS volume in another Availability Zone, placing both behind an Application Load Balancer. After completing this change, users reported that, each time they refreshed the website, they could see one subset of their documents or the other, but never all of the documents at the same time.
What should a solutions architect propose to ensure users see all of their documents at once?
explanation_en:
There is a simple explanation for the symptoms: an EBS volume is attached only to a single instance, so each machine has its own file collection, and the load balancer shows one of the sets on which machine it is requested to be placed. What is needed is a shared storage that can be accessed by both machines at the same time - through NFS to mount Amazon EFS in all available cases. The existing file is copied to the EFS, the application starts writing here, and the complete list of files is available to the user regardless of which instance it is requested to reach.
Option A: A one-time copy will only synchronize the volume at the moment of the copy: the next document to be uploaded will still be on only one machine.
Option B: Fixed the user to their server is not helpful: the single user's document has been scattered over two volumes, and if the server fails, access to its file will be lost.
Option D: The load balancer will send the request to a target server. It is unable to divide requests and collide responses.

options.text: Copy the data so both EBS volumes contain all the documents
Configure the Application Load Balancer to direct a user to the server with the documents
Copy the data from both EBS volumes to Amazon EFS. Modify the application to save new documents to Amazon EFS
Configure the Application Load Balancer to send the request to both servers. Return each document from the correct server

question_text:
A company uses NFS to store large video files in on-premises network attached storage. Each video file ranges in size from 1 MB to 500 GB. The total storage is 70 TB and is no longer growing. The company decides to migrate the video files to Amazon S3. The company must migrate the video files as soon as possible while using the least possible network bandwidth.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Two binding conditions apply: to move as quickly as possible and to minimize the use of network bandwidth. The second condition directly excludes any network transmission, so 70 TB data is transmitted offline - via AWS Snowball Edge equipment (about 80 TB, i.e., individual orders). The data was copied locally to the device, the equipment was returned to AWS and the data eventually entered S3. A useful rule of estimation: a Gbps ⁇ 10 TB per day, so it takes a week to transmit 70 TB via the network, even if it has a totally free gigabytes connection, which is not the case.
Option A: Copying through CLI will use the company ' s Internet connection: it is completely contrary to the requirement to minimize bandwidth use.
Option C: S3 File Gateway is designed for ongoing mixed access rather than a one-time migration, and data will still be transmitted through the network.
Option D: DirectConect takes months to set it up and the data will still be transmitted through that link. It does not meet the need for a one-time 'quick 'transmission 70 TB.

options.text: Create an S3 bucket. Create an IAM role that has permissions to write to the S3 bucket. Use the AWS CLI to copy all files locally to the S3 bucket.

Create an AWS Snowball Edge job. Receive a Snowball Edge device on premises. Use the Snowball Edge client to transfer data to the device. Return the device so that AWS can import the data into Amazon S3.

Deploy an S3 File Gateway on premises. Create a public service endpoint to connect to the S3 File Gateway. Create an S3 bucket. Create a new NFS file share on the S3 File Gateway. Point the new file share to the S3 bucket. Transfer the data from the existing NFS file share to the S3 File Gateway.

Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises network and AWS. Deploy an S3 File Gateway on premises. Create a public virtual interface (VIF) to connect to the S3 File Gateway. Create an S3 bucket. Create a new NFS file share on the S3 File Gateway. Point the new file share to the S3 bucket. Transfer the data from the existing NFS file share to the S3 File Gateway.

question_text:
A company has an application that ingests incoming messages. Dozens of other applications and microservices then quickly consume these messages. The number of messages varies drastically and sometimes increases suddenly to 100,000 each second. The company wants to decouple the solution and increase scalability.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
Dozens of stand-alone applications consume information, each of which requires its own copy. A SNS theme distributes messages to all subscribers, while the SQS queue for each consumer smooths the peak of up to 100,000 messages per second and allows each consumer to process them at its own pace. It's classic radio mode.
Option A: Kinesis Data Analytics handles data streams by searching; it does not store messages by ten independent consumers.
Option B: Based on the CPU load extension example, it is not possible to decorate the producer with the consumer or to cope with sudden peaks in flows.
Option C: A single Kinesis fraction has a record limit of about 1,000 per second, well below 100,000, and the middle table adds complexity without real benefit.

options.text: Persist the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics. Configure the consumer applications to read and process the messages.
Deploy the ingestion application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to scale the number of EC2 instances based on CPU metrics.

Write the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a single shard. Use an AWS Lambda function to preprocess messages and store them in Amazon DynamoDB. Configure the consumer applications to read from DynamoDB to process the messages.

Publish the messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SOS) subscriptions. Configure the consumer applications to process the messages from the queues.

question_text:
A company is migrating a distributed application to AWS. The application serves variable workloads. The legacy platform consists of a primary server that coordinates jobs across multiple compute nodes. The company wants to modernize the application with a solution that maximizes resiliency and scalability.
How should a solutions architect design the architecture to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The operation coordinator is a bottleneck and a single point failure. The operation is placed in a SQS queue, the calculation node runs in an automatic extension group, the size of which is driven by the queue length. This would allow the system to respond to actual workloads and to withstand any node failure.
Option A: Time extension cannot respond to variable loads specified in the demand.
Option C: CloudTrail records API calls, cannot be the target of the operation and the main server remains single-point failure.
Option D: EventBridge route events without working queues, and the main server is still in design.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling to use scheduled scaling.

Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the size of the queue.

Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure AWS CloudTrail as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the primary server.

Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the compute nodes.

question_text:
A company is running an SMB file server in its data center. The file server stores large files that are accessed frequently for the first few days after the files are created. After 7 days the files are rarely accessed.
The total data size is increasing and is close to the company's total storage capacity. A solutions architect must increase the company's available storage space without losing low-latency access to the most recently accessed files. The solutions architect must also provide file lifecycle management to avoid future storage issues.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
There are three requirements: additional storage space, maintenance of low delays in recent access documents, and life-cycle management. Amazon S3 File Gateway provides SMB sharing to local clients, stores data in S3 and keeps recently used files in local caches - hence the low delay in new data. A life-cycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive in seven days addresses the growth of costs and data volumes.
Option A: DataSync copys data, but does not allow local applications transparent access to the migrated data and does not manage the life cycle itself.
Option C: FSx for Windows File Server provides storage space and SMB protocols, but is a fully paid file storage and does not automatically transition to a cheaper archive storage category.
Option D: The deployment of a tool on each user computer means that work processes need to be changed and familiar network sharing abandoned, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retriev is more expensive than Deep Archive for the same needs.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to copy data that is older than 7 days from the SMB file server to AWS.
Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway to extend the company's storage space. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.
Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system to extend the company's storage space.
Install a utility on each user's computer to access Amazon S3. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 7 days.

question_text:
A company is building an ecommerce web application on AWS. The application sends information about new orders to an Amazon API Gateway REST API to process. The company wants to ensure that orders are processed in the order that they are received.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Only the SQS FIFO queue ensures the order of order: it maintains a sequence in the message group and guarantees an accurate one-time processing. The API Gateway places the order in such a queue, and the Lambda function reads and sequentially processes the order.
Option A: SNS does not guarantee the order in which the message will be delivered: the message can reach the subscriber in any order.
Option C: Blocking all requests while handling an order would undermine the amount of throughput in the application.
Option D: Standard SQS queue is treated in the order in which you try, but allows for reordering: it does not provide for strict serialization.

options.text: Use an API Gateway integration to publish a message to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the application receives an order. Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the topic to perform processing.

Use an API Gateway integration to send a message to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue when the application receives an order. Configure the SQS FIFO queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function for processing.
Use an API Gateway authorizer to block any requests while the application processes an order.

Use an API Gateway integration to send a message to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue when the application receives an order. Configure the SQS standard queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function for processing.

question_text:
A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances and uses an Amazon Aurora database. The EC2 instances connect to the database by using user names and passwords that are stored locally in a file. The company wants to minimize the operational overhead of credential management.
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this goal?
explanation_en:
The password is stored in a document on an example, which means that someone has to distribute it, change it on each machine and ensure that it does not leak along with the mirror. AWS Securitys Manager removes all of these problems: the key is encrypted with KMS keys, the key is obtained through the API through the identity of the example role, the built-in rotation function changes the password in both the Aurora database and the key itself, using off-the-shelf functions for supporting the database. There was no need to write any code -- so "minimize operating expenses". The key difference with Parameter Store is that only Secrets Manager has a rotational function.
Option B: Parameter Store can store the password as SecureString, but it has no built-in automatic rotation -- it cannot be opened by tickbox; you need to write and maintain your own functions.
Option C: The document in the encrypted S3 bucket remains the same file: the password in the database and the password in the object still need to be changed manually or by your own code.
Option D: Encrypted EBS volumes provide protection only when static data is stored, but do not solve any problems in document management: there is no rotation function and the file now exists in each instance.

options.text: Use AWS Secrets Manager. Turn on automatic rotation.
Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Turn on automatic rotation.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store objects that are encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Migrate the credential file to the S3 bucket. Point the application to the S3 bucket.

Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume for each EC2 instance. Attach the new EBS volume to each EC2 instance. Migrate the credential file to the new EBS volume. Point the application to the new EBS volume.

question_text:
A global company hosts its web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).
The web application has static data and dynamic data. The company stores its static data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
The company wants to improve performance and reduce latency for the static data and dynamic data. The company is using its own domain name registered with Amazon Route 53.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The same service accelerates static and dynamic content: CloudFront can have multiple sources and is provided through a path-based behavioural route request - static files are provided from S3 S3 buckets and dynamic requests are proxyd to load balancers. The performance of dynamic content is not derived from caches, but from TLS being terminated at the nearest edge and then requested to be transmitted through the AWS core network. Route 53 uses aliases to identify the company ' s domain name to this distribution configuration.
Option B: The global accelerator does not support S3 as an endpoint: it is only compatible with ALB, NLB, EC2 and flexible IP addresses. This design is not feasible.
Option C: There is no point in adding an accelerator to the claudFront: two services already provide a global network and the design will add complexity without any benefit.
Option D: The use of two stand-alone domain names for static and dynamic content increases the complexity of applications, and S3 is still not an end point for global accelerators.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the S3 bucket and the ALB as origins. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the ALB as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the S3 bucket as an endpoint Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the S3 bucket as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the ALB and the CloudFront distribution as endpoints. Create a custom domain name that points to the accelerator DNS name. Use the custom domain name as an endpoint for the web application.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has the ALB as an origin. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator that has the S3 bucket as an endpoint. Create two domain names. Point one domain name to the CloudFront DNS name for dynamic content. Point the other domain name to the accelerator DNS name for static content. Use the domain names as endpoints for the web application.

question_text:
A company performs monthly maintenance on its AWS infrastructure. During these maintenance activities, the company needs to rotate the credentials for its Amazon RDS for MySQL databases across multiple AWS Regions.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Two requirements: the same certificates need to be used in more than one region and they must be rotated according to a predetermined schedule, while minimizing manual operations. Secrets Manager happens to provide both mechanisms: multi-regional key copy will keep a copy of the key in the desired area and will automatically update the copy as the primary key changes; and the built-in rotation function for RDS will change passwords as planned. Applications in each region read local copies and no cross-regional calls were required to avoid delays.
Option B: Systems Manager Parameter Store does not support cross-regional replication or built-in rotations. Both mechanisms need to be built on their own from scratch.
Option C: A file stored in a barrel with a custom function triggered by EventBridge means that it needs to create its own code to perform the functions in the Secrets Manager configuration and does not have an off-the-shelf cross-regional reproduction function.
Option D: A multi-area KMS key, a DynamoDB global table and a custom rotation function are feasible, but involve three services and a manual build process rather than a single configuration.

options.text: Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Secrets Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Systems Manager by creating a secure string parameter. Use multi- Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Systems Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket that has server-side encryption (SSE) enabled. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to invoke an AWS Lambda function to rotate the credentials.

Encrypt the credentials as secrets by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) multi-Region customer managed keys. Store the secrets in an Amazon DynamoDB global table. Use an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the secrets from DynamoDB. Use the RDS API to rotate the secrets.

question_text:
A company runs an ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The Auto Scaling group scales based on CPU utilization metrics. The ecommerce application stores the transaction data in a MySQL 8.0 database that is hosted on a large EC2 instance.
The database's performance degrades quickly as application load increases. The application handles more read requests than write transactions. The company wants a solution that will automatically scale the database to meet the demand of unpredictable read workloads while maintaining high availability.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Reading operations are significantly more numerous than writing operations, loads are unpredictable and require high availability. Aurora MySQL is compatible with existing databases and is deployed across multiple available areas and can automatically add and remove read copies based on the load through Aurora. The application can switch to the reading end without changing any query.
Option A: Redshift is an analytical data repository for complex queries on large-scale data sets, is not a service database for online stores and cannot provide high availability at single nodes.
Option B: Single-usable area configuration contradicts high-availability requirements, and RDS reading copies are not automatically added according to load.
Option D: Memcached is a cache that does not have data durability and copying; it is not a database and the Spot example is not suitable for data storage.

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.
Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.
Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.

question_text:
A company recently migrated to AWS and wants to implement a solution to protect the traffic that flows in and out of the production VPC. The company had an inspection server in its on-premises data center. The inspection server performed specific operations such as traffic flow inspection and traffic filtering. The company wants to have the same functionalities in the AWS Cloud.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The local check server did two things: checking traffic and filtering traffic. In AWS, this corresponds to AWS Network Firewall - a managed, state-based VPC-level firewall that supports the Suricat compatible rules, domain filtering and depth protocol checks. It is deployed in a dedicated subnet, and VPC traffic flows by its endpoint. The difference is that Network Firewall filter traffic, WAF protects HTTP applications, Firewall Manager centralizes management strategies in multiple accounts, and GuardDuty only performs testing.
Option A: GuardDuty analyzes logs and reports suspicious activities. It doesn't stop anything, it doesn't filter the flow.
Option B: Traffic Mirroring copys the flow to the analyser, but it does not filter or block anything when used alone - it is an observable tool.
Option D: Firewall Manager manages the WAF, Shield and Network Firewall policies in multiple accounts, but does not carry out the check itself: it needs a bottom-up service, namely Network Firewall.

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty for traffic inspection and traffic filtering in the production VPC.
Use Traffic Mirroring to mirror traffic from the production VPC for traffic inspection and filtering.
Use AWS Network Firewall to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.
Use AWS Firewall Manager to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.

question_text:
A company hosts a data lake on AWS. The data lake consists of data in Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company needs a reporting solution that provides data visualization and includes all the data sources within the data lake. Only the company's management team should have full access to all the visualizations. The rest of the company should have only limited access.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
What is needed is visualization across multiple data sources (S3 and RDS) and isolation of access: managing users have full access and others have restricted access. Amazon QuickSight connects to S3 via Athena, directly to RDS, and the release dashboard is shared with QuickSight's own users and groups - the service owns its own user and group model. This is the key difference between the correct and similar options: the dashboard cannot be shared to the IAM role.
Option A: QuickSight dashboards are posted to QuickSight users and groups instead of IAM roles. Role Control Service access to data sources, rather than the visibility of the dashboard.
Option C: The Glue operation generates the report file, but this is not interactive visualization and access control achieved through the storage barrel policy is more crude than permissions at the dashboard level.
Option D: Athena federal query solves data access problems, but it still generates tables and files rather than visualization. Cannot meet the need for dashboards.

options.text: Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate IAM roles.
Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate users and groups.

Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Create an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job to produce reports. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.

Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena Federated Query to access data within Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Generate reports by using Amazon Athena. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.

question_text:
A company is implementing a new business application. The application runs on two Amazon EC2 instances and uses an Amazon S3 bucket for document storage. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the EC2 instances can access the S3 bucket.
What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
An EC2 instance can only be granted permission in one way - i.e. through the IAM role attached to the example (technically through the case profile). Application takes temporary vouchers from case metadata that are automatically refreshed and the key will never be saved in a file or environment variable. The strategy is attached to the role rather than the example; the group is used only by the user.
Option B: A policy cannot be attached to an instance: a strategy is attached to the user, group and role. The example gets a role, which carries a strategy.
Option C: An IAM group is a user container. Examples cannot be attached to them.
Option D: An IAM user is a long-term voucher for an individual or external system. The user is unable to attach the example and saving the key on disk is an inverse mode.

options.text: Create an IAM role that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.
Create an IAM policy that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the policy to the EC2 instances.
Create an IAM group that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the group to the EC2 instances.
Create an IAM user that grants access to the S3 bucket. Attach the user account to the EC2 instances.

question_text:
An application development team is designing a microservice that will convert large images to smaller, compressed images. When a user uploads an image through the web interface, the microservice should store the image in an Amazon S3 bucket, process and compress the image with an AWS Lambda function, and store the image in its compressed form in a different S3 bucket.
A solutions architect needs to design a solution that uses durable, stateless components to process the images automatically.
Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
durable storage and stateless components are required. S3 The information is placed in the SQS queue by notification at the time of uploading, thus enabling the document information to be stored reliably and maintained in case of malfunction (A). This queue is the calling source for the Lambda function, where messages are deleted after successful processing; if the processing fails, the queue is returned and retry (B).
Option C: The text file in the function memory disappears while the environment disappears, and the function itself does not have an built-in way to interrogate the drum.
Option D: An EC2 instance with a log file increases state and infrastructure maintenance.
Option E: Mail sent to the application owner is an act of notifying the individual rather than automating image processing.

options.text: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the S3 bucket to send a notification to the SQS queue when an image is uploaded to the S3 bucket.
Configure the Lambda function to use the Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the invocation source. When the SQS message is successfully processed, delete the message in the queue.

Configure the Lambda function to monitor the S3 bucket for new uploads. When an uploaded image is detected, write the file name to a text file in memory and use the text file to keep track of the images that were processed.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to monitor an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. When items are added to the queue, log the file name in a text file on the EC2 instance and invoke the Lambda function.

Configure an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) event to monitor the S3 bucket. When an image is uploaded, send an alert to an Amazon ample Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with the application owner's email address for further processing.

question_text:
A company has a three-tier web application that is deployed on AWS. The web servers are deployed in a public subnet in a VPC. The application servers and database servers are deployed in private subnets in the same VPC.
The company has deployed a third-party virtual firewall appliance from AWS Marketplace in an inspection VPC.
The appliance is configured with an IP interface that can accept IP packets.
A solutions architect needs to integrate the web application with the appliance to inspect all traffic to the application before the traffic reaches the web server.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Third-party testing equipment received data packages on the IP level - AWS happens to provide a dedicated service for this scenario. The gateway load balancer is deployed to detect VPC at the front end of the device and creates a gateway load balancer end point in the VPC of the application: traffic is routed to that end, transferred transparently to the device via GENEVE and then back to the original route. The source address is kept and the load balancer is responsible for the extension and health check of the equipment - operating costs are minimal.
Option A: A network load equalizer operates on the 4th floor and changes the target of the connection: it does not provide transparent detection of the full flow and the return path of the package must be built manually.
Option B: An application of the load balancer to resolve HTTP and to terminate the connection itself, while the device expects the original IP package.
Option C: The transfer gateway is used to connect the network, but it is not possible to transmit traffic to the detection device when used separately, or to balance loads between multiple device examples. Routes must be maintained manually.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer in the public subnet of the application's VPC to route the traffic to the appliance for packet inspection.
Create an Application Load Balancer in the public subnet of the application's VPC to route the traffic to the appliance for packet inspection.
Deploy a transit gateway in the inspection VPConfigure route tables to route the incoming packets through the transit gateway.
Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer in the inspection VPC. Create a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint to receive the incoming packets and forward the packets to the appliance.

question_text:
A company wants to improve its ability to clone large amounts of production data into a test environment in the same AWS Region. The data is stored in Amazon EC2 instances on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Modifications to the cloned data must not affect the production environment. The software that accesses this data requires consistently high I/O performance.
A solutions architect needs to minimize the time that is required to clone the production data into the test environment.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
A roll recovered from a snapshot was loaded from S3 lazy when the block was first visited, and therefore is usually slow. The snapshot restoration function eliminates this behaviour: once it is activated, the volume created by the snapshot provides integrity at the time it is created. The process is therefore to create a snapshot, enable the functionality, create a new volume from the snapshot and attach it to the test instance, a copy that is independent and achieves high performance from the first second.
Option A: A snapshot cannot be restored to the instance storage: the local disk of the instance is not created from the EBS snapshot.
Option B: Multiple mounts connect the same volume to multiple examples, which means that the test environment will write production data — a direct violation of requirements.
Option C: Each block is read individually for a long time by starting a manual scroll, and time is a factor that needs to be minimized. The presentation has also been reordered.

options.text: Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Restore the snapshots onto EC2 instance store volumes in the test environment.

Configure the production EBS volumes to use the EBS Multi-Attach feature. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Attach the production EBS volumes to the EC2 instances in the test environment.

Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Create and initialize new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment before restoring the volumes from the production EBS snapshots.

Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Turn on the EBS fast snapshot restore feature on the EBS snapshots. Restore the snapshots into new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment.

question_text:
An ecommerce company wants to launch a one-deal-a-day website on AWS. Each day will feature exactly one product on sale for a period of 24 hours. The company wants to be able to handle millions of requests each hour with millisecond latency during peak hours.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Millions of requests per hour, millisecond response times and extremely low operating expenses indicate the introduction of a server-free structure. Static contents are stored in S3 and cached at edges through CloudFront, dynamic calls are processed by API Gateway and Lambda, and order data are stored in DynamoDB, with response times of only a few milliseconds. The system can be expanded automatically without having to manage any server.
Option A: A completely static website cannot handle purchase operations and it is not feasible to store order data in S3: service processing and fast key-based access are required.
Option B: A set of examples, two load equalizers and one RDS database represent the highest operating expenses and require manual configuration of peak hours.
Option C: An EKS cluster implies the need to manage nodes and auto-extension settings, while RDS still has bottlenecks under peak loads.

options.text: Use Amazon S3 to host the full website in different S3 buckets. Add Amazon CloudFront distributions. Set the S3 buckets as origins for the distributions. Store the order data in Amazon S3.

Deploy the full website on Amazon EC2 instances that run in Auto Scaling groups across multiple Availability Zones. Add an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute the website traffic. Add another ALB for the backend APIs. Store the data in Amazon RDS for MySQL.

Migrate the full application to run in containers. Host the containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to increase and decrease the number of pods to process bursts in traffic. Store the data in Amazon RDS for MySQL.

Use an Amazon S3 bucket to host the website's static content. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Set the S3 bucket as the origin. Use Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions for the backend APIs. Store the data in Amazon DynamoDB.

question_text:
A solutions architect is using Amazon S3 to design the storage architecture of a new digital media application. The media files must be resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone. Some files are accessed frequently while other files are rarely accessed in an unpredictable pattern. The solutions architect must minimize the costs of storing and retrieving the media files.
Which storage option meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The two requests are here to work together. "Resistence in loss of serviceable areas" excludes any storage class that exists in a single serviceable area, i.e., single serviceable area standard storage (One Zone-IA). The "access mode is unpredictable" excludes those storage categories that charge for retrieval: if you cannot predict when the document will be needed, then every unexpected visit costs the standard storage category (IA). This leaves only S3 Intelligent-Tiering: it automatically moves objects between different levels according to actual access, without a charge for retrieval, and stores copies in three available areas. Excerpt Law: "Unforeseeable access patterns" almost always refer to the storage of intelligent layers.
Option A: S3 standard storage can resist the loss of a single available area, but it does not solve another problem: for documents that are rarely visited, you still have to pay the full cost. This does not meet the requirement to reduce costs.
Option C: Standard-IA storage costs are lower, but it charges a fee for search of each Gia byte and at least 30 days for storage. In cases where the pattern of visits is unpredictable, these costs can easily offset the cost savings.
Option D: Single Available Area-IA stores data in a single Available Area. This option does not meet the first requirement at all — that of being able to withstand the loss of a usable area.

options.text: S3 Standard
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

question_text:
A company is storing backup files by using Amazon S3 Standard storage. The files are accessed frequently for 1 month. However, the files are not accessed after 1 month. The company must keep the files indefinitely.
Which storage solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The pattern of access here is clearly known: after a month of use, the document will no longer be read but will have to be retained permanently. When the model is known, the explicit life-cycle rule is the least costly option, and the target storage category is selected according to the search speed required - which is not mentioned at all in the title. Therefore, the cheapest filing level, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, is the best option: approximately $1 per month per terabyte, compared with the $20 standard storage. In comparison to Question 126, part of the latter data must always be readily accessible, so the answer will be different.
Option A: Intelligent-Tiering charges the monitoring fees per object per month and moves the data according to actual access. When plans for visits are known, this leads to additional costs and additional uncertainty, compared to simple life-cycle rules.
Option C: Standard-IA costs approximately one order of magnitude higher than Deep Archive. It applies to situations where data are still to be read and where immediate access is required, but in this scenario the documents are not visited at all after the first month.
Option D: One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA, but is still much higher than Deep Archive, and it stores only one copy in a single usable area - a bad trade-off for indefinite backup.

options.text: Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically migrate objects.
Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 month.
Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 1 month.
Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 1 month.

question_text:
A company observes an increase in Amazon EC2 costs in its most recent bill. The billing team notices unwanted vertical scaling of instance types for a couple of EC2 instances. A solutions architect needs to create a graph comparing the last 2 months of EC2 costs and perform an in-depth analysis to identify the root cause of the vertical scaling.
How should the solutions architect generate the information with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
A two-month graph and analysis of the underlying causes are required, with minimal input. Cost Explorer (Cost Explorer) originals provide these two functions: providing ready-made graphs over time, supporting filtering and grouping by service, case type, label, account and area, and daily and hourly particle size. No content needs to be exported or constructed. Service boundaries: Cost explorers are used for interactive cost analysis, budgets (Budgets) are used for setting thresholds and alarms, and cost reports (CUR) provide raw data for self-defined analysis.
Option A: AWS Budgets tracking threshold and notify when you have exceeded it. It is not a tool for analysing the causes of cost increases.
Option C: Billing Dashboard shows aggregate gross values, but does not support flexible filtering by type of example or cycle-to-cycle comparisons at the required level of detail.
Option D: CUR, S3 and QuickSight provide maximum flexibility, but need to set the export, directory and dashboard. This is unnecessary for one-time analysis.

options.text: Use AWS Budgets to create a budget report and compare EC2 costs based on instance types.
Use Cost Explorer's granular filtering feature to perform an in-depth analysis of EC2 costs based on instance types.
Use graphs from the AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard to compare EC2 costs based on instance types for the last 2 months.
Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon S3 as a source to generate an interactive graph based on instance types.

question_text:
A company is designing an application. The application uses an AWS Lambda function to receive information through Amazon API Gateway and to store the information in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database.
During the proof-of-concept stage, the company has to increase the Lambda quotas significantly to handle the high volumes of data that the company needs to load into the database. A solutions architect must recommend a new design to improve scalability and minimize the configuration effort.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The problem is that during the surge in traffic, the number of functional calls carried out at the same time reaches the quota limit and the database cannot keep up with the writing operation. The correct solution is to use a queue to decorate data intake and writing: one function receives data and puts messages into SQS, the other functions read messages from the queue and write to the database at a controlled rate. The queue absorbs peak traffic, does not lose any data and hardly requires configuration.
Option A: Rewrite the data to Tomcat on the EC2 instance, which requires both a lot of work and a return to server management.
Option B: Switching the database to DynamoDB and matching the DAX cluster means that the data model and all queries need to be redesigned and that the reference to "existing DynamoDB API caller" contradicts the demand because the database here is Aurora.
Option C: SNS immediately sends a message to the subscriber without buffering the message: the second function will experience exactly the same overload during the surge, and failure to send will cause the message to be lost.

options.text: Refactor the Lambda function code to Apache Tomcat code that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Connect the database by using native Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) drivers.
Change the platform from Aurora to Amazon DynamoDProvision a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Use the DAX client SDK to point the existing DynamoDB API calls at the DAX cluster.

Set up two Lambda functions. Configure one function to receive the information. Configure the other function to load the information into the database. Integrate the Lambda functions by using Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).

Set up two Lambda functions. Configure one function to receive the information. Configure the other function to load the information into the database. Integrate the Lambda functions by using an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.

question_text:
A company needs to review its AWS Cloud deployment to ensure that its Amazon S3 buckets do not have unauthorized configuration changes.
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this goal?
explanation_en:
The task is to detect unauthorized configuration changes on the drums. This is precisely the function of AWS Config: it captures resource allocation, keeps historical records for each resource change and compares them with management rules (e.g., s3-buchet-public-read-prohibited, s3-buchet-changing-enabled, s3-buchet-ssl-requests-only, etc.). In case of non-compliance, it may give notice or automatically repair. It needs to be distinguished: Config is responsible for state and compliance checks, CloudTrail records who called which API, GuardDuty was responsible for threat detection.
Option B: Trusted Advisor provides regular recommendations for a limited range of inspections. It does not provide continuous configuration monitoring or changes in historical records.
Option C: Amazon Inspect scans the load for bugs; it does not check the drum configuration.
Option D: Object access log shows data access, not changes to the S3 bucket settings.

options.text: Turn on AWS Config with the appropriate rules.
Turn on AWS Trusted Advisor with the appropriate checks.
Turn on Amazon Inspector with the appropriate assessment template.
Turn on Amazon S3 server access logging. Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon Cloud Watch Events).

question_text:
A company is launching a new application and will display application metrics on an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard. The company's product manager needs to access this dashboard periodically. The product manager does not have an AWS account. A solutions architect must provide access to the product manager by following the principle of least privilege.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The person does not have an AWS account and the creation of the account is unnecessary to view a dashboard: Cloudwatch can share the dashboard with an outside user. Select the "shared dashboard" in the console, enter an e-mail address, and the service will create an independent certificate to view the dashboard only and send a link. Access rights are limited to individual resources and read-only — the most pure and minimal entitlement principle.
Option B: An IAM user with a Cloudwatch ReadOnly Access policy will expose all indicators, logs and dashboards in the account, not just what is required. It will also create long-term and valid evidence for outsiders.
Option C: The ViewOnlyAccess policy grants access to all service resources in the account — a much broader, far from minimal privileges principle.
Option D: A jumpboard host with caches in the browser is neither secure nor time-consuming: a server needs to be built, the server closed and access granted through RDP.

options.text: Share the dashboard from the CloudWatch console. Enter the product manager's email address, and complete the sharing steps. Provide a shareable link for the dashboard to the product manager.

Create an IAM user specifically for the product manager. Attach the CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess AWS managed policy to the user. Share the new login credentials with the product manager. Share the browser URL of the correct dashboard with the product manager.

Create an IAM user for the company's employees. Attach the ViewOnlyAccess AWS managed policy to the IAM user. Share the new login credentials with the product manager. Ask the product manager to navigate to the CloudWatch console and locate the dashboard by name in the Dashboards section.

Deploy a bastion server in a public subnet. When the product manager requires access to the dashboard, start the server and share the RDP credentials. On the bastion server, ensure that the browser is configured to open the dashboard URL with cached AWS credentials that have appropriate permissions to view the dashboard.

question_text:
A company is migrating applications to AWS. The applications are deployed in different accounts. The company manages the accounts centrally by using AWS Organizations. The company's security team needs a single sign-on (SSO) solution across all the company's accounts. The company must continue managing the users and groups in its on-premises self-managed Microsoft Active Directory.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Users and groups are kept in local Active Directory and are required to log in to each account within the organization. Standard Configuration: Enable IAM Infrastructure Center (formerly AWS SSO) to deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and build confidence with local forests. The test here requires that this integration requires a two-way forest trust — Identity Center must be able to identify and authenticate users, and one-way trust does not. Alternatives without trust can be AD Contractor or external SAML providers, but none of these options appear.
Option A: One-way trust is not enough to integrate Identity Center with self-managed Active Directory: the document clearly requires the use of two-way forest trust.
Option C: The directory service itself provides only a directory function, but cannot achieve single-point access to the organization's accounts - the allocation of access to the account is the responsibility of the Identity Center.
Option D: The deployment of a local identity provider is feasible, but requires that users continue to be managed in the existing Active Directory rather than constructing a new login system.

options.text: Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console. Create a one-way forest trust or a one- way domain trust to connect the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory with AWS SSO by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.

Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console. Create a two-way forest trust to connect the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory with AWS SSO by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.
Use AWS Directory Service. Create a two-way trust relationship with the company's self-managed Microsoft Active Directory.
Deploy an identity provider (IdP) on premises. Enable AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO) from the AWS SSO console.

question_text:
A company provides a Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) service that uses UDP connections. The service consists of Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group. The company has deployments across multiple AWS Regions.
The company needs to route users to the Region with the lowest latency. The company also needs automated failover between Regions.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
UDP traffic rules exclude Cloud Front and Application Load Balancer - both based on HTTP work. Only one Network Load Balancer is left in each region, which is directed by AWS Global Accerator to: it provides static on-board IP addresses, links users to the lowest delayed area of the AWS backbone network and automatically switch traffic when the regional endpoint group fails. The failure switch is completed in a few seconds and does not depend on the client 's DNS cache -- this is an important advantage compared to the route based on Route 53.
Option B: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP and HTTPS, but the service is based on UDP running.
Option C: CloudFront does not support UDP and cannot use Route 53 as a source for this type of traffic. The DNS-based failure switch also depends on the TTL solver cache.
Option D: The load balancer is wrong, and the weighted route does not select the lowest delayed area - and CloudFront is again not applicable to UDP.

options.text: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the NLB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the ALB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.

Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 latency record that points to aliases for each NLB. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the latency record as an origin.

Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 weighted record that points to aliases for each ALB. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the weighted record as an origin.

question_text:
A development team runs monthly resource-intensive tests on its general purpose Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with Performance Insights enabled. The testing lasts for 48 hours once a month and is the only process that uses the database. The team wants to reduce the cost of running the tests without reducing the compute and memory attributes of the DB instance.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The database requires 48 hours of operation per month, and the type of case cannot be changed. The key detail is that the stopped RDS example will be automatically restarted in seven days, so the mere "stop case" for one month is not valid. A more economical approach would be to take a snapshot, remove the example and then restore it from the snapshot for the next round of tests — you would simply have to pay for the cache.
Option A: Stop the instance only for a maximum of seven days: AWS will automatically restart the instance in seven days and the fee will resume.
Option B: RDS does not calculate the automatic extension of the resource, and storage resources can only be expanded upwards.
Option D: The narrowing of the case type is explicitly prohibited: the computational properties cannot be changed.

options.text: Stop the DB instance when tests are completed. Restart the DB instance when required.
Use an Auto Scaling policy with the DB instance to automatically scale when tests are completed.
Create a snapshot when tests are completed. Terminate the DB instance and restore the snapshot when required.
Modify the DB instance to a low-capacity instance when tests are completed. Modify the DB instance again when required.

question_text:
A company that hosts its web application on AWS wants to ensure all Amazon EC2 instances. Amazon RDS DB instances. and Amazon Redshift clusters are configured with tags. The company wants to minimize the effort of configuring and operating this check.
What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?
explanation_en:
Checking whether all resources carry the required labels should be the responsibility of the hosting service, rather than the custom code. The AWS Config required-tags rule specifies which label keys are necessary and which resource types are applicable, and these labels are evaluated at each change and a compliance historical record is maintained. If needed, the rule can be triggered by SSM Automation. Settings take only a few minutes to run automatically when they are complete.
Option B: Cost explorers can show expenditure and support grouping by label, but it is not an inventory tool for unmarked resources, and then manually labeling the resource cannot be extended.
Option C: The deployment of a custom code on a running example means that both the development work and the operation of an additional machine are required.
Option D: The planned task function removes the example, but the code still needs to be maintained by you: page breaks, new resource types, error processing. An off-the-shelf Config rule can do this without any development.

options.text: Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.
Use Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Tag those resources manually.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Periodically run the code on an EC2 instance.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Schedule an AWS Lambda function through Amazon CloudWatch to periodically run the code.

question_text:
A development team needs to host a website that will be accessed by other teams. The website contents consist of HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images.
Which method is the MOST cost-effective for hosting the website?
explanation_en:
The content is completely static: HTML, CSS, client JavaScript and pictures. Such a site can be hosted directly in the S3 storage barrels that enable the static website to be hosted - you only have to pay for storage and requests, there is no server, and the service itself will deal with extension issues.
Option A: Packagings on Fargate will continue to charge time for the task, even if they have no work to do.
Option C: The Web server on the EC2 instance means an ongoing hourly cost plus patches and monitoring expenses.
Option D: A load balancer with the Lambda function to provide static content means the hourly cost of the load balancer and the cost of each call, and the mere use of a S3 bucket is sufficient to meet the demand.

options.text: Containerize the website and host it in AWS Fargate.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket and host the website there.
Deploy a web server on an Amazon EC2 instance to host the website.
Configure an Application Load Balancer with an AWS Lambda target that uses the Express.js framework.

question_text:
A company runs an online marketplace web application on AWS. The application serves hundreds of thousands of users during peak hours. The company needs a scalable, near-real-time solution to share the details of millions of financial transactions with several other internal applications. Transactions also need to be processed to remove sensitive data before being stored in a document database for low-latency retrieval.
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
An extended near real-time ingestion capacity is required, along with the removal of sensitive data and their distribution to multiple internal applications. Kinesis Data Streets consumer transaction data are kept and one Lambda function removes sensitive fields and writes the results to DynamoDB for quick access. Other applications can read data independently from the same stream, and each application is read in its own location.
Option A: DynamoDB does not have data conversion rules at the time of writing, and the watch stream is not designed for ten independent historical data consumers.
Option B: Firehose has a buffer of tens of seconds for data transfer and does not allow multiple applications to read stream data from their respective locations.
Option D: Write a file volume to S3 is not close to real time, and rewriting the file will introduce the risk of data inconsistency.

options.text: Store the transactions data into Amazon DynamoDB. Set up a rule in DynamoDB to remove sensitive data from every transaction upon write. Use DynamoDB Streams to share the transactions data with other applications.

Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to store data in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Use AWS Lambda integration with Kinesis Data Firehose to remove sensitive data. Other applications can consume the data stored in Amazon S3.

Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use AWS Lambda integration to remove sensitive data from every transaction and then store the transactions data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume the transactions data off the Kinesis data stream.

Store the batched transactions data in Amazon S3 as files. Use AWS Lambda to process every file and remove sensitive data before updating the files in Amazon S3. The Lambda function then stores the data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume transaction files stored in Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company hosts its multi-tier applications on AWS. For compliance, governance, auditing, and security, the company must track configuration changes on its AWS resources and record a history of API calls made to these resources.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Two different issues require two different services. AWSConfig tracks resource allocation changes: it records the history of the state and shows you how and when it happened. AWS CloudTrail will record the API call history: who did what and where it was initiated.
Option A: Two services are swapped: CloudTrail will not record configuration history, and Config will not record API calls.
Option C: Config is the right choice, but Cloudwatch collects indicators and logs instead of the API call history record.
Option D: Both parts are wrong here.

options.text: Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and AWS Config to record API calls.
Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and AWS CloudTrail to record API calls.
Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.
Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.

question_text:
A company is preparing to launch a public-facing web application in the AWS Cloud. The architecture consists of Amazon EC2 instances within a VPC behind an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB). A third-party service is used for the DNS. The company's solutions architect must recommend a solution to detect and protect against large-scale DDoS attacks.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
AWS provides two levels of protection against large-scale DDoS attacks. Shield Standard is free for everyone and can withstand frequent cyber and transmission-level attacks. Shield Advanced is a fee-paying subscription service that provides protection against complex attacks, DDoS response team support 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, protection of the cost of amplification during an attack, and detailed attack diagnosis; resources that clearly require protection (in this case, load balancers) need to be added to the subscription. Since DNS are the responsibility of third-party providers, Route 53 is not part of the structure and it is the load balancer that needs to be protected.
Option A: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity from the log, but does not absorb or mitigate DDoS flows.
Option B: Inspector scans cases. It has nothing to do with the prevention of sexual assault.
Option C: Route 53 is not used in this scene - DNS is provided by a third-party service, and it is ERB that needs to be protected. In addition, Shield Standard has been defaulted on without any resources being allocated to it.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty on the account.
Enable Amazon Inspector on the EC2 instances.
Enable AWS Shield and assign Amazon Route 53 to it.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced and assign the ELB to it.

question_text:
A company is building an application in the AWS Cloud. The application will store data in Amazon S3 buckets in two AWS Regions. The company must use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt all data that is stored in the S3 buckets. The data in both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key. The data and the key must be stored in each of the two Regions.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
All other options are excluded: "Two S3 drums must be encrypted and decrypted using the same KMS key" and the key must physically exist in two areas. An ordinary KMS key is limited to its area and is reencrypted using a different key when the object is copied to another area. The only mechanism that can provide multiple interregional equivalent keys (the same key ID and key material) is the multi-area KMS key. Of the given options, only B used one. The ideal solution is to combine multi-area keys with SSE-KMS, but this option is not available, so we choose the option to meet the core requirements.
Option A: SSE-S3 Encryptes with S3 self-managed keys. The requirement to use the KMS key managed by the client is not met at all.
Option C: A KMS key has been created, but the drum is configured to SSE-S3 and therefore the key created has never been actually used. This option is contradictory.
Option D: SSE-KMS is correctly configured, but there are two separate keys - one in each region. In cross-regional copying, the object uses the source key to decrypt, reencrypt the key from the target area, and requires that the same key be used throughout the process.

options.text: Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.

Create a customer managed multi-Region KMS key. Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the application to use the KMS key with client-side encryption.
