question_text:
A company recently launched a variety of new workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in its AWS account. The company needs to create a strategy to access and administer the instances remotely and securely. The company needs to implement a repeatable process that works with native AWS services and follows the AWS Well- Architected Framework.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The company needs a repeatable, secure way to use original AWS service management examples. AWS Systems Manyager Session Manager is designed for this purpose: the proxy on the example is connected to the service from the outside, so there is no need to open the port, fort host or SSH key; access is granted through the IAM policy, and the entire session is recorded and can be transferred to Cloudwatch Logs or S3. The example only needs a role with AmazonSSMManaged InstanceCore -- that's what the answer means by "the proper IAM role."
Option A: The EC2 Serial Console is an emergency tool to screen for start-up issues, rather than a way to manage a cluster of examples on a daily basis.
Option C: The use of a fort host with shared SSH keys means an open port for the Internet, additional expenses for key management, and servers that require extra running. Well-Architected Framework expressly recommended abandoning this model.
Option D: A VPN connection plus a direct SSH connection for each administrator means that the infrastructure needs to be built and the key distributed, rather than managing access rights through the IAM policy.

options.text: Use the EC2 serial console to directly access the terminal interface of each instance for administration.
Attach the appropriate IAM role to each existing instance and new instance. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to establish a remote SSH session.
Create an administrative SSH key pair. Load the public key into each EC2 instance. Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet to provide a tunnel for administration of each instance.
Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. Instruct administrators to use their local on-premises machines to connect directly to the instances by using SSH keys across the VPN tunnel.

question_text:
A company is hosting a static website on Amazon S3 and is using Amazon Route 53 for DNS. The website is experiencing increased demand from around the world. The company must decrease latency for users who access the website.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The site is static and is hosted in S3 and therefore requires only the configuration of CloudFront in front of the barrel: content is cached at the edges of the world, delayed and the cost of transmitting data from CloudFront is lower than the cost of providing services directly from S3. An alias record of Route 53 points the domain to distribution configuration. This is the least expensive model for the global distribution of static content.
Option A: Reproduction of drums in each area means multiple payments for storage costs, plus ongoing synchronized costs, and geographic access is not guaranteed.
Option B: The global accelerator does not support S3 as an endpoint and is designed to accelerate TCP and UDP applications, rather than to provide static content.
Option D: The S3 Transfer Acceleration will speed up the uploading of the object to the barrel through the edge position - it does not serve the end-user website and will add additional costs.

options.text: Replicate the S3 bucket that contains the website to all AWS Regions. Add Route 53 geolocation routing entries.
Provision accelerators in AWS Global Accelerator. Associate the supplied IP addresses with the S3 bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the IP addresses of the accelerators.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the CloudFront distribution.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. Edit the Route 53 entries to point to the new endpoint.

question_text:
A company maintains a searchable repository of items on its website. The data is stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database table that contains more than 10 million rows. The database has 2 TB of General Purpose SSD storage. There are millions of updates against this data every day through the company's website.
The company has noticed that some insert operations are taking 10 seconds or longer. The company has determined that the database storage performance is the problem.
Which solution addresses this performance issue?
explanation_en:
The bottlenecks are clearly identified: there is insufficient storage at high writing loads. In this volume level, the generic SSD volume will reach its I/ O limit, while the SSD storage that keeps IOPS allows you to specify the IOPS number independently of the volume size and to provide a consistent low delay.
Option B: More memory helps to read the cache, but the bottlenecks to insert the operation are on disk rather than memory.
Option C: Burstable example groups provide worse continuity - the situation will only get worse once the sudden credit lines have run out.
Option D: Read a copy to share the reading of the query, but a problem arises with the insertion on the main example.

options.text: Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD.
Change the DB instance to a memory optimized instance class.
Change the DB instance to a burstable performance instance class.
Enable Multi-AZ RDS read replicas with MySQL native asynchronous replication.

question_text:
A company has thousands of edge devices that collectively generate 1 TB of status alerts each day. Each alert is approximately 2 KB in size. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to ingest and store the alerts for future analysis.
The company wants a highly available solution. However, the company needs to minimize costs and does not want to manage additional infrastructure. Additionally, the company wants to keep 14 days of data available for immediate analysis and archive any data older than 14 days.
What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
A small warning byte per day does not have to manage the infrastructure on its own and is extremely low-cost. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose receives data streams, automatically expands and delivers the data to S3 without running any server, while an S3 life cycle rule transfers objects to Glacier after 14 days. Data for the last two weeks can still be analysed directly in S3 instantaneously.
Option B: A set of examples to install a load balancer and run a custom script, which is the additional infrastructure explicitly excluded by the demand.
Option C: OpenSearch clusters need to be managed and paid on a continuous basis, and creating a snapshot manually every day is manual.
Option D: A SQS queue is not a reservoir for analysis, and it is neither easy nor reliable for consumers to check the age of the message and act accordingly.

options.text: Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon S3 bucket. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.

Launch Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones and place them behind an Elastic Load Balancer to ingest the alerts. Create a script on the EC2 instances that will store the alerts in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.

Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster. Set up the Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster to take manual snapshots every day and delete data from the cluster that is older than 14 days.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to ingest the alerts, and set the message retention period to 14 days. Configure consumers to poll the SQS queue, check the age of the message, and analyze the message data as needed. If the message is 14 days old, the consumer should copy the message to an Amazon S3 bucket and delete the message from the SQS queue.

question_text:
A company's application integrates with multiple software-as-a-service (SaaS) sources for data collection. The company runs Amazon EC2 instances to receive the data and to upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for analysis. The same EC2 instance that receives and uploads the data also sends a notification to the user when an upload is complete. The company has noticed slow application performance and wants to improve the performance as much as possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
These examples carry out three tasks simultaneously: extracting data from external SaaS data sources, uploading them to S3 and sending notifications. Amazon AppFlow is a hosting integration service for SaaS data sources: it pulls data and transmits them to S3 buckets without involving any single server. Complete notification of an original event from S3 sent, which was sent to the SNS theme. These examples have disappeared completely.
Option A: Automatic expansion groups can speed up processing, but examples and their maintenance remain - the operational burden is not reduced.
Option C: EventBridge usually cannot write data directly to the S3 S3 bucket as a rule target and does not process the ingestion of data from any SaaS data source.
Option D: The container is still the computing environment that you need to manage, and the Container Insights collects indicators -- it does not notify when the S3 upload is complete.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group so that EC2 instances can scale out. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.

Create an Amazon AppFlow flow to transfer data between each SaaS source and the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.

Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule for each SaaS source to send output data. Configure the S3 bucket as the rule's target. Create a second EventBridge (Cloud Watch Events) rule to send events when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as the second rule's target.

Create a Docker container to use instead of an EC2 instance. Host the containerized application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.

question_text:
A company runs a highly available image-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances in a single VPC. The EC2 instances run inside several subnets across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances do not communicate with each other. However, the EC2 instances download images from Amazon S3 and upload images to Amazon S3 through a single NAT gateway. The company is concerned about data transfer charges.
What is the MOST cost-effective way for the company to avoid Regional data transfer charges?
explanation_en:
As long as traffic flows to S3 via the NAT gateway, the company incurs two costs: the cost of each gigabyte of traffic handled by the gateway, and the cost of each hour of the gateway operation. A VPC endpoint for S3 eliminates both costs: it directly adds a path to S3 prefix in the route chart, traffic is transmitted through the AWS internal network, and no cost is incurred by the endpoint itself and through its data. Access to S3 traffic through endpoints in the same region is completely excluded as data transfer costs. The same technique is reflected in questions 91, 497, 612.
Option A: Each available area will be equipped with a NAT gateway to eliminate transmission across the available area, but the main cost factor — the hourly cost per gateway and the processing cost per gigabyte — will be retained. The greater the number of gateways, the higher the cost, not the lower.
Option B: An NAT example replaces a management gateway with a common example: you need to pay for the example and its traffic, and now you need to be responsible for its tolerance and throughput.
Option D: The dedicated host is a physical server reserved for your example - involving licensing and isolation. It has nothing to do with the cost of data transmission.

options.text: Launch the NAT gateway in each Availability Zone.
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance.
Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3.
Provision an EC2 Dedicated Host to run the EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company has an on-premises application that generates a large amount of time-sensitive data that is backed up to Amazon S3. The application has grown and there are user complaints about internet bandwidth limitations. A solutions architect needs to design a long-term solution that allows for both timely backups to Amazon S3 and with minimal impact on internet connectivity for internal users.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
Complaints about Internet bandwidth for internal users mean that backup and office traffic are competing for the same connection. The long-term solution uses a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection to transmit backup traffic: bandwidth becomes predictable, delays remain stable and Internet connections are released to other people. At the same time, the cost of transmitting outbound data has been reduced.
Option A: A VPN is still running on the same Internet connection: bandwidth does not increase, encryption increases costs. A gateway endpoint can only be accessed from within the VPC.
Option C: Daily transport of Snowball equipment does not meet the time-sensitive requirement for data to be described — delivery takes days.
Option D: There is no S3 restriction working here; bottlenecks are the company's own connection. The submission of the support forms will not change this.

options.text: Establish AWS VPN connections and proxy all traffic through a VPC gateway endpoint.
Establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection and direct backup traffic through this new connection.
Order daily AWS Snowball devices. Load the data onto the Snowball devices and return the devices to AWS each day.
Submit a support ticket through the AWS Management Console. Request the removal of S3 service limits from the account.

question_text:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains critical data. The company must protect the data from accidental deletion.
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The function in S3 to prevent accidental deletion consists of two layers. Version control (A) makes deletion reversible: it does not remove objects directly, but creates a delete mark, and the original version remains unchanged. The multiple-factor deletion (B) adds a second-heavy validation factor to the irreversible operation (i.e. permanently deletes the object version and disables the version control), making it difficult for even the owner of the drum (the root owner) to perform the operation by error and not even if the document is leaked. Version control must be enabled first: the multiple-factor authentication deletion can only be opened on the activated version-controlled drum.
Option C: The barrel policy controls which users can call which API operations. It does not prevent users with valid deletion permission from deleting objects by error, nor can it restore objects that have been deleted.
Option D: Default encryption protects content from unauthorized users. It has nothing to do with the possibility of the object being deleted.
Option E: The life cycle rule automatically deletes objects according to the plan - which is completely contrary to the functions required for this scenario.

options.text: Enable versioning on the S3 bucket.
Enable MFA Delete on the S3 bucket.
Create a bucket policy on the S3 bucket.
Enable default encryption on the S3 bucket.
Create a lifecycle policy for the objects in the S3 bucket.

question_text:
A company has a data ingestion workflow that consists of the following:
• An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications about new data deliveries
• An AWS Lambda function to process the data and record metadata The company observes that the ingestion workflow fails occasionally because of network connectivity issues.
When such a failure occurs, the Lambda function does not ingest the corresponding data unless the company manually reruns the job.
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to ensure that the Lambda function ingests all data in the future? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
A SNS theme immediately sends the message and discards it after several failures. To ensure that no message is lost, a SQS queue is placed between the SNS and the function: the queue subscribes to the theme (B), while the function reads the message (E) from the queue. Messages will remain in line until they are successfully processed, and if repeated attempts fail, they will be routed to the Death Line.
Option A: The Lambda function is by default running between more than one available area - no configuration required, not related to the loss of the message.
Option C: More CPUs and memory will speed up implementation, but information will still be lost when network failure occurs.
Option D: Preset and co-opt will pre-prepared the implementation environment, but will not enhance the reliability of the message.

options.text: Deploy the Lambda function in multiple Availability Zones.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue, and subscribe it to the SNS topic.
Increase the CPU and memory that are allocated to the Lambda function.
Increase provisioned throughput for the Lambda function.
Modify the Lambda function to read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.

question_text:
A company has an application that provides marketing services to stores. The services are based on previous purchases by store customers. The stores upload transaction data to the company through SFTP, and the data is processed and analyzed to generate new marketing offers. Some of the files can exceed 200 GB in size.
Recently, the company discovered that some of the stores have uploaded files that contain personally identifiable information (PII) that should not have been included. The company wants administrators to be alerted if PII is shared again. The company also wants to automate remediation.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
explanation_en:
The requirement is that personal identity information can be found in uploaded documents without the need for a customized detection code. Amazon Macie is designed to find PII in an object of S3: it categorizes data, reports the type and location of PII and posts it to EventBridge, so that it can easily trigger SNS notifications or automating repairs. There is no need to construct a self-defined search logic - hence minimal development workload.
Option A: Inspector will check the gaps in the task load, but will not analyse the object content. The life-cycle rules also do not remove objects based on scanning results.
Option C: Develop a custom algorithm to test PII in a function as the most time-consuming part of this task -- and this is what Macie has already handled as a hosting service.
Option D: The same self-defined test algorithm, combined with an attempt to remove objects using life-cycle rules, which operate only on the basis of age and prefixes, not content.

options.text: Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Inspector to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the objects that contain PII.

Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Macie to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.

Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.

Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to trigger a notification to the administrators and trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the meats that contain PII.

question_text:
A company needs guaranteed Amazon EC2 capacity in three specific Availability Zones in a specific AWS Region for an upcoming event that will last 1 week.
What should the company do to guarantee the EC2 capacity?
explanation_en:
The Guaranteed EC2 capacity is provided at the required capacity and is always reserved for a specific available area. Therefore, the company created a reservation in each of the three available areas required: the capacity would be retained throughout the event, regardless of the overall needs of the region.
Option A: Leave an example of a financial commitment in exchange for a discount; they will not guarantee capacity unless linked to a specific area of availability.
Option B: Cannot reserve capacity for a region - it always applies to a specific available area.
Option C: Even examples of district-level reservation are for long-term commitment (one or three years), which is inappropriate compared to a week-long activity.

options.text: Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region needed.
Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation that specifies the Region needed.
Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region and three Availability Zones needed.
Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation that specifies the Region and three Availability Zones needed.

question_text:
A company's website uses an Amazon EC2 instance store for its catalog of items. The company wants to make sure that the catalog is highly available and that the catalog is stored in a durable location.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
One example of storage is that of loss and loss: when the case stops, the data will disappear and therefore will not be sustainable at all. The directory needs to be migrated to a storage that is viable in case of case failure and can be accessed by multiple machines at the same time — that is, Amazon EFS: the file system is duplicated between available areas and can be mounted by all Web servers.
Option A: ElastiCache is a memory cache. It is not a persistent storage: re-starting clusters without the use of durability loses data.
Option B: The larger example simply means more space for loss of access - the problem is not in terms of capacity, but in terms of data disappearing as the example disappears.
Option C: Glacier Deep Archive is an archive, which is retrieved in hours. A site directory that was read at the time of each request could not be stored there.

options.text: Move the catalog to Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
Deploy a larger EC2 instance with a larger instance store.
Move the catalog from the instance store to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Move the catalog to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system.

question_text:
A company stores call transcript files on a monthly basis. Users access the files randomly within 1 year of the call, but users access the files infrequently after 1 year. The company wants to optimize its solution by giving users the ability to query and retrieve files that are less than 1-year-old as quickly as possible. A delay in retrieving older files is acceptable.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Document access was irregular in the previous year and has since been virtually non-accessible, making storage costs and quick access to recent documents important. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between different storage levels according to the actual access mode, without the cost of searching, and after a year, moving them to S3 Glacier Flexiblé Retrieval via the life cycle rule, the delay in searching is acceptable. Query for recent data via Athena and for archived data via S3 Glacier Select.
Option A: Glacier Instant Retrieval has a higher storage cost than the archive level, and searching through labels is not a mechanism for searching for content.
Option C: S3 Standard has been stored in the previous year at a higher cost than Inteligent-Tiering due to irregular access, and metadata stored in the same S3 storage can not provide easy search.
Option D: Deep Archive recovery objects take hours and separate RDS databases for metadata add unnecessary costs and operating costs.

options.text: Store individual files with tags in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Query the tags to retrieve the files from S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

Store individual files in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year. Query and retrieve the files that are in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena. Query and retrieve the files that are in S3 Glacier by using S3 Glacier Select.

Store individual files with tags in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Store search metadata for each archive in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 year. Query and retrieve the files by searching for metadata from Amazon S3.

Store individual files in Amazon S3 Standard storage. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year. Store search metadata in Amazon RDS. Query the files from Amazon RDS. Retrieve the files from S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

question_text:
A company has a production workload that runs on 1,000 Amazon EC2 Linux instances. The workload is powered by third-party software. The company needs to patch the third-party software on all EC2 instances as quickly as possible to remediate a critical security vulnerability.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The software is a third-party software, so the standard base patch set cannot cover it — a custom command needs to be run. AWS Systems Manager Run Comand can immediately execute the order in all selected examples without SSH connections or third-party agents, which is the function required to quickly repair the loophole.
Option A: The Lambda function does not by itself perform any operation on the example - it still needs a mechanism like Run Comand.
Option B: The patch manager works only with the operating system updated and supported software package and cannot process any third-party software.
Option C: The maintenance window will delay implementation until the scheduled time, but the loophole needs to be closed as soon as possible.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.
Configure AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.
Schedule an AWS Systems Manager maintenance window to apply the patch to all EC2 instances.
Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to run a custom command that applies the patch to all EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company is developing an application that provides order shipping statistics for retrieval by a REST API. The company wants to extract the shipping statistics, organize the data into an easy-to-read HTML format, and send the report to several email addresses at the same time every morning.
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The task is divided into two steps. A timed EventBridge rule triggers the Lambda function once a day, which calls the API of the application to get data (D). The function then formats the data into an HTML report and sends them to multiple recipients (B) through Amazon SES.
Option A: Firehose delivers current data to storage destinations, unrelated to the generation of daily reports.
Option C: AWS Glue is an ETL service used to process data sets instead of a tool to call the application RET API.
Option E: SNS sends a notification in plain text, not an email in HTML format, and the S3 event is not associated with the daily schedule.

options.text: Configure the application to send the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose.
Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to format the data and to send the report by email.
Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Glue job to query the application's API for the data.
Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Lambda function to query the application's API for the data.
Store the application data in Amazon S3. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as an S3 event destination to send the report by email.

question_text:
A company wants to migrate its on-premises application to AWS. The application produces output files that vary in size from tens of gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes. The application data must be stored in a standard file system structure. The company wants a solution that scales automatically. is highly available, and requires minimum operational overhead.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The definitional requirement is the "standard file system structure", coupled with automatic expansion and high availability, with minimal operation. Amazon EFS can automatically grow and shrink, data are stored across multiple available areas and mounted through NFS to each example in the automatic extension group. It's not a problem for it to have a volume capacity ranging from dozens of gypsies to hundreds of bits.
Option A: S3 is the object storage: it lacks a familiar directory hierarchy and file operation, so the application must be rewrited.
Option B: An EBS volume is connected to a single available area, usually to a single instance: there is no shared access and there is no automatic ability to extend to hundreds of bits.
Option D: The same problem as the previous option: EBS will not be shared among the examples in the group, nor will it be automatically extended.

options.text: Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon S3 for storage.
Migrate the application to run as containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.
Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) for storage.
Migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) for storage.

question_text:
A company needs to store its accounting records in Amazon S3. The records must be immediately accessible for 1 year and then must be archived for an additional 9 years. No one at the company, including administrative users and root users, can be able to delete the records during the entire 10-year period. The records must be stored with maximum resiliency.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Distinction by three requirements. First, there was immediate access in the previous year, followed by archiving for nine years: this required a life-cycle rule that moved objects from the standard storage category to the archive storage category of Glacier Deep Archive in the first year. Second, no one can delete these records, including administrators and root users: this can only be ensured if the S3 object locks are in compliance mode, as the governance model can normally be bypassed by anyone holding the S3: BypassGovernanceRetenance permission. Third, maximum tolerance error: this means that the storage class will retain a copy between the three available areas, which excludes the archive storage of the single available area (One Zone-IA). The fulfilment of these three conditions points to option C.
Option A: The entire cycle of storing all content in Glacier is contrary to the requirement of immediate access in the previous year, and the visit strategy is not really protected: any person who prepares the strategy can modify it at any time.
Option B: Administrator or root user can change IAM policy at any time, so "no one can delete" cannot actually be guaranteed. The mere use of an intelligent stratification cannot in itself prohibit deletion.
Option D: The governance model can be bypassed by users holding bypass privileges, and One Zone-IA is stored in a single area for archiving only one copy - both requirements are violated.

options.text: Store the records in S3 Glacier for the entire 10-year period. Use an access control policy to deny deletion of the records for a period of 10 years.
Store the records by using S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Use an IAM policy to deny deletion of the records. After 10 years, change the IAM policy to allow deletion.
Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the records from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for a period of 10 years.
Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition the records from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 1 year. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode for a period of 10 years.

question_text:
A company runs multiple Windows workloads on AWS. The company's employees use Windows file shares that are hosted on two Amazon EC2 instances. The file shares synchronize data between themselves and maintain duplicate copies. The company wants a highly available and durable storage solution that preserves how users currently access the files.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The key phrase is "Maintenance of current user access to files": User access to Windows file sharing through SMB protocols, using NTFS privileges, usually in conjunction with Active Directory. Only Amazon FSx for Windows File Server retains this access, while Multi-AZ configurations create a synchronized copy in the second available area and effect automatic downtime transfer. When the two examples are decommissioned, the customized synchronization mechanism between them disappears.
Option A:S3 is the object stored via API: the user must change the way the file is handled and the familiar file sharing will disappear.
Option B: S3 File Gateway provides SMB interfaces, but behind them are objects rather than Windows file systems: lock semantics and NTFS privileges will be lost. Examples and their maintenance still exist.
Option D: EFS is a file system using NFS protocols that the Windows client cannot use.

options.text: Migrate all the data to Amazon S3. Set up IAM authentication for users to access files.
Set up an Amazon S3 File Gateway. Mount the S3 File Gateway on the existing EC2 instances.
Extend the file share environment to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ configuration. Migrate all the data to FSx for Windows File Server.
Extend the file share environment to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a Multi-AZ configuration. Migrate all the data to Amazon EFS.

question_text:
A solutions architect is developing a VPC architecture that includes multiple subnets. The architecture will host applications that use Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon RDS DB instances. The architecture consists of six subnets in two Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone includes a public subnet, a private subnet, and a dedicated subnet for databases. Only EC2 instances that run in the private subnets can have access to the RDS databases.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The principle of minimum authority is realized here through the security group: the entry rules for databases allow access only to the security group assigned to the example of a private subnet. The rule refers to a security unit rather than an IP address, and therefore remains valid regardless of how the convoy members change, and only these examples can be connected to the database.
Option A: Removes the route to the public subnet CIDR block without any effect: the path between the VPC internal subnet is always achieved by local route and cannot be deleted.
Option B: The security team does not support the rule of denial - they only allow traffic. Such a rule cannot be created.
Option D: Reciprocal connections are created between VPCs, not between subnets within the same VPCs: connectivity within VPCs already exists.

options.text: Create a new route table that excludes the route to the public subnets' CIDR blocks. Associate the route table with the database subnets.
Create a security group that denies inbound traffic from the security group that is assigned to instances in the public subnets. Attach the security group to the DB instances.
Create a security group that allows inbound traffic from the security group that is assigned to instances in the private subnets. Attach the security group to the DB instances.
Create a new peering connection between the public subnets and the private subnets. Create a different peering connection between the private subnets and the database subnets.

question_text:
A company has registered its domain name with Amazon Route 53. The company uses Amazon API Gateway in the ca-central-1 Region as a public interface for its backend microservice APIs. Third-party services consume the APIs securely. The company wants to design its API Gateway URL with the company's domain name and corresponding certificate so that the third-party services can use HTTPS.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
For API to respond to a company's own domain name via HTTPS, three conditions are required: the custom domain name in API Gateway, the certificate to configure it, and a DNS record. The key detail is the area of the certificate: for the regional endpoint, the ACM certificate must be issued in the same area as the API (in this case, ca-central-1) - only at the edge optimisation end point will it be required in us-east-1. Once the certificate is attached, the aliases of Route 53 point the domain at the API Gateway endpoint.
Option A: Phase variables pass values to integration and do not change the URL that API can access. Custom domain name is configured as your own custom domain name resource.
Option B: For area endpoints, the certificate must be issued in the same area, not in us-east-1, and if the custom domain name is not configured, there is no pointer to the alias record.
Option D: The same error as the certificate area, plus A records should point to the API Gateway endpoint, not to the `domain name of the company'.

options.text: Create stage variables in API Gateway with Name="Endpoint-URL" and Value="Company Domain Name" to overwrite the default URL. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).

Create Route 53 DNS records with the company's domain name. Point the alias record to the Regional API Gateway stage endpoint. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region.

Create a Regional API Gateway endpoint. Associate the API Gateway endpoint with the company's domain name. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the same Region. Attach the certificate to the API Gateway endpoint. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the API Gateway endpoint.

Create a Regional API Gateway endpoint. Associate the API Gateway endpoint with the company's domain name. Import the public certificate associated with the company's domain name into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-1 Region. Attach the certificate to the API Gateway APIs. Create Route 53 DNS records with the company's domain name. Point an A record to the company's domain name.

question_text:
A company is running a popular social media website. The website gives users the ability to upload images to share with other users. The company wants to make sure that the images do not contain inappropriate content. The company needs a solution that minimizes development effort.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The task is to identify the inappropriate content of the images and to develop the smallest amount of work. Amazon Rekognation has built-in content clearance functions and therefore does not require training, while Amazon Augmented AI provides manual clearance for low confidence predictions.
Option A: Comprehend analyzes text, not images.
Option C: SageMaker means developing and training a self-defined model - which is completely contrary to the minimum development workload required.
Option D: Self-defined models deployed on Fargate mean more development work, plus the need to manage the base infrastructure.

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.
Use Amazon Rekognition to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.
Use Amazon SageMaker to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.
Use AWS Fargate to deploy a custom machine learning model to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.

question_text:
A company wants to run its critical applications in containers to meet requirements for scalability and availability.
The company prefers to focus on maintenance of the critical applications. The company does not want to be responsible for provisioning and managing the underlying infrastructure that runs the containerized workload.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The company wishes to focus on its applications rather than on infrastructure under containers. The Fargate start-up type using ECS removes the node completely: AWS will be responsible for computing, patching and extending.
Option A: An example of manually installing Docker - the largest amount of maintenance.
Option B: EC2 work nodes in the ECS cluster still need to be updated, expanded and monitored for health status.
Option D: Optimized AMI using ECS can simplify settings, but the example itself needs to be maintained by the company.

options.text: Use Amazon EC2 instances, and install Docker on the instances.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 worker nodes.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.
Use Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)-optimized Amazon Machine Image (AMI).

question_text:
A company hosts more than 300 global websites and applications. The company requires a platform to analyze more than 30 TB of clickstream data each day.
What should a solutions architect do to transmit and process the clickstream data?
explanation_en:
The 30-byte click stream data per day requires current ingestion and analysis. Kinesis Data Streets consumes the data stream, and Kinesis Data Firehose transmits it to the data lake on S3 without any management action, and Redshift loads the data for analytical query. This is a standard model that can be expanded as the volume of data increases.
Option A: AWS Data Pipeline is an outdated batch scheduler that must create and pay for EMR clusters - both more complex and more expensive.
Option B: A custom cluster of examples is required to ingestion data streams, which requires manual extension, monitoring and trouble management.
Option C: ClaudFront distributes content to users, it is not a mechanism for ingestion of click stream data, and the use of the Lambda function to process each object cannot replace the current conduit.

options.text: Design an AWS Data Pipeline to archive the data to an Amazon S3 bucket and run an Amazon EMR cluster with the data to generate analytics.
Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the data and send it to an Amazon S3 data lake for Amazon Redshift to use for analysis.
Cache the data to Amazon CloudFront. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. When an object is added to the S3 bucket. run an AWS Lambda function to process the data for analysis.
Collect the data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit the data to an Amazon S3 data lake. Load the data in Amazon Redshift for analysis.

question_text:
A company has a website hosted on AWS. The website is behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is configured to handle HTTP and HTTPS separately. The company wants to forward all requests to the website so that the requests will use HTTPS.
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
Apply the load balancer to execute re-direction on your own: create a rule on a listening device at port 80, which contains a re-directional action to HTTPS, usually using 301 status code. No layer changes are required, and all traffic eventually arrives through a security agreement.
Option A: A network ACL will only discard HTTP traffic: the user will receive an error instead of reorienting.
Option B: A rule "Replace HTTP with HTTPS in URL" describes the same reorientation, but does not specify the location of the configuration of the rule; the standard mechanism for achieving this function is called the listening rules.
Option D: The Network Load Balancer is running on the 4th floor and will not execute the HTTP redirection.

options.text: Update the ALB's network ACL to accept only HTTPS traffic.
Create a rule that replaces the HTTP in the URL with HTTPS.
Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer configured to use Server Name Indication (SNI).

question_text:
A company is developing a two-tier web application on AWS. The company's developers have deployed the application on an Amazon EC2 instance that connects directly to a backend Amazon RDS database. The company must not hardcode database credentials in the application. The company must also implement a solution to automatically rotate the database credentials on a regular basis.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Requirements are almost literally a description of Secrets Manager: do not encode the password in the code and rotate automatically as planned. Keys are stored in encrypted form, and examples are obtained through their roles (with no embedded key in the application), while RDS rotations are processed by the built-in AWS function, which updates the passwords in the database and key at the same time. Please note the details of the structure: Access rights are granted to the EC2 role rather than to the user, and therefore the evidence obtained is provisional.
Option A: Empirical metadata are accessible to any process on the machine and are not suitable for storage of key, and you have to prepare the RDS sync password update logic and updates in metadata.
Option B: A configuration file stored in a barrel with a custom rotor function means that codes, plans and error processing are required, rather than just one setting. Version control allows only the value before rolling - it does not eliminate the development work.
Option D: Parameter Store store encryption parameters, but it does not have an "Auto Wheel" switch: rotation has to be written by yourself.

options.text: Store the database credentials in the instance metadata. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rules to run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that updates the RDS credentials and instance metadata at the same time.

Store the database credentials in a configuration file in an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rules to run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that updates the RDS credentials and the credentials in the configuration file at the same time. Use S3 Versioning to ensure the ability to fall back to previous values.
Store the database credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Turn on automatic rotation for the secret. Attach the required permission to the EC2 role to grant access to the secret.

Store the database credentials as encrypted parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Turn on automatic rotation for the encrypted parameters. Attach the required permission to the EC2 role to grant access to the encrypted parameters.

question_text:
A company is deploying a new public web application to AWS. The application will run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application needs to be encrypted at the edge with an SSL/TLS certificate that is issued by an external certificate authority (CA). The certificate must be rotated each year before the certificate expires.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The certificate is issued by an external certificate issuing authority, so ACM can only import the certificate. ACM does not automatically renew imported certificates - this is the responsibility of the certificate owner. Therefore, the certificate is imported and attached to the load balancer, and the EventBridge rules trigger a notification when the certificate is about to expire, so that the certificate can be replaced manually.
Option A: Only ACM's own certificates are supported for automatic renewal, while the demand is for certificates from external CAs.
Option B: Cannot import "key materials" into ACM-issued certificates: certificates are issued by ACM or imported in full.
Option C: Certificate browsers issued by a private certificate issuer do not trust: Web applications for the public will not work properly.

options.text: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALUse the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.

question_text:
A company runs its infrastructure on AWS and has a registered base of 700,000 users for its document management application. The company intends to create a product that converts large .pdf files to .jpg image files.
The .pdf files average 5 MB in size. The company needs to store the original files and the converted files. A solutions architect must design a scalable solution to accommodate demand that will grow rapidly over time.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The load is event-driven and uneven: a file is uploaded and converted. The most economical option is to store both the original file and the conversion results in S3 and trigger a Lambda function to perform the conversion operation when an S3 PUT event occurs. You only pay for the actual milliseconds of time and storage costs, and there are no free cases, and the automatic extension is realized as the user base increases.
Option B: DynamoDB is not suitable for storing files: the project size is limited to 400 KB and the average PDF file size is 5 MB. This design cannot be achieved.
Option C: Examples of cases stored with EBS will be billed on a continuous basis, regardless of load, and the cost of EBS will be much higher than S3 as the number of files increases.
Option D: Same problem: The example of ongoing operations plus a combination of documents storage costs higher than S3 and Lambda, and the presentation itself is contradictory - it suggests that the files be stored in both EFS and EBS.

options.text: Save the .pdf files to Amazon S3. Configure an S3 PUT event to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in Amazon S3.
Save the .pdf files to Amazon DynamoDUse the DynamoDB Streams feature to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in DynamoDB.

Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the files to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.

Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the file to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.

question_text:
A company has more than 5 TB of file data on Windows file servers that run on premises. Users and applications interact with the data each day.
The company is moving its Windows workloads to AWS. As the company continues this process, the company requires access to AWS and on-premises file storage with minimum latency. The company needs a solution that minimizes operational overhead and requires no significant changes to the existing file access patterns. The company uses an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for connectivity to AWS.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Three constraints were established simultaneously: access from cloud and local environments, with minimal delays and minimal management costs, and "no significant change in the pattern of access to existing documents". The last condition is decisive: the Windows load uses SMB and NTFS privileges and Active Directory, so the target storage must be FSx for Windows File Server, not object storage like S3. FSx File Gateway eliminates local environmental delays caused by VPN: it is deployed locally, caches hotspot files and provides services via SMB, while complete copies of documents are kept in the cloud FSx. This creates twinning schemes: FSx for Windows File Server in the cloud environment for cloud loads, and FSx File Gateway in the local environment for local loads.
Option A: Use FSx only instead of the gateway, which means that local users access files via Site-to-Site VPN. This does not meet local environmental requirements for the minimization of delays.
Option B: S3 File Gateway provides the SMB interface, but behind it is the object storage, not the Windows filesystem: NTFS ACL, Active Directory integration and lock semantics are lost. This will require significant re-engineering for Windows work loads that need to be relocated without change.
Option C: Part of the load is migrated to a direct access S3, which means that it needs to be rewritten as an object API. Significant changes in the way documents are accessed are explicitly prohibited in the title.

options.text: Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Move the on-premises file data to FSx for Windows File Server. Reconfigure the workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS.

Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the S3 File Gateway. Reconfigure the on-premises workloads and the cloud workloads to use the S3 File Gateway.

Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to Amazon S3. Reconfigure the workloads to use either Amazon S3 directly or the S3 File Gateway. depending on each workload's location.

Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Deploy and configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the FSx File Gateway. Configure the cloud workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Configure the on-premises workloads to use the FSx File Gateway.

question_text:
A hospital recently deployed a RESTful API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The hospital uses API Gateway and Lambda to upload reports that are in PDF format and JPEG format. The hospital needs to modify the Lambda code to identify protected health information (PHI) in the reports.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The report arrives in PDF and JPEG files, so the text must first be extracted and then scanned to find protected health information. Amazon Text identifies text in documents and images, while Amazon Comprehend Medical has PHI detection functionality. No training is required - just two calls in the same function.
Option A: The custom library means that you need to develop and maintain the logic of text extraction and detection — best efforts.
Option B: SageMaker needs to train a custom model, and the hosting service already knows how to find PHI.
Option D: Rekognition can recognize the text in the image, but cannot parse multipage PDF documents: these require Text.

options.text: Use existing Python libraries to extract the text from the reports and to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon SageMaker to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Rekognition to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.

question_text:
A company has an application that generates a large number of files, each approximately 5 MB in size. The files are stored in Amazon S3. Company policy requires the files to be stored for 4 years before they can be deleted.
Immediate accessibility is always required as the files contain critical business data that is not easy to reproduce.
The files are frequently accessed in the first 30 days of the object creation but are rarely accessed after the first 30 days.
Which storage solution is MOST cost-effective?
explanation_en:
Dismantling on demand. The rule of 'immediate access is always necessary' excludes Glacier Flexible Retrieval, as its retrieval takes minutes to hours. " Hard to repeat" means that the data cannot be lost, which requires a type of storage in which copies are kept between the three available areas - excluding One Zone-IA. `Assisted within the first 30 days, very few thereafter' is the model designed by the life cycle rules: using Standard the first 30 days, then converting to Standard-IA. Corporate policy requires the document to be deleted after four years, so the rules also need to include obsolete operations. Always compare to question 890: This is the same scenario, but the option contains Glacier Instant Retrieval - the correct answer becomes this option at this time.
Option A: S3 Glacier (Flexible Retrieval) takes minutes and hours for standard searches when the rush search is enabled. The need for continuous and immediate access constitutes a violation.
Option B: One Zone-IA keeps a copy of the single available area. This risk is unacceptable in the case of key data and difficult to repeat, and its savings relative to Standard-IA are only about 20 per cent.
Option D: This rule moves the file to Glacier in the fourth year instead of deleting it. The company policy allows for deletion after four years, but in this programme storage costs will be paid indefinitely.

options.text: Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.
Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Delete the files 4 years after object creation.

Create an S3 bucket lifecycle policy to move files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 30 days from object creation. Move the files to S3 Glacier 4 years after object creation.

question_text:
A company hosts an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue, writes to an Amazon RDS table, and deletes the message from the queue. Occasional duplicate records are found in the RDS table. The SQS queue does not contain any duplicate messages.
What should a solutions architect do to ensure messages are being processed once only?
explanation_en:
The existence of duplicate entries in the database and the absence of duplicate items in the queue means that the message is processed longer than visible time: the message becomes visible again and is captured by another working node, while the first node is still processing the message. The solution is to increase the visible time out of time by calling ChangeMessageVisibility and setting its value to a value greater than the processing time.
Option A: The new queue will not change the root cause: the visible timeout will remain unchanged.
Option B: Permissions have nothing to do with duplicate processing.
Option C: Long-duration queries reduce the number of empty responses and the cost of requests, but do not prevent information from being re-delivered.

options.text: Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.
Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.
Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.
Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API call to increase the visibility timeout.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a new hybrid architecture to extend a company's on-premises infrastructure to AWS. The company requires a highly available connection with consistent low latency to an AWS Region. The company needs to minimize costs and is willing to accept slower traffic if the primary connection fails.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Demand always requires low delay, high availability and minimal cost, and slow flow is acceptable if the main connection fails. This suggests that direct connection is the main link because of its predictable delays, while the VPN on the Internet is backed up: it is activated quickly, at minimal cost and only in case of failure.
Option B: VPN operates via the public Internet, where delays are unpredictable and demand requires continued low delays.
Option C: The second DirectConnect connection is more reliable, but it doubles the cost of the port, and the need explicitly allows for a slower backup.
Option D: DirectConnect does not have any such failure switch properties that automatically create a backup connection.

options.text: Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a VPN connection as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.
Provision a VPN tunnel connection to a Region for private connectivity. Provision a second VPN tunnel for private connectivity and as a backup if the primary VPN connection fails.
Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a second Direct Connect connection to the same Region as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.

Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Use the Direct Connect failover attribute from the AWS CLI to automatically create a backup connection if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.

question_text:
A company is running a business-critical web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database that is deployed in a single Availability Zone. The company wants the application to be highly available with minimum downtime and minimum loss of data.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
explanation_en:
High availability requires minimum downtime and minimum data to be lost, with the least operational complexity. For applications, this means that automatic extension teams will be deployed across multiple available areas; for databases, the deployment of Aurora (multi-usable area model), with a backup copy, the failure switch will be done automatically in a few seconds and the data will not be lost. The design was further refined by RDS Proxy: it maintains the connect pool and accelerates the recovery of the application following a failure switch. All of this is at the configuration level rather than a top-up structure.
Option A: A multi-area setting with Route 53 health checkup operations are clearly more complex and more costly, DNS-based failure switching speeds are slower and rely on the solver cache. For `minimum operational complexity' requirements, this is over-designed.
Option C: A single available area with an hourly snapshot means that there is a stoppage time during the recovery period and that data will be lost for up to one hour.
Option D: Write the data to S3, and then load it in the database by a function, which means that the application needs to be rewritten, leading to a significant change in consistency.

options.text: Place the EC2 instances in different AWS Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks to redirect traffic. Use Aurora PostgreSQL Cross-Region Replication.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple Availability Zones. Configure the database as Multi-AZ. Configure an Amazon RDS Proxy instance for the database.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use one Availability Zone. Generate hourly snapshots of the database. Recover the database from the snapshots in the event of a failure.

Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple AWS Regions. Write the data from the application to Amazon S3. Use S3 Event Notifications to launch an AWS Lambda function to write the data to the database.

question_text:
A company's HTTP application is behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The NLB's target group is configured to use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with multiple EC2 instances that run the web service.
The company notices that the NLB is not detecting HTTP errors for the application. These errors require a manual restart of the EC2 instances that run the web service. The company needs to improve the application's availability without writing custom scripts or code.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
A network load equalizer works on the fourth floor and knows nothing about the HTTP response code: as long as the TCP connection is established successfully, its health check will pass. The application of the load balancer allows for the checking of a specific URL and the expected response code, and the automatic extension group using the load balancer's health check automatically replaces an unhealthy example - no custom code is required.
Option A: NLB supports HTTP health check-ups, but the demand also requires automatic case substitution, which NLB does not itself trigger; furthermore, application layers are more naturally deployed behind ALB.
Option B: A timed task script for restarting applications is the type of custom script that is explicitly excluded from the demand.
Option D: The unhealthy number of hosts is only triggered once when the 4th floor health examination determines the death - it will never see HTTP errors.

options.text: Enable HTTP health checks on the NLB, supplying the URL of the company's application.
Add a cron job to the EC2 instances to check the local application's logs once each minute. If HTTP errors are detected. the application will restart.
Replace the NLB with an Application Load Balancer. Enable HTTP health checks by supplying the URL of the company's application. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances.
Create an Amazon Cloud Watch alarm that monitors the UnhealthyHostCount metric for the NLB. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances when the alarm is in the ALARM state.

question_text:
A company runs a shopping application that uses Amazon DynamoDB to store customer information. In case of data corruption, a solutions architect needs to design a solution that meets a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour.
What should the solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
This relates to data damage rather than regional failure, and the loss of data for up to 15 minutes is acceptable. The DynamoDB time point restoration will keep the last 35 days of backup and allow you to restore the table to any second, accurate to the minute - sufficient to meet the recovery point and recovery time requirements.
Option A: The global table will copy the data, including the damaged data: Switching to another area will only return the same damaged records.
Option C: A daily export recovery point is one day, far less than the 15 minutes required, and it takes hours to import from the archive.
Option D: DynamoDB is a hosting service with no EBS volume: there is no form requiring snapshots.

options.text: Configure DynamoDB global tables. For RPO recovery, point the application to a different AWS Region.
Configure DynamoDB point-in-time recovery. For RPO recovery, restore to the desired point in time.
Export the DynamoDB data to Amazon S3 Glacier on a daily basis. For RPO recovery, import the data from S3 Glacier to DynamoDB.
Schedule Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots for the DynamoDB table every 15 minutes. For RPO recovery, restore the DynamoDB table by using the EBS snapshot.

question_text:
A company runs a photo processing application that needs to frequently upload and download pictures from Amazon S3 buckets that are located in the same AWS Region. A solutions architect has noticed an increased cost in data transfer fees and needs to implement a solution to reduce these costs.
How can the solutions architect meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
Data transfer costs arise because traffic access to S3 passes through the Internet gateway or the NAT gateway. The end point of the S3 gateway will add a route to the prefix of the service, so the flow will be kept within the AWS network at no cost, and the end-point strategy will limit access to the required S3 buckets. As the drums are located in the same area, there are no cross-regional costs.
Option A: API Gateway is not a network device that can pass the requested route to access S3: there is no route entry that can point to it.
Option B: NAT gateway charges each byte processed - this increases costs rather than lowers them, and it has no end-point strategy.
Option C: Public subnets and Internet gateways maintain the same Internet access and reduce safety.

options.text: Deploy Amazon API Gateway into a public subnet and adjust the route table to route S3 calls through it.
Deploy a NAT gateway into a public subnet and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.
Deploy the application into a public subnet and allow it to route through an internet gateway to access the S3 buckets.
Deploy an S3 VPC gateway endpoint into the VPC and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.

question_text:
A company recently launched Linux-based application instances on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet and launched a Linux-based bastion host on an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet of a VPC. A solutions architect needs to connect from the on-premises network, through the company's internet connection, to the bastion host, and to the application servers. The solutions architect must make sure that the security groups of all the EC2 instances will allow that access.
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Access to the Internet comes from an enterprise network, so that the fort host must accept a connection from the company's external IP scope — as specified in the entry rules (C). Examples of applications in private subnets should only be accepted from the fort host, which accesses them through its private address, so the rules refer to the private address of the fort host (D).
Option A: Allowing the fort host to accept an entry connection from the application example is meaningless: the connection is in the opposite direction.
Option B: The internal IP scope of the company will be translated on the path to the Internet: the host of the fort is an external address and the rule will never match.
Option E: Fortress hosts access private examples of VPC through their private addresses; their public network addresses do not play any role in this flow.

options.text: Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the application instances.
Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the internal IP range for the company.
