A solutions architect must design a system to process these messages from the sensors. The solution must be highly available, and the results must be made available for the company’s security team to analyze.
Which system architecture should the solutions architect recommend?
explanation_en:
Readers send messages via HTTPS, which requires a managed HTTPS terminal and a serverless processor. API Gateway receives requests and calls the Lambda function, which parses messages and writes the results to DynamoDB - the three components are by default highly usable, are self-extensible and do not require any management. The data in DynamoDB can be exported to S3 and made available to the security team for analysis if needed.
Option A: A single EC2 instance is a single point failure that requires patching, extension and monitoring. The high availability requirement cannot be met.
Option C: Route 53 cannot call the Lambda function: it is a DNS service. A HTTP terminal is required between the client and the function, e. g. API Gateway.
Option D: Readers send HTTPS requests, not files written to the S3 buckets, and VPNs built to build buildings for this purpose are over-designed.

options.text: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to serve as the HTTPS endpoint and to process the messages. Configure the EC2 instance to save the results to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an HTTPS endpoint in Amazon API Gateway. Configure the API Gateway endpoint to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Use Amazon Route 53 to direct incoming sensor messages to an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.

Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Configure a Site-to-Site VPN connection from the facility network to the VPC so that sensor data can be written directly to an S3 bucket by way of the VPC endpoint.

question_text:
A company wants to implement a disaster recovery plan for its primary on-premises file storage volume. The file storage volume is mounted from an Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) device on a local storage server. The file storage volume holds hundreds of terabytes (TB) of data.
The company wants to ensure that end users retain immediate access to all file types from the on-premises systems without experiencing latency.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the company's existing infrastructure?
explanation_en:
End-users must maintain instant access to all document types without delay and changes to existing infrastructure must be minimized. The storage roll gateway is connected to the existing file server in the same iSCSI protocol in the memory volume mode, and the entire data set is kept on a local disk and sent to AWS with a periodic snapshot. In the event of a disaster, the note returns to EBS and is attached to the example.
Option A: This involves switching the protocol to NFS and modifying the application - a direct violation of the minimum change requirement.
Option B: Tape gateways are designed for backup to virtual tape libraries and do not provide instant local access to documents.
Option C: Cache roll mode only keeps 10 TB caches in hundreds of bits: access to the remaining data will be done through the cloud, with significant delays.

options.text: Provision an Amazon S3 File Gateway as a virtual machine (VM) that is hosted on premises. Set the local cache to 10 TB. Modify existing applications to access the files through the NFS protocol. To recover from a disaster, provision an Amazon EC2 instance and mount the S3 bucket that contains the files.

Provision an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway. Use a data backup solution to back up all existing data to a virtual tape library. Configure the data backup solution to run nightly after the initial backup is complete. To recover from a disaster, provision an Amazon EC2 instance and restore the data to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume from the volumes in the virtual tape library.

Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway cached volume. Set the local cache to 10 TB. Mount the Volume Gateway cached volume to the existing file server by using iSCSI, and copy all files to the storage volume. Configure scheduled snapshots of the storage volume. To recover from a disaster, restore a snapshot to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and attach the EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance.

Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway stored volume with the same amount of disk space as the existing file storage volume. Mount the Volume Gateway stored volume to the existing file server by using iSCSI, and copy all files to the storage volume. Configure scheduled snapshots of the storage volume. To recover from a disaster, restore a snapshot to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and attach the EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance.

question_text:
A company is hosting a web application from an Amazon S3 bucket. The application uses Amazon Cognito as an identity provider to authenticate users and return a JSON Web Token (JWT) that provides access to protected resources that are stored in another S3 bucket.
Upon deployment of the application, users report errors and are unable to access the protected content. A solutions architect must resolve this issue by providing proper permissions so that users can access the protected content.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
A Cognito token does not per se grant any AWS privileges. The process works as follows: the user performs authentication in the user pool and receives a JWT, and then the token is exchanged in the identification pool as a temporary IAM role certificate, which gives S3:GetObject permission to the protected drum. An error in access means that the role of the identification pool assigned to the certified user does not exist (or is misconfigured). Remember the difference: the user pool is responsible for "Who is this" and the identification pool is responsible for "what AWS privileges are granted to them." "
Option B: ACL is a legacy S3 mechanism that cannot be granted permission based on Cognito authentication results. Modern methods are the use of a storage barrel strategy with a user role.
Option C: S3 has long provided strong post-writing consistency, which has nothing to do with access errors.
Option D: Custom attribute mapping helps to pass on user information, but independently it does not grant any AWS privileges: permissions come from the role granted by the identification pool.

options.text: Update the Amazon Cognito identity pool to assume the proper IAM role for access to the protected content.
Update the S3 ACL to allow the application to access the protected content.
Redeploy the application to Amazon S3 to prevent eventually consistent reads in the S3 bucket from affecting the ability of users to access the protected content.
Update the Amazon Cognito pool to use custom attribute mappings within the identity pool and grant users the proper permissions to access the protected content.

question_text:
An image hosting company uploads its large assets to Amazon S3 Standard buckets. The company uses multipart upload in parallel by using S3 APIs and overwrites if the same object is uploaded again. For the first 30 days after upload, the objects will be accessed frequently. The objects will be used less frequently after 30 days, but the access patterns for each object will be inconsistent. The company must optimize its S3 storage costs while maintaining high availability and resiliency of stored assets.
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
There are two separate cost items. The first is the object itself: after 30 days, visits become scarce but "unconsistent", i.e. unpredictable, which requires the use of Intelligent-Tiering(A) rather than the type of fee-based access search. The second is incomplete multi-part upload (B): In multiple simultaneous uploads, the suspended parts remain in S3 buckets, do not appear in the list of objects and are still charged for storage costs until they are removed from the life cycle rules ( "AbortIncomplete MultiPartUpload"). For large assets, such invisible cost items may sometimes represent a significant share of the billing.
Option C: It is important to clear expired deletion marks in the versioned S3 buckets. The scene describes the overlay of the object, and the removal of the mark itself does not occupy any storage space - there are no cost savings.
Option D: Standard-IA charges access costs, and visits after 30 days are described as inconsistent. Each unexpected visit would incur costs, which would make it more cost-effective in this scenario.
Option E: Individual Area-IA stores a copy in a usable area, while the problem requires high availability and error tolerance.

options.text: Move assets to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to clean up incomplete multipart uploads.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to clean up expired object delete markers.
Move assets to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.
Move assets to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.

question_text:
A solutions architect must secure a VPC network that hosts Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances contain highly sensitive data and run in a private subnet. According to company policy, the EC2 instances that run in the VPC can access only approved third-party software repositories on the internet for software product updates that use the third party’s URL. Other internet traffic must be blocked.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
This limitation is expressed in the form of a domain name ( "third party URL"), while the security group and the Network ACL only support the address and port. AWS Network Firewall can distinguish between domain names: a statusful fulgation corresponds to a list of domain names, allows traffic to the names listed, prevents all other traffic, and private sub-network traffic is routed from the end of the firewall. This is the standard method for constructing export filters based on domain names.
Option B: AWS WAF protects HTTP requests that are brought to your application, without filtering out the flow of the instance.
Option C: The security group rules cannot specify a URL or domain name - only CIDR blocks, prefix lists and other security groups can be specified.
Option D: Load Balancer distributes the entry request to your target. The Internet traffic outside the site will not pass through it.

options.text: Update the route table for the private subnet to route the outbound traffic to an AWS Network Firewall firewall. Configure domain list rule groups.
Set up an AWS WAF web ACL. Create a custom set of rules that filter traffic requests based on source and destination IP address range sets.
Implement strict inbound security group rules. Configure an outbound rule that allows traffic only to the authorized software repositories on the internet by specifying the URLs.

Configure an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the EC2 instances. Direct all outbound traffic to the ALB. Use a URL-based rule listener in the ALB’s target group for outbound access to the internet.

question_text:
A company is hosting a three-tier ecommerce application in the AWS Cloud. The company hosts the website on Amazon S3 and integrates the website with an API that handles sales requests. The company hosts the API on three Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The API consists of static and dynamic front-end content along with backend workers that process sales requests asynchronously.
The company is expecting a significant and sudden increase in the number of sales requests during events for the launch of new products.
What should a solutions architect recommend to ensure that all the requests are processed successfully?
explanation_en:
A sharp and sudden surge in traffic is expected, and all orders must be processed. CloudFront removes static content from the example and receives a SQS queue of purchase requests: this queue can receive requests immediately and save them until the processor is finished. This would not result in any requests being lost, even if the examples were temporarily unable to keep up with traffic flows.
Option A: The manual addition of examples does not respond to sudden surges in flows, and the benefits of dynamic content via the CloudFront cache are minimal.
Option B: An automatic extension group based on network traffic takes several minutes to expand, and requests that arrived earlier during this period will still be discarded during overload.
Option C: The cache in front of the load balancer does not help to write the orders, and the ClaudFront is used for dynamic content that does not solve the problem of keeping these orders.

options.text: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the dynamic content. Increase the number of EC2 instances to handle the increase in traffic.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the static content. Place the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on network traffic.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the dynamic content. Add an Amazon ElastiCache instance in front of the ALB to reduce traffic for the API to handle.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the static content. Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to receive requests from the website for later processing by the EC2 instances.

question_text:
A security audit reveals that Amazon EC2 instances are not being patched regularly. A solutions architect needs to provide a solution that will run regular security scans across a large fleet of EC2 instances. The solution should also patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule and provide a report of each instance’s patch status.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
There are two requirements, which are met by two different services. Hole scanning is achieved by Amazon Inspector: an ongoing scan of the software packages on the example is performed through SSM Agent, and priority results are provided. The state of patches is regularly updated and reported by Patch Manager (as part of the system management service): this includes patches baseline, maintenance window and compliance reporting for each instance. Both components are achieved through management and do not require a self-defined code.
Option A: Macie analyzes data in S3, while the cron operation on each instance is a manual scheme without reporting or compliance tracking.
Option B: GuardDuty does not scan software packages to detect holes, while Session Manager provides access to examples, but does not manage patches.
Option C: Amazon Detective helps investigate events from the log instead of identifying loopholes, while the movement of EventBridge alone does not apply any patches.

options.text: Set up Amazon Macie to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up a cron job on each EC2 instance to patch the instance on a regular schedule.

Turn on Amazon GuardDuty in the account. Configure GuardDuty to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.
Set up Amazon Detective to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.

Turn on Amazon Inspector in the account. Configure Amazon Inspector to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.

question_text:
A company is planning to store data on Amazon RDS DB instances. The company must encrypt the data at rest.
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
The static data encryption in RDS is opened when the instance is created (or recovered from the encrypted snapshot) and depends on a KMS key - either the client key that you manage yourself, or the AWS default key. This will encrypt data on disks, autobacks, snapshots and read copies simultaneously. Do not confuse this with encryption in the transfer - encryption in the transmission is handled by the TLS connection to the database, which is another independent matter.
Option B: Secrets Manager storage keys, such as database passwords. It does not provide a key for encryption of RDS storage -- this is KMS 's duty.
Option C: Certificates from ACM provide encryption for connections, that is, protection of data in transfer. It does not encrypt data on disk.
Option D: The same problem exists, plus IAM certificate storage is an outdated mechanism that has been replaced by ACM.

options.text: Create a key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Enable encryption for the DB instances.
Create an encryption key. Store the key in AWS Secrets Manager. Use the key to encrypt the DB instances.
Generate a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Enable SSL/TLS on the DB instances by using the certificate.
Generate a certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Enable SSL/TLS on the DB instances by using the certificate.

question_text:
A company must migrate 20 TB of data from a data center to the AWS Cloud within 30 days. The company’s network bandwidth is limited to 15 Mbps and cannot exceed 70% utilization.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The problem is solved by arithmetic. The available bandwidth is 70 per cent of 15 Mbps, about 10.5 Mbps, and about 113 GB/day. At this rate, it takes about 180 days for the 20 bytes, but the deadline is 30 days. No matter how convenient the online method is, it cannot be completed within the time frame, so the remaining option is offline transfer: Snowball. Remember this rule of experience: 100 Mbps ⁇ 1 TB, 1 Gbps ⁇ 10 TB per day -- that's enough to exclude the line options in 10 seconds.
Option B: DataSync transmits data via the same link. It accelerates and validates the transmission process, but does not change the bottom physical limit of 10.5 Mbps.
Option C: VPN is the same link plus the cost of encryption. In such a short deadline, its feasibility is even less feasible.
Option D: Transfer Acceleration optimizes the path from the edge position to the S3 bucket, but the bottlenecks here are the uplink of the data centre itself, and the acceleration does not reach the bottleneck.

options.text: Use AWS Snowball.
Use AWS DataSync.
Use a secure VPN connection.
Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.

question_text:
A company needs to provide its employees with secure access to confidential and sensitive files. The company wants to ensure that the files can be accessed only by authorized users. The files must be downloaded securely to the employees’ devices.
The files are stored in an on-premises Windows file server. However, due to an increase in remote usage, the file server is running out of capacity.
.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The file is stored on Windows shared with domain fundamentals, the space is running out and the staff is working remotely. Migration to FSx for Windows File Server retains familiar SMB and NTFS privileges and maintains the same authorization mechanism as the existing Active Directory integration, while Clean VPN provides secure access to VPC for remote employees, where the file system is located. Downloads are carried out through encrypted tunnels, not through an open Internet.
Option A: A file server located in a public subnet with an IP-based filter means that SMB is exposed to the Internet and needs to maintain the address list manually. This is neither safe nor convenient for remote work.
Option C: Private endpoints can only be accessed from within VPC, and employees are located outside of them, so they cannot access the endpoint. Moving to object storage also changes how people operate their files.
Option D: There is no known "public VPC endpoint". Access to Internet Center does not solve the problem of sending files safely to the device.

options.text: Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.
Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).

question_text:
A company’s application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. On the first day of every month at midnight, the application becomes much slower when the month-end financial calculation batch runs. This causes the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances to immediately peak to 100%, which disrupts the application.
What should a solutions architect recommend to ensure the application is able to handle the workload and avoid downtime?
explanation_en:
This peak is known in advance: midnight on the first day of the month. This means that the example needs to be expanded before it begins, rather than being reactive. The planned expansion strategy of the auto-extension group increases capacity before the known time and reduces capacity thereafter, so CPU utilization will never be fixed at 100 per cent.
Option A: CloudFront cache content is available to users, while the load is generated by a batch calculation within the application.
Option B: A simple CPU-based extension strategy will only trigger when the utilization rate has reached 100 per cent: the application will not be available within minutes of the new example being launched.
Option D: Cache will read traffic separately, but the peak load here comes from a calculation task rather than a data request.

options.text: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB.
Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling simple scaling policy based on CPU utilization.
Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled scaling policy based on the monthly schedule.
Configure Amazon ElastiCache to remove some of the workload from the EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company wants to give a customer the ability to use on-premises Microsoft Active Directory to download files that are stored in Amazon S3. The customer’s application uses an SFTP client to download the files.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead and no changes to the customer’s application?
explanation_en:
There is an unalterable SFTP client, as well as the local Active Directory where the user is located. AWS Transport Family can provide a managed SFTP endpoint over S3 drums and can authenticate an external directory, including Active Directory identification through Microsoft AD managed by AWS or a custom identity provider. The application can continue to run through the SFTP without running any infrastructure at the bottom.
Option B: AWS DMS Migration Database. It provides neither SFTP nor synchronisation of documents.
Option C: DataSync copys the data according to plan, but does not provide SFTP endpoints to the client to download the file.
Option D: Deployment of a custom SFTP server on the Windows instance is a machine that needs maintenance, patches and extensions. The hosting service, on the other hand, can perform the same functions without a server.

options.text: Set up AWS Transfer Family with SFTP for Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.
Set up AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to synchronize the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.
Set up AWS DataSync to synchronize between the on-premises location and the S3 location by using AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).
Set up a Windows Amazon EC2 instance with SFTP to connect the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Integrate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).

question_text:
A company is experiencing sudden increases in demand. The company needs to provision large Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Machine Image (AMI). The instances will run in an Auto Scaling group. The company needs a solution that provides minimum initialization latency to meet the demand.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The start-up delay occurred at the time of the mirror start-up instance, as the block of the root roll was pulled from the snapshot during the first visit. Quickshot restoration eliminates this: the volume created by the snapshot that enabled the function can be fully performance at start-up. This is a snapshot of the created AMI, and the automatic extension group is switched to the AMI.
Option A: The initialization process will not be expedited by registration of a snapshot image alone, and StepFunctions will only be used to coordinate the steps.
Option C: Amazon DLM automated timing mirror creation, but it does not affect the start speed of the first start.
Option D: AWS Backup is responsible for backup and the capacity limits of the auto-scaling group are not sources of EventBridge events.

options.text: Use the aws ec2 register-image command to create an AMI from a snapshot. Use AWS Step Functions to replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.
Enable Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) fast snapshot restore on a snapshot. Provision an AMI by using the snapshot. Replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group with the new AMI.
Enable AMI creation and define lifecycle rules in Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM). Create an AWS Lambda function that modifies the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.
Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke AWS Backup lifecycle policies that provision AMIs. Configure Auto Scaling group capacity limits as an event source in EventBridge.

question_text:
A company hosts a multi-tier web application that uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster for storage. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The company’s IT security guidelines mandate that the database credentials be encrypted and rotated every 14 days.
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?
explanation_en:
The requirement is that the database be encrypted and rotate every 14 days, with minimal operating costs. This was achieved through configuration: the key is encrypted using the KMS key associated with the Aurora cluster and the rotation schedule is set at any number of days - 14 days is set as a custom cycle. AWS itself provides a rotational function for the supporting database and therefore does not need to prepare a rotation code. Each of the other options suggests that the same result be achieved through a custom code.
Option B: Parameter Store stores encrypted passwords, but rotation must be performed and maintained by yourself in the Lambda function. This is significantly more than the establishment of a rotation cycle in the Secrets Manager.
Option C: A file on a shared file system plus a custom rotation function increases the development workload, requires managing file access rights and risks that databases and files are not synchronized.
Option D: Regular downloads of password files from a S3 bucket mean that the application will use outdated passwords for a certain period of time and will again require a custom rotation code.

options.text: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to create a new secret that uses the KMS key with the appropriate credentials. Associate the secret with the Aurora DB cluster. Configure a custom rotation period of 14 days.

Create two parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: one for the user name as a string parameter and one that uses the SecureString type for the password. Select AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption for the password parameter, and load these parameters in the application tier. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password every 14 days.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system in all EC2 instances of the application tier. Restrict the access to the file on the file system so that the application can read the file and that only super users can modify the file. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the key in Aurora every 14 days and writes new credentials into the file.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon S3 bucket that the application uses to load the credentials. Download the file to the application regularly to ensure that the correct credentials are used. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the Aurora credentials every 14 days and uploads these credentials to the file in the S3 bucket.

question_text:
A company has deployed a web application on AWS. The company hosts the backend database on Amazon RDS for MySQL with a primary DB instance and five read replicas to support scaling needs. The read replicas must lag no more than 1 second behind the primary DB instance. The database routinely runs scheduled stored procedures.
As traffic on the website increases, the replicas experience additional lag during periods of peak load. A solutions architect must reduce the replication lag as much as possible. The solutions architect must minimize changes to the application code and must minimize ongoing operational overhead.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Copies in RDS for MySQL are delayed to increase under load because they are made through binary logs and are applied independently on each copy. Aurora works differently: a copy is read from the same shared storage and is therefore delayed in milliseconds and is almost unrelated to the load. Auto-extension Aurora adds a copy as the flow increases and the storage process is replaced by the original Aurora MySQL function - very small changes in the application.
Option B: Cache before the database requires the rewrite of the application logic, which does not reduce the delay in the copy itself.
Option C: The self-managed MySQL example means the largest operating cost, while the reproduction mechanism remains the same and the delay is the same.
Option D: DynamoDB means that data models and queries need to be rewrited, and DynamoDB streams do not replace storage processes.

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Replace the read replicas with Aurora Replicas, and configure Aurora Auto Scaling. Replace the stored procedures with Aurora MySQL native functions.

Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of the database. Modify the application to check the cache before the application queries the database. Replace the stored procedures with AWS Lambda functions.
Migrate the database to a MySQL database that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Choose large, compute optimized EC2 instances for all replica nodes. Maintain the stored procedures on the EC2 instances.

Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Provision a large number of read capacity units (RCUs) to support the required throughput, and configure on-demand capacity scaling. Replace the stored procedures with DynamoDB streams.

question_text:
A solutions architect must create a disaster recovery (DR) plan for a high-volume software as a service (SaaS) platform. All data for the platform is stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster.
The DR plan must replicate data to a secondary AWS Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Reference answer: D; disputed option: B.
The AWS document refers to the no-example configuration of the Aurora global database: a stand-by cluster with no example is duplicated at the storage level and is less costly. Strictly interpreted, "most economical" prefers option B; option D argues that, in the absence of examples, the spare area cannot carry the load immediately.
Aurora Global Database supports headless secondary without DB access: storage continues to be copied across regions, but not for subregional costing. The drying requires only cross-regional replication and the most cost-effective, so B is more relevant than retaining the original answer D for the subregional example; it is more time-consuming to add the example when failure shifts.
Source answer D's original resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
The issue is controversial. The answer to the exercise information is option D: Aurora Global Database copying data at the storage level to the second area, with a delay of about one second, and retaining at least one example so that the region can carry the load immediately. A strong alternative is option B, i.e. no instance configuration: AWS clearly documents an exampleless back-up cluster, which is cheaper because you only have to pay for storage and reproduction. Strictly read, "most economical" prefers option B; option D is better if read as "disaster recovery plans must be ready for immediate use".
Source old option A: MySQL binary copying is a slower way to copy Aurora across regions and needs manual maintenance, while the global database completes this at the storage level.
Old Source Option B: This configuration is technically effective and cheaper than the response to the exercise of information, and the question is therefore marked as controversial: the only reason to oppose it is that regions without examples cannot receive traffic immediately after a disaster has occurred.
The old source option C:DMS is a migration tool, not a standard mechanism used by Aurora for continuous cross-regional replication: it is an additional component and may fail itself.

options.text: Use MySQL binary log replication to an Aurora cluster in the secondary Region. Provision one DB instance for the Aurora cluster in the secondary Region.
Set up an Aurora global database for the DB cluster. When setup is complete, remove the DB instance from the secondary Region.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to continuously replicate data to an Aurora cluster in the secondary Region. Remove the DB instance from the secondary Region.
Set up an Aurora global database for the DB cluster. Specify a minimum of one DB instance in the secondary Region.

question_text:
A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance. Management says the application must be made more secure with the least amount of programming effort.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The limit to doing so is "the least programming workload". AWS Securitys Manager supports RDS MySQL to rotate automatically: You set a plan, AWS will provide a function to modify the database password and update the key. The application can only call GetSecretValue once without hard-coding proof. This is the key difference between the right option and the need to prepare a similar option for the same rotation function on its own.
Option A: KMS manages encryption keys rather than database documents. You cannot load usernames and passwords from KMS.
Option B: The design is valid, but the preparation of a self-defined rotation function is precisely the programming workload that the title requires to avoid: it needs to be prepared, tested and maintained.
Option D: Parameter Store does not have an built-in rotation mechanism, so it is not possible to set up a rotation scheme through Parameter Store.

options.text: Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to create keys. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation.

Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Create an AWS Lambda function that rotates the credentials in Secret Manager.

Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Secrets Manager.

Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Parameter Store.

question_text:
A media company hosts its website on AWS. The website application’s architecture includes a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a database that is hosted on Amazon Aurora. The company’s cybersecurity team reports that the application is vulnerable to SQL injection.
How should the company resolve this issue?
explanation_en:
SQL injection is an attack at the HTTP request level filtered by AWS WAF at the front end of the application. A Web ACL was added to the application load balancer, and the Management Rules Group (especially the SQL database rule book) was activated, and malicious requests were blocked before the arrival of the instance. This is a remedial control: at the same time, codes should be repaired to use parameterized queries, but the specific way in which the title requirements are met is through WAF.
Option B: The AALB listener rules use routers according to path, host name, head and method, but do not check if there is an injection sign in the request contents.
Option C: Shield Advanced defends against a serviceable attack and does not parse SQL injections.
Option D: Inspector is used to detect and report a loophole, but it does not filter traffic or block anything.

options.text: Use AWS WAF in front of the ALB. Associate the appropriate web ACLs with AWS WAF.
Create an ALB listener rule to reply to SQL injections with a fixed response.
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced to block all SQL injection attempts automatically.
Set up Amazon Inspector to block all SQL injection attempts automatically.

question_text:
A company has an Amazon S3 data lake that is governed by AWS Lake Formation. The company wants to create a visualization in Amazon QuickSight by joining the data in the data lake with operational data that is stored in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The company wants to enforce column-level authorization so that the company’s marketing team can access only a subset of columns in the database.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The key requirement is level access control, with minimal operating costs. Lake Formation precisely achieved this: it maintains a catalogue, grants privileges at table, column and row levels and disseminates these privileges to its search engine, mainly Athena. Therefore, Aurora data is imported into the lake by Lake Formation blueprints, with row permissions, QuickSight is connected through Athena, and only allowed columns are automatically visible. There is no barrel strategy and no need to create data sets for each team.
Option A: EMR for data import is a heavy device and does not provide a row access control - you must manually prepare a separate extraction data.
Option B: The IAM policy cannot limit access to individual columns in the S3 file - the particle size is the object and prefix.
Option C: The barrel policy does not even distinguish between columns within the object. In addition, Glue Elastic Views is a service that has never reached general availability.

options.text: Use Amazon EMR to ingest the data directly from the database to the QuickSight SPICE engine. Include only the required columns.

Use AWS Glue Studio to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Attach an IAM policy to the QuickSight users to enforce column-level access control. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.

Use AWS Glue Elastic Views to create a materialized view for the database in Amazon S3. Create an S3 bucket policy to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon S3 as the data source in QuickSight.

Use a Lake Formation blueprint to ingest the data from the database to the S3 data lake. Use Lake Formation to enforce column-level access control for the QuickSight users. Use Amazon Athena as the data source in QuickSight.

question_text:
A transaction processing company has weekly scripted batch jobs that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The number of transactions can vary, but the baseline CPU utilization that is noted on each run is at least 60%. The company needs to provision the capacity 30 minutes before the jobs run.
Currently, engineers complete this task by manually modifying the Auto Scaling group parameters. The company does not have the resources to analyze the required capacity trends for the Auto Scaling group counts. The company needs an automated way to modify the Auto Scaling group’s desired capacity.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
These operations are run weekly, the base load is known (at least 60 per cent) and there is no manual analysis of load patterns. Predictive expansion can automatically accomplish this: it builds projections based on historical data of the indicator and starts with examples of early start-up, with a clear time frame for pre-start — here, 30 minutes before the start of the operation.
Option A: A dynamic expansion policy only reacts after the load has arrived: it does not provide you with 30 minutes in advance.
Option B: Time extension is feasible, but it requires a manual identification and maintenance of the required capacity, and the scenario description makes it clear that there are no resources to carry out such an analysis.
Option D: The self-defined function triggered by the alarm adds both additional codes and an after-action rather than a proactive expansion.

options.text: Create a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on the CPU utilization metric. Set the target value for the metric to 60%.

Create a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Set the appropriate desired capacity, minimum capacity, and maximum capacity. Set the recurrence to weekly. Set the start time to 30 minutes before the batch jobs run.

Create a predictive scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on forecast. Set the scaling metric to CPU utilization. Set the target value for the metric to 60%. In the policy, set the instances to pre-launch 30 minutes before the jobs run.

Create an Amazon EventBridge event to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the CPU utilization metric value for the Auto Scaling group reaches 60%. Configure the Lambda function to increase the Auto Scaling group’s desired capacity and maximum capacity by 20%.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a company’s disaster recovery (DR) architecture. The company has a MySQL database that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet with scheduled backup. The DR design needs to include multiple AWS Regions.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Disaster recovery must be designed across multiple AWS areas at minimal operational cost. Aurora GDB supports this: the main database cluster operates in the main area, the backup cluster operates in the disaster recovery area, duplicates occur in storage, usually delayed at the subsecond level, and upgrading the backup cluster is a single operation. The self-managed MySQL deployment and all its operational burdens have completely disappeared.
Option A: Self-management examples combined with manual configuration replication means the highest volume of work and the highest risk, and the failure switch is also manual.
Option B: Multi-usable area configuration and read-only copies of different available areas are operating within a single area: not meeting multi-area requirements.
Option D: Recovery from backup stored in drums takes hours and manual steps are required, and data is delayed between backup intervals.

options.text: Migrate the MySQL database to multiple EC2 instances. Configure a standby EC2 instance in the DR Region. Turn on replication.
Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS. Use a Multi-AZ deployment. Turn on read replication for the primary DB instance in the different Availability Zones.
Migrate the MySQL database to an Amazon Aurora global database. Host the primary DB cluster in the primary Region. Host the secondary DB cluster in the DR Region.
Store the scheduled backup of the MySQL database in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for S3 Cross- Region Replication (CRR). Use the data backup to restore the database in the DR Region.

question_text:
A company has a Java application that uses Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to parse messages. The application cannot parse messages that are larger than 256 KB in size. The company wants to implement a solution to give the application the ability to parse messages as large as 50 MB.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the code?
explanation_en:
The KB restriction is a rigid limitation of the SQS service itself and cannot be changed. The standard solution is to expand the client library using the Java version of Amazon SQS: The main message content is stored in S3 and only references to objects are sent to the queue and processed transparently by the library. There are very few changes to the application code - you just have to replace it with an extended client.
Option B: EventBridge itself has an event limit of 256 KB, so it cannot solve this problem, and this means that the entire message delivery model needs to be changed.
Option C: 256 KB is a hard service limit that cannot be raised by configuration or support request.
Option D: Theoretically it is feasible to quote files stored in EFS, but you have to prepare all the logic of writing, reading and cleaning documents yourself, and the ready-made library will do these for you.

options.text: Use the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java to host messages that are larger than 256 KB in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon EventBridge to post large messages from the application instead of Amazon SQS.
Change the limit in Amazon SQS to handle messages that are larger than 256 KB.
Store messages that are larger than 256 KB in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Configure Amazon SQS to reference this location in the messages.

question_text:
A company wants to restrict access to the content of one of its main web applications and to protect the content by using authorization techniques available on AWS. The company wants to implement a serverless architecture and an authentication solution for fewer than 100 users. The solution needs to integrate with the main web application and serve web content globally. The solution must also scale as the company's user base grows while providing the lowest login latency possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
With fewer than 100 users, global content distribution was achieved using a server-free structure, with the lowest delays in login. Cognito is responsible for authentication (almost free of charge in that number of users), while CloudFront provides application services from the edge, while the token authentication runs in Lambda@Edge — that is, execution at the edge of the user's connection without the need to return to the source area. This is the key to minimizing the delay in login.
Option B: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a catalogue service that is hourlyly and too complex and costly for 100 users and that ARB cannot achieve global content distribution.
Option C: S3 Transfer Acceleration can speed up the uploading of data to the S3 bucket, but does not speed up the availability of content on the site and the regular Lambda function operates only in a single area, which increases the delay.
Option D: Once again the AD directory appears too complex and expensive, while Elastic Beanstalk means that a server is needed — contrary to the absence of a server structure.

options.text: Use Amazon Cognito for authentication. Use [email protected] for authorization. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the web application globally.
Use AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory for authentication. Use AWS Lambda for authorization. Use an Application Load Balancer to serve the web application globally.
Use Amazon Cognito for authentication. Use AWS Lambda for authorization. Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to serve the web application globally.
Use AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory for authentication. Use [email protected] for authorization. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to serve the web application globally.

question_text:
A company has an aging network-attached storage (NAS) array in its data center. The NAS array presents SMB shares and NFS shares to client workstations. The company does not want to purchase a new NAS array. The company also does not want to incur the cost of renewing the NAS array’s support contract. Some of the data is accessed frequently, but much of the data is inactive.
A solutions architect needs to implement a solution that migrates the data to Amazon S3, uses S3 Lifecycle policies, and maintains the same look and feel for the client workstations. The solutions architect has identified AWS Storage Gateway as part of the solution.
Which type of storage gateway should the solutions architect provision to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Client workstations need to maintain the same appearance and feeling, and data must move to S3 and be subject to life-cycle rules. This is Amazon S3 File Gateway: it is achieved by exposing NFS and SMB sharing, while storing each file as an object in a S3 bucket, so life cycle rules can be applied normally, frequently accessed data can be cached locally, and workstations do not detect any difference.
Option A: Volume Gateway provides a block through iSCSI and stores data in a snapshot instead of a single object: this does not allow the application of life-cycle rules to user files and the workstation will lose its familiar shared access.
Option B: Tape Gateway Simulates virtual tape libraries for backup software; it has nothing to do with network sharing at the workstation.
Option C: FSx File Gateway cache access to FSx filesystems instead of S3, so there is no S3 life cycle rule in this setting.

options.text: Volume Gateway
Tape Gateway
Amazon FSx File Gateway
Amazon S3 File Gateway

question_text:

The company wants to maximize cost savings for the application over the next 3 years. The company needs to be able to change the instance family and sizes in the next 6 months based on application popularity and usage.

explanation_en:
The commitment period is three years, but within six months there may be changes in family and specifications. A savings calculation scheme provides a discount of up to 66 per cent, which is not tied to the example family, specification, area or even service - the discount remains valid when you migrate to different examples, Fargate or Lambda.

Standard Reserved Instances

question_text:
A company collects data from a large number of participants who use wearable devices. The company stores the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table and uses applications to analyze the data. The data workload is constant and predictable. The company wants to stay at or below its forecasted budget for DynamoDB.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The workload is constant and predictable and the budget needs to be controlled. Under the pre-retention model, which defines the unit of reading and writing capacity, costs are lower than on demand and generate predictable billings for a stable load of work: you pay the cost of the pre-retention capacity, rather than the fee as requested.
Option A: Standard-IA Tables reduce storage costs, but raise the request cost - not economical under a stable work load - and the description of "retention capacity" here is not accurate.
Option C: You are not allowed to set up a unit of capacity in an as-needed mode at a higher cost than the reserved mode under a stable load of work.
Option D: As required, support neither the specified unit of capacity nor the reserved capacity - there is no such configuration.

options.text: Use provisioned mode and DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA). Reserve capacity for the forecasted workload.
Use provisioned mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs).
Use on-demand mode. Set the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) high enough to accommodate changes in the workload.
Use on-demand mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) with reserved capacity.

question_text:
A company stores confidential data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database in the ap-southeast-3 Region. The database is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. The company was recently acquired and must securely share a backup of the database with the acquiring company’s AWS account in ap-southeast-3.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The snapshot is encrypted using KMS keys, so sharing it again takes two steps: allowing another account to use the key (update the key policy and add authorization if necessary) and explicitly sharing the snapshot itself with the account. The recipient usually immediately creates a copy of the snapshot and re-encodes it using its own key to avoid relying on your key. An important limitation that often emerges from the subject of the examination is that snapshots encrypted with default AWS management keys (ws/rds) cannot be shared — only if they are encrypted with your own key.
Option A: You cannot copy encrypted snapshots to unencrypted RDS examples - this is not the way to decrypt the data. For sensitive data, this would also lead to lower security levels.
Option C: You cannot share a snapshot using the AWS managed key encryption, while the key alias is just a convenient name -- it does not grant access to anyone.
Option D: You cannot download the RDS snapshot to disk -- this service does not provide this option. Alternative options for uploading S3 are more complex and less secure, and it is preferable to share snapshot security directly.

options.text: Create a database snapshot. Copy the snapshot to a new unencrypted snapshot. Share the new snapshot with the acquiring company’s AWS account.
Create a database snapshot. Add the acquiring company’s AWS account to the KMS key policy. Share the snapshot with the acquiring company’s AWS account.
Create a database snapshot that uses a different AWS managed KMS key. Add the acquiring company’s AWS account to the KMS key alias. Share the snapshot with the acquiring company's AWS account.
Create a database snapshot. Download the database snapshot. Upload the database snapshot to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from the acquiring company’s AWS account.

question_text:
A company uses a 100 GB Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server Single-AZ DB instance in the us-east-1 Region to store customer transactions. The company needs high availability and automatic recovery for the DB instance.
The company must also run reports on the RDS database several times a year. The report process causes transactions to take longer than usual to post to the customers’ accounts. The company needs a solution that will improve the performance of the report process.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Multi-AZ decision of RDS for SQL Server provides an automatic failure transfer, but its standby does not accept reading; a new read report can be carried for occasional reading. Source AC corresponds to the two requirements of high-availability and read load segregation, with attention to the selected SQL Server version and permission for read repica support.
There are two requirements here. High availability and automatic recovery mean the conversion of examples to multi-usable area deployments (A) with simultaneous replication and automatic failure switching. Accelerating the report query without compromising the transaction means creating a read-only copy in another available area, and all the report queries point to that copy (C).
Option B: Creates an independent copy from the snapshot restoration, which immediately begins to become obsolete and does not provide an automatic failure switch.
Option D: RDS Custom is the solution that requires access to the bottom operating system; it has nothing to do with usability and reporting.
Option E: RDS Proxy manages the connective pool and cannot delay the query to the maintenance window.

options.text: Modify the DB instance from a Single-AZ DB instance to a Multi-AZ deployment.
Take a snapshot of the current DB instance. Restore the snapshot to a new RDS deployment in another Availability Zone.
Create a read replica of the DB instance in a different Availability Zone. Point all requests for reports to the read replica.

question_text:
A company is moving its data management application to AWS. The company wants to transition to an event-driven architecture. The architecture needs to be more distributed and to use serverless concepts while performing the different aspects of the workflow. The company also wants to minimize operational overhead.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The demand is a non-server-based, event-driven and distributed structure with minimal operating costs. AWS Step Function describes the workflow as a status machine, calls the Lambda function in each step and handles errors, retrys and branch operations - the whole process does not require a single server or a custom organization code.
Option A: AWS Glue is an ETL service for data processing, not an organiser for any workflow.
Option B: The EC2 instance of a workstream step will lead to infrastructure that needs to be maintained.
Option C: EventBridge ' s planned implementation means a cyclical call, not an event-driven workflow with a state and branch.

options.text: Build out the workflow in AWS Glue. Use AWS Glue to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the workflow steps.
Build out the workflow in AWS Step Functions. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Step Functions to invoke the workflow steps on the EC2 instances.
Build out the workflow in Amazon EventBridge. Use EventBridge to invoke AWS Lambda functions on a schedule to process the workflow steps.

question_text:
A company is designing the network for an online multi-player game. The game uses the UDP networking protocol and will be deployed in eight AWS Regions. The network architecture needs to minimize latency and packet loss to give end users a high-quality gaming experience.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
UDP transfers between eight regions with requests for minimization delays and loss of data packages. The global accelerator creates UDP listening and endpoint groups in each region: when players enter the AWS network, they reach the nearest edge, and then transmit via the AWS backbone network, with a significantly lower rate of discarding and shaking than the public Internet. Any Cast IP address remains static and the area will be removed from the inquiry in a few seconds when an area fails.
Option A: Transit Gateway and interregional equivalence connects the AWS network. They have no impact on the path from the player to the nearest region.
Option C: CloudFront does not support UDP: it only supports HTTP and HTTPS.
Option D: VPC reciprocal connections provide internal AWS connectivity rather than external user access improvements. There is no "open UDP" expression in the peer connection.

options.text: Setup a transit gateway in each Region. Create inter-Region peering attachments between each transit gateway.
Set up AWS Global Accelerator with UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region.
Set up Amazon CloudFront with UDP turned on. Configure an origin in each Region.
Set up a VPC peering mesh between each Region. Turn on UDP for each VPC.

question_text:
A company hosts a three-tier web application on Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. The web application uses a self-managed MySQL database that is hosted on an EC2 instance to store data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The MySQL database currently uses a 1 TB Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume. The company expects traffic of 1,000 IOPS for both reads and writes at peak traffic.
The company wants to minimize any disruptions, stabilize performance, and reduce costs while retaining the capacity for double the IOPS. The company wants to move the database tier to a fully managed solution that is highly available and fault tolerant.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The peak traffic is 1,000 IOPS, leaving twice as much space as 2,000. A 1 TB gp2 volume provides 3,000 IOPS based on the formula for each GB 3 IOPS, which leaves a residual amount of capacity and is clearly less than io2. The database was also migrated to the MySQL-based Multi-AZ management example, which provided fault tolerance and removed the management burden.
Option A: O2 Block Express is designed for tens of thousands of operations per second and is expensive: it is wasteful to use 2,000 IOPS.
Option C:S3 is an object storage -- it cannot be used as a database.
Option D: Two large-scale examples run in the master mode and are still a self-managed database, while demand requires a fully managed solution.

options.text: Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with an io2 Block Express EBS volume.
Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume.
Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers.
Use two large EC2 instances to host the database in active-passive mode.

question_text:
A company hosts a serverless application on AWS. The application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The company notices an increase in application errors that result from database connection timeouts during times of peak traffic or unpredictable traffic. The company needs a solution that reduces the application failures with the least amount of change to the code.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The error stems from the depletion of the connection: in the surge, Lambda initiates a large number of simultaneous examples, each of which opens its own database connection. RDS Proxy will maintain and reuse a connection pool, and the only code change that is required is to point the connection to the proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.
Option A: Lowering the simultaneous permission value of the function limits the amount of throughput in the application and leads to another type of failure.
Option C: The use of a larger type of example will increase connectivity restrictions, but the problem will still take the form of an unpredictable peak and you will continue to pay for it.
Option D: Migration to DynamoDB means that data models and queries need to be rewrited - the maximum possible number of code changes.

options.text: Reduce the Lambda concurrency rate.
Enable RDS Proxy on the RDS DB instance.
Resize the RDS DB instance class to accept more connections.
Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand scaling.

question_text:
A company is migrating an old application to AWS. The application runs a batch job every hour and is CPU intensive. The batch job takes 15 minutes on average with an on-premises server. The server has 64 virtual CPU (vCPU) and 512 GiB of memory.
Which solution will run the batch job within 15 minutes with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
This operation requires 64 vCPU and 512 GiB memory and runs for 15 minutes - well beyond Lambda limits and beyond the scale of the typical Fargate task. AWS Watch automatically selects the type of instance that meets the operational requirements on EC2, initiates the example, runs the calculation task and releases the resource after completion - the service handles the queue and the schedule for you.
Option A: The memory limit for the Lambda function is approximately 10 GB and the execution time limit is 15 minutes - these requirements do not meet the requirements.
Option B: Fargate missions are much lower than 64 vCPU and 512 GiB RAMs.
Option C: Lightsail provides a small and fixed configuration that does not apply to such tasks loads.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda with functional scaling.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.
Use Amazon Lightsail with AWS Auto Scaling.
Use AWS Batch on Amazon EC2.

question_text:
A company stores its data objects in Amazon S3 Standard storage. A solutions architect has found that 75% of the data is rarely accessed after 30 days. The company needs all the data to remain immediately accessible with the same high availability and resiliency, but the company wants to minimize storage costs.
Which storage solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The phrase "same high availability and error tolerance" addresses the selection of three available areas and instant access, so decision-making ultimately falls between Standard Storage (Standard) and Standard Low Frequency Storage (Standard-IA). Age determines the choice: 75 per cent of the data is rarely read after 30 days, while Standard Low Frequency Storage (Standard-IA) is about 45 per cent cheaper with the same persistence and the same search speed. Therefore, a life-cycle rule is used to move objects on the 30th day.
Option A: S3 Glacier Deep Archive returns the object after an hour. This undermines the requirement that data be immediately accessible.
Option C: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single available area: 99.5 per cent availability, while Standard Low Frequency Storage (Standard-IA) is 99.9 per cent loss of the available area means data is lost. This is contrary to the requirement of the same tolerance.
Option D: There is also the problem of single available areas here, and the immediate migration of all data will also touch 25 per cent of the data that are still frequently read, which will incur search costs.

options.text: Move the data objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately.

question_text:
A gaming company is moving its public scoreboard from a data center to the AWS Cloud. The company uses Amazon EC2 Windows Server instances behind an Application Load Balancer to host its dynamic application. The company needs a highly available storage solution for the application. The application consists of static files and dynamic server-side code.
Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The application is divided into two parts, each of which requires independent storage. Static files are stored in S3 and cache (A) at edges via CloudFront. Server end-end codes need to be shared between all examples, which run Windows Servers - this requires a SMB sharing, using Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, which is mounted on each instance (D).
Option B: ElastiCache is a memory cache within an area; it does not cache objects at the edge or provide static file services.
Option C: EFS uses the NFS protocol to build for Linux - it is not a original access to Windows instance.
Option E: A gp2 volume is mounted inside a single available area and is not designed to be mounted simultaneously by multiple instances: there is no shared access and no high availability.

Store the static files on Amazon S3. Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache objects at the edge.

question_text:

explanation_en:
Resize and convert images in real time at edge nodes, processing thousands of requests per second, and best practice is implemented at edges. A Lambda@Edge function attached to the CloudFront cache behaviour, combined with the Image Processing Library: it receives requests, generates the required variant and returns the result, which is subsequently cached. Do not have to run the server on its own.

Option B: The source requests policy to control which head and parameters are forwarded to the source. It doesn't convert images.

question_text:
A hospital needs to store patient records in an Amazon S3 bucket. The hospital’s compliance team must ensure that all protected health information (PHI) is encrypted in transit and at rest. The compliance team must administer the encryption key for data at rest.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Demand has been broken down into three parts. "Construction in transfer" means that HTTPS (otherwise available but not mandatory) is enforced by using the ws:SecureTransport condition in the storage barrel policy. "static storage encryption" refers to the default encryption of the S3 bucket. "The compliance team must manage the encryption key" is the decisive detail - only the KMS key can be managed because it has key tactics, rotation mechanisms, logs and access rights that can be revoked. SSE-S3 does not have these functions: the service itself manages these keys.
Option A: Could not attach an ACM certificate to S3: The service provides data via HTTPS with its own certificate. There is no mechanism to enforce TLS.
Option B: SSE-S3 does not allow anyone to "manage key": these keys are invisible, have no strategy and cannot be revoked. The requirements of the compliance team were not met.
Option D: Macie can detect and classify sensitive data, but will not encrypt them. The static storage encryption requirement has not been resolved.

options.text: Create a public SSL/TLS certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Associate the certificate with Amazon S3. Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Assign the compliance team to manage the SSE-S3 keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Use Amazon Macie to protect the sensitive data that is stored in Amazon S3. Assign the compliance team to manage Macie.

question_text:
A company uses Amazon API Gateway to run a private gateway with two REST APIs in the same VPC. The BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service to ensure that enough funds are available before a stock can be purchased. The company has noticed in the VPC flow logs that the BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service over the internet instead of through the VPC. A solutions architect must implement a solution so that the APIs communicate through the VPC.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the code?
explanation_en:
The private API in the API Gateway can only be accessed internally from VPC via the interface endpoint: it creates a network interface with a private address and a DNS record, so one service calls another service through a private network. There is no need to change the code -- just resolve the API name to a private address.
Option A: API keys are relevant to the authorization and have no impact on the network path.
Option C: Gateway endpoints only apply to S3 and DynamoDB; the API Gateway does not have this endpoint type.

options.text: Add an X-API-Key header in the HTTP header for authorization.
Use an interface endpoint.
