Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance with a read replica in a single Availability Zone. Promote the read replica to replace the primary DB instance if the primary DB instance fails.

Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy the primary and secondary database servers on EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach to create shared storage between the instances.

question_text:
A company needs to ingest and handle large amounts of streaming data that its application generates. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and sends data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which is configured with default settings. Every other day, the application consumes the data and writes the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for business intelligence (BI) processing. The company observes that Amazon S3 is not receiving all the data that the application sends to Kinesis Data Streams.
What should a solutions architect do to resolve this issue?
explanation_en:
The application only pulls the data every two days, but Kinesis defaults to keep the record for 24 hours - any data earlier than the time the consumer arrives will be discarded. The extension of the retention period (up to 7 days under the standard model and longer use of the extended reservation) is sufficient to prevent the loss of data.
Option B: The Kinesis producer bank has improved the efficiency of writing, but has no effect on the length of time that the data already written is retained.
Option C: The missing fraction will be shown as writing failed, but writing here is successful and the data is lost while reading.
Option D: The S3 version control will retain the version of the object that has been uploaded to S3 but will not save the data that has been removed from the stream.

options.text: Update the Kinesis Data Streams default settings by modifying the data retention period.
Update the application to use the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) to send the data to Kinesis Data Streams.
Update the number of Kinesis shards to handle the throughput of the data that is sent to Kinesis Data Streams.
Turn on S3 Versioning within the S3 bucket to preserve every version of every object that is ingested in the S3 bucket.

question_text:
A developer has an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to upload files to Amazon S3 and needs the required permissions to perform the task. The developer already has an IAM user with valid IAM credentials required for Amazon S3.
What should a solutions architect do to grant the permissions?
explanation_en:
The Lambda function acquires its privileges by performing the role that is assigned to the function and attaches the required permission policies (e.g. s3 for a specific drum: PutObject) to that role. When running, the function automatically acquires a temporary voucher for the character and therefore does not need to store anything in the code. The current IAM user here is just a interference: putting a personal key in the service code is a counter-model. Do not confuse Lambda's two strategies - the executive role defines the action that a function can perform, and the resource-based strategy defines who can call the function.
Option A: The resource policy of the function defines which services and accounts are allowed to call it. It does not grant permission to write to S3.
Option B: Signing a request using the key of an existing user means embedding a long-standing key into a function code. This, while feasible, is contrary to recognized best practice and does not address the issue of competence management.
Option C: A new user and its key is the same error: store a long-term document in the code, rather than take a temporary certificate from the character.

options.text: Add required IAM permissions in the resource policy of the Lambda function.
Create a signed request using the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.
Create a new IAM user and use the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.
Create an IAM execution role with the required permissions and attach the IAM role to the Lambda function.

question_text:
A company has deployed a serverless application that invokes an AWS Lambda function when new documents are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. The application uses the Lambda function to process the documents. After a recent marketing campaign, the company noticed that the application did not process many of the documents.
What should a solutions architect do to improve the architecture of this application?
explanation_en:
During the surge, the direct call function from S3 is subject to the simultaneous limitation of the function, and the redundant event is lost because of the limited number of retries that are used by the step. A SQS queue receives every event, saves it and transmits it to a function at a rate that it can process - no document will be discarded.
Option A: A 15-minute running timeout does not help when the event never reaches the initial stage of the function.
Option B: Copying will copy the object into another S3 bucket, but will not perform any handling and will not keep the event.
Option C: The second function does not increase the balance of the account, nor does it provide a buffer function, and it does not allow a load balance for Lambda calls in this way.

options.text: Set the Lambda function's runtime timeout value to 15 minutes.
Configure an S3 bucket replication policy. Stage the documents in the S3 bucket for later processing.
Deploy an additional Lambda function. Load balance the processing of the documents across the two Lambda functions.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Send the requests to the queue. Configure the queue as an event source for Lambda.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing the architecture for a software demonstration environment. The environment will run on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The system will experience significant increases in traffic during working hours but is not required to operate on weekends.
Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to ensure that the system can scale to meet demand? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Workloads have risen and have completely disappeared on weekends. On working days, target-tracking expansion strategies based on average CPU utilization are appropriate - capacity changes with actual demand (D). On weekends, the planned expansion will set the minimum, expected and maximum capacity of the automatic expansion group to zero, and then restore the value (E) prior to the start of the week.
Option A: The application load balancer is automatically expanded as a hosting service; its capacity does not need to be configured.
Option B: The Internet gateway is a logical structure, with no bar-off limit, and therefore there is no content that needs to be expanded.
Option C: Multi-regional deployment addresses global availability rather than daily load fluctuations and is significantly more costly.

options.text: Use AWS Auto Scaling to adjust the ALB capacity based on request rate.
Use AWS Auto Scaling to scale the capacity of the VPC internet gateway.
Launch the EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions to distribute the load across Regions.
Use a target tracking scaling policy to scale the Auto Scaling group based on instance CPU utilization.
Use scheduled scaling to change the Auto Scaling group minimum, maximum, and desired capacity to zero for weekends. Revert to the default values at the start of the week.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a two-tiered architecture that includes a public subnet and a database subnet.
The web servers in the public subnet must be open to the internet on port 443. The Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the database subnet must be accessible only to the web servers on port 3306.
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The two-layer structure is based on the security team: the Web Server Open Port 443 for Internet access as a whole, as public websites require visitors (C); the database allows port 3306 by quoting the Web Server Security Team - access is granted only to those examples, regardless of address, and no one is granted other access rights.
Option A: Network ACL operates at the subnet level and is not required here; banning port 3306 port traffic will undermine the connection of the Web server to the database.
Option B: Allowing traffic through the address range of the subnet will open the database to any resources within the subnet, not just the Web server.
Option E: The security group does not have a rule of refusal — only those elements that are expressly permitted are allowed — and therefore cannot create such a rule.

options.text: Create a network ACL for the public subnet. Add a rule to deny outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the public subnet CIDR block on port 3306.
Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to deny all traffic except traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.

question_text:
A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud.
The company needs the ability to use Lustre clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The key phrase to re-emphasize is the Lustre client. The only hosting file system in AWS that supports the protocol is Amazon FSx for Lustre. It can provide a millisecond-scale delay and load per second byte, while AWS is responsible for all operations. Similar processes are described in Question 99.
Option A: DataSync is used to move data between storage systems and does not create a mounted file system.
Option B: Process Gateway provides resources through NFS and SMB; it does not support the Lustre protocol.
Option C: EFS does not support Lustre - there is no such configuration.

options.text: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.

question_text:
A company runs an application that receives data from thousands of geographically dispersed remote devices that use UDP. The application processes the data immediately and sends a message back to the device if necessary. No data is stored.
The company needs a solution that minimizes latency for the data transmission from the devices. The solution also must provide rapid failover to another AWS Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
UDP transmission, minimum delay and rapid failure to move to a network load equalizer in each region, achieved by a global accelerator. The accelerator receives data packages at the nearest edge, routes through the AWS global network backbone and switchs to healthy areas within seconds, without relying on DNS caches. Achieves the objective of a load equalizer without a server through the ECS on the Fargate. Applying the load balancer is inappropriate in this scenario - it does not support UDP.
Option A: The rate of transfer via Route 53 is slower because of the existence of a TTL solver cache and the network load balancer cannot target the Lambda function.
Option C: Application of a load balancer does not support UDP: Device cannot send data at all.
Option D: Application of the load balancer is not appropriate for UDP and failure transfer based on DNS does not provide a fast, high-availability switch.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions. Configure the NLB to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the data.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the NLProcess the data in Amazon ECS.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.

Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.

question_text:
A solutions architect must migrate a Windows Internet Information Services (IIS) web application to AWS. The application currently relies on a file share hosted in the user's on-premises network-attached storage (NAS). The solutions architect has proposed migrating the IIS web servers to Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones that are connected to the storage solution, and configuring an Elastic Load Balancer attached to the instances.
Which replacement to the on-premises file share is MOST resilient and durable?
explanation_en:
IS applications run on Windows and are shared via SMB protocols. The most robust and durable alternative is Amazon FSx for Windows File Server ' s Multi-AZ configuration: The data are synchronized between the available areas, supporting Windows ACLs and Active Directory, where the same file is available for each available area.
Option A: RDS is a relationship database; it cannot be shared as a file.
Option B: Storange Gateway is designed for a mixed scene and relies on a local virtual machine, which itself is a single point failure. It does not need to fully migrate to the AWS work load.
Option D: EFS uses NFS protocols: This is not original access for IS applications running on Windows and does not support Windows ACLs.

options.text: Migrate the file share to Amazon RDS.
Migrate the file share to AWS Storage Gateway.
Migrate the file share to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
Migrate the file share to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).

question_text:
A company is deploying a new application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application writes data to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company needs to ensure that all data that is written to the EBS volumes is encrypted at rest.
Which solution will meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
For EBS volumes, encryption is set at the time of creation and covers data on disks, data transmitted between volumes and examples, snapshots and volumes created from these snapshots. For existing unencrypted volumes, encryption cannot be opened - instead, you need to take a snapshot, specify a KMS key when copying the snapshot, and then create a new volume from an encrypted copy. Therefore, it is right to set the volume as encrypted when it is created; at the account level, this can be easily enforced by the EC2 "EBS Default Encryption".
Option A: An IAM character describes the actions the subject is allowed to perform. It has no attribute to "encrypted scrolls" and does not affect how they are created.
Option C: Label is only a tag for tracking and searching. Use it alone will not turn on any functionality; at most you can build on it, but the volume will not be encrypted because of the label.
Option D: KMS Key Policy defines who can use the key - it does not force the encryption of volumes across the account. Encryption enforcement is done by default EBS encryption settings or SCP policies containing ec2: Encrypted conditions.

options.text: Create an IAM role that specifies EBS encryption. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.
Create the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes. Attach the EBS volumes to the EC2 instances.
Create an EC2 instance tag that has a key of Encrypt and a value of True. Tag all instances that require encryption at the EBS level.
Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key policy that enforces EBS encryption in the account. Ensure that the key policy is active.

question_text:
A company has a web application with sporadic usage patterns. There is heavy usage at the beginning of each month, moderate usage at the start of each week, and unpredictable usage during the week. The application consists of a web server and a MySQL database server running inside the data center. The company would like to move the application to the AWS Cloud, and needs to select a cost-effective database platform that will not require database modifications.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Emergency loads are unpredictable, databases cannot be changed and costs are critical. MySQL-compatible Aurora Servers is the best solution to this problem: applications can run without modifications, capacity will automatically expand to respond to peaks at the beginning of the month and week, and then automatically shrink during low loads, so companies do not have to pay for peak capacity on a continuous basis.
Option A: DynamoDB is a non-relative storage: queries and data models need to be rewrited.
Option B: RDS for MySQL needs to select an example type for a peak load and to continue to pay for the example, even if there is no actual load.
Option D: Relationship database cannot be extended through the EC2 Autoscaling Group: new examples do not share bottom data.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora Serverless
MySQL deployed on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group

question_text:
An image-hosting company stores its objects in Amazon S3 buckets. The company wants to avoid accidental exposure of the objects in the S3 buckets to the public. All S3 objects in the entire AWS account need to remain private.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is that none of the objects in the account as a whole should be made public, even if the strategy is wrongly configured. The first level is the account level S3 to block public access: it will cover any public ACL or storage barrel strategy, regardless of content. The second layer is a SCP, which rejects s3: PutAccountPublicAccessBlock (and disables stop settings on individual S3 buckets) and is therefore unable to close the settings from inside the account. This is a form of preventive protection, not an after-action test.
Option A: GuardDuty analyzes threats and suspicious activities, but does not monitor the storage barrel strategy or roll it back.
Option B: Trusted Advisor found and sent a notification after the incident, and the repair still needs to be manual. Data may be exposed during this period.
Option C: Resources Access Manager shares resources between accounts and is not relevant to the discovery of open S3 buckets.

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor S3 bucket policies. Create an automatic remediation action rule that uses an AWS Lambda function to remediate any change that makes the objects public.

Use AWS Trusted Advisor to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Configure email notifications in Trusted Advisor when a change is detected. Manually change the S3 bucket policy if it allows public access.

Use AWS Resource Access Manager to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a change is detected. Deploy a Lambda function that programmatically remediates the change.

Use the S3 Block Public Access feature on the account level. Use AWS Organizations to create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents IAM users from changing the setting. Apply the SCP to the account.

question_text:
An ecommerce company is experiencing an increase in user traffic. The company’s store is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances as a two-tier web application consisting of a web tier and a separate database tier. As traffic increases, the company notices that the architecture is causing significant delays in sending timely marketing and order confirmation email to users. The company wants to reduce the time it spends resolving complex email delivery issues and minimize operational overhead.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The problem was mail delivery, and the company wished to stop dealing with its complexity. Amazon SES is a hosting mail service: the sender's reputation, delivery queues, rejections and complaints are handled by the service — the application simply calls API.
Option A: Specialized e-mail EC2 instances leave all delivery complexities on the company and add more infrastructure.
Option C: SNS sends a notice to the subscriber, but it is not a complete client-oriented mail delivery tool: no template, no reputation management.
Option D: Same as option A, except for Auto Scaling: Operating costs will not decrease, but will increase.

options.text: Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing.
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).
Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing. Place the instances in an Auto Scaling group.

question_text:
A company has a business system that generates hundreds of reports each day. The business system saves the reports to a network share in CSV format. The company needs to store this data in the AWS Cloud in near-real time for analysis.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
explanation_en:
The business system can only write data into a network shared directory, cannot modify them, and data need to be transferred to the cloud in near real time. S3 File Gateway is exactly the type of web-sharing directory that is available, but each file that it saves is moved to an object S3 — essentially done in real time and without having to create any automated code. The system simply points to a new shared directory.
Option A: Tasks performed once a day are not near real time: reports need to be processed until the end of the day.
Option C: A custom application to call DataSync API requires the preparation and maintenance of a code, while the gateway can perform the same function without any code.
Option D: The script that monitors new files and uploads them through SFTP is once again a custom automation, with its own problems of failure and retry management.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create a scheduled task that runs at the end of each day.
Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway. Update the business system to use a new network share from the S3 File Gateway.
Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create an application that uses the DataSync API in the automation workflow.
Deploy an AWS Transfer for SFTP endpoint. Create a script that checks for new files on the network share and uploads the new files by using SFTP.

question_text:
A company is storing petabytes of data in Amazon S3 Standard. The data is stored in multiple S3 buckets and is accessed with varying frequency. The company does not know access patterns for all the data. The company needs to implement a solution for each S3 bucket to optimize the cost of S3 usage.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
When access mode is unknown, the mode is "MOST accessal economy". Inteligent-Tiering does not need to analyse or make decisions manually: it monitors access to each object and moves between levels without any search costs. Each drum requires only one life cycle rule to manage several bytes of data. Please note that objects less than 128 KB will never move to the archive level and will always be charged to the level of frequent access.
Option B: Storage class analysis generates only one report. Moving objects bytes based on their results must be done manually, and repeated operations are required each time a mode of access is changed - this is the most expensive operation of all options.
Option C: Glacier Instant Retrieval provides instant access, but will incur obvious search costs and have a minimum storage period of 90 days. Some of the byte data are frequently read, and the cost is ultimately higher than that of Standard.
Option D: A Zone-IA reduces error tolerance to a single area with a fee for retrieval - this is a bad option for access to data that is not known in the mode.

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 Intelligent- Tiering.
Use the S3 storage class analysis tool to determine the correct tier for each object in the S3 bucket. Move each object to the identified storage tier.
Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration with a rule to transition the objects in the S3 bucket to S3 One Zone- Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).

question_text:
A rapidly growing global ecommerce company is hosting its web application on AWS. The web application includes static content and dynamic content. The website stores online transaction processing (OLTP) data in an Amazon RDS database The website’s users are experiencing slow page loads.
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to resolve this issue? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Pages are loaded slowly from two sources. CloudFront accelerates static content and some dynamic content: content is cached at the edge, requesting transmission to the area via the AWS backbone network (B). Read-only copies of RDS share the load of the database, absorb the search and release the main example for transaction processing
Option A: Redshift is an analytical data repository that is not related to the speed at which the pages of the transactional website are loaded.
Option C: Dynamic content by definition cannot be hosted in S3: it is generated by an application.
Option E: Multi-AZ configuration increases usability, but the backup case does not process the request and therefore does not enhance performance.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Redshift cluster.
Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution.
Host the dynamic web content in Amazon S3.
Create a read replica for the RDS DB instance.
Configure a Multi-AZ deployment for the RDS DB instance.

question_text:
A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions to run its application. The company has VPCs with public subnets and private subnets in its AWS account. The EC2 instances run in a private subnet in one of the VPCs. The Lambda functions need direct network access to the EC2 instances for the application to work.
The application will run for at least 1 year. The company expects the number of Lambda functions that the application uses to increase during that time. The company wants to maximize its savings on all application resources and to keep network latency between the services low.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The company needs to save costs on examples and functions, and functions need to be directly networked to access examples. The calculation savings plan covers EC2, Lambda and Fargate, and provides discounts for all calculations of the application. Direct access comes from the same private subnet that connects a function to an instance - the flow is kept in VPC and the delay is minimal.
Option A: The EC2 instance economy plan only provides discounts for the example only: in the case of an increasing number of functions, the cost of the function remains at the full price.
Option B: The same limited savings scheme, which connects functions to the public subnet does not bring them closer to the example - simply adds to the complexity of the route.
Option D: Stay in the VPC service in Lambda means that the function does not have direct access to the network in the private subnet.

options.text: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage and the number of invocations. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnet that contains the EC2 instances.

Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan Optimize the Lambda functions' duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Connect the Lambda functions to a public subnet in the same VPC where the EC2 instances run.

Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnet that contains the EC2 instances.

Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Optimize the Lambda functions’ duration and memory usage, the number of invocations, and the amount of data that is transferred. Keep the Lambda functions in the Lambda service VPC.

question_text:
A solutions architect needs to allow team members to access Amazon S3 buckets in two different AWS accounts:
a development account and a production account. The team currently has access to S3 buckets in the development account by using unique IAM users that are assigned to an IAM group that has appropriate permissions in the account.
The solutions architect has created an IAM role in the production account. The role has a policy that grants access to an S3 bucket in the production account.
Which solution will meet these requirements while complying with the principle of least privilege?
explanation_en:
Classic cross-account access is not achieved by copying the user - it is based on a role: the target account has a role that has the right to store drums, and the role ' s confidence strategy lists the subjects that allow the assumption of that role. The role in the production environment already exists, so the remaining task is to add the development account as the subject to its trust policy (and to allow users to assume the role by sts: AssumeRole on the side of the development account). Users remain in a single account and are issued temporary vouchers during sessions, with privileges limited to what is awarded by the role strategy - which is in line with the principle of minimum privileges.
Option A: Administrator Access grants full access to the entire development account and does not open the S3 buckets in the production environment. This is a direct violation of the principle of minimum competence.
Option C: Closing the public access limit exposes the drums to the outside world and has nothing to do with granting team access. It is a security degradation, not a solution.
Option D: Separation of users in a production environment means that each person needs to create, rotate and cancel a long-term group of vouchers. The role solves the same problem by means of a temporary certificate.

options.text: Attach the Administrator Access policy to the development account users.
Add the development account as a principal in the trust policy of the role in the production account.
Turn off the S3 Block Public Access feature on the S3 bucket in the production account.
Create a user in the production account with unique credentials for each team member.

question_text:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and runs multiple Amazon EC2 workloads in the ap-southeast-2 Region. The company has a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any resources from being created in any other Region. A security policy requires the company to encrypt all data at rest.
An audit discovers that employees have created Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for EC2 instances without encrypting the volumes. The company wants any new EC2 instances that any IAM user or root user launches in ap-southeast-2 to use encrypted EBS volumes. The company wants a solution that will have minimal effect on employees who create EBS volumes.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Reference answer: CE; dispute option: AC.
Option E describes a non-existent settings: the default EBS encryption is enabled separately by account and region (belongs to EC2 settings), not at the Organization's Management Account level - the correct pairs are A and C.
EBS encryption by default is an account-by-account, region-by-area EC2 setting and is not an organization-wide switch for an Organization management account, so the E in the original CE does not exist. Enables the default encryption A for each account to avoid disrupting the normal creation process; in conjunction with SCP, rejecting unencrypted creation as forming an organisation-level constraint, change to an AC.
Source answer for original CE resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
This issue was marked as controversial, as there was a problem with the presentation of one of the options. The intended solution is to ban the creation of unencrypted volumes for all users (including root users of member accounts), only through a SCP with an ec2: Encrypted condition equal to false(C) - the account's own administrator can rewrite the IAM policy at any time and the permission boundaries cannot be attached to the organizational unit. The other part is to make encryption undetected when it is used: the default EBS encryption means that new volumes are automatically encrypted and that users are not subject to rejected requests. But the key is that this is configured separately by account and region (option A), while option E, as described in the answer key, is used as an organizational management account setting, but in practice the organization management account does not exist.
Source old option A: This is actually an accurate description of the default encryption configuration: an account attribute in the EC2 console plus a default KMS key. That's why options A and C are more accurate than the answer keys to the subject.
Source old option B: Permission borders are attached to the user or character and limit the maximum permissions. It cannot be attached to an organizational unit.
Source old option D: The IAM policy in each account can be changed by the account ' s own administrator and is not suitable for the root user of the account. This does not provide any preventive guarantees.

options.text: In the Amazon EC2 console, select the EBS encryption account attribute and define a default encryption key.

Create an IAM permission boundary. Attach the permission boundary to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the boundary to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Create an SCP. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the SCP to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action whenthe ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Update the IAM policies for each account to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
In the Organizations management account, specify the Default EBS volume encryption setting.

question_text:
A company wants to use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB cluster to simplify time-consuming database administrative tasks for production database workloads. The company wants to ensure that its database is highly available and will provide automatic failover support in most scenarios in less than 40 seconds. The company wants to offload reads off of the primary instance and keep costs as low as possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The key requirement is that the failure switch be completed within 40 seconds and that the read load share be achieved at the lowest cost. A multi-usable RDS database cluster (Multi-AZ) contains one main example and two alternative examples, which are also readable when running simultaneously: the failure switch is usually completed within approximately 35 seconds, and all reading traffic can be accessed by way of the reading end, without the need for additional examples.
Option A: The failure switch for deployment in a multi-usable area (Multi-AZ) database takes between one and two minutes, and reading a copy is another example of what you need to pay for.
Option B: The cluster selection is correct, but two additional reading copies are redundant: the cluster nodes are already readable in themselves and the requirements are the lowest.
Option C: In multi-usable area (Multi-AZ) database case deployment, the backup case does not process the request.

options.text: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB duster deployment Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instances in the Multi-AZ pair.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.

question_text:
A company runs a highly available SFTP service. The SFTP service uses two Amazon EC2 Linux instances that run with elastic IP addresses to accept traffic from trusted IP sources on the internet. The SFTP service is backed by shared storage that is attached to the instances. User accounts are created and managed as Linux users in the SFTP servers.
The company wants a serverless option that provides high IOPS performance and highly configurable security. The company also wants to maintain control over user permissions.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Requirements include no server service, high I/O performance, finely configured security, and continuous control of user privileges. AWS Transport Family eliminates the need for self-managed examples, stores an encrypted EFS file system with familiar POSIX privileges, and endpoints are deployed within VPC, with Internet-oriented access and flexible IP addresses, so that a security group can be attached to allow access to a trusted address only.
Option A: EBS Volume cannot be attached to Transfer Family Service: S3 and EFS are only supported as storage. Public endpoints are also not allowed to apply security units.
Option C: S3 as a storage backend does not provide familiar POSIX privileges and does not have the same I/O performance features, and the public endpoint will remove the ability to exercise precision control over network access through the security team.
Option D: Endpoints that are located in a private subnet and are not accessible on the Internet will prevent access to a trusted source on the public Internet that is explicitly required in the scene.

options.text: Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EBS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with elastic IP addresses and a VPC endpoint that has internet-facing access. Attach a security group to the endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the EFS volume to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a public endpoint that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption enabled. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP service with a VPC endpoint that has internal access in a private subnet. Attach a security group that allows only trusted IP addresses. Attach the S3 bucket to the SFTP service endpoint. Grant users access to the SFTP service.

question_text:
A company is developing a new machine learning (ML) model solution on AWS. The models are developed as independent microservices that fetch approximately 1 GB of model data from Amazon S3 at startup and load the data into memory. Users access the models through an asynchronous API. Users can send a request or a batch of requests and specify where the results should be sent.
The company provides models to hundreds of users. The usage patterns for the models are irregular. Some models could be unused for days or weeks. Other models could receive batches of thousands of requests at a time.
Which design should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
SQS buffers a large number of irregular motions, and ECS services can be consumed in queues and scaled up to the depths of queues; title C The so-called increase in the number of vCPUs in Lambda by Queue Size by Auto Scaling is not an effective independent scaling mechanism. D better meets the requirements of long idle and sudden requests.
The load pattern is extremely uneven: a model may remain idle for weeks and then suddenly receives tens of thousands of requests. A SQS queue receives and temporarily saves all requests, while the model is used as an ECS service to read data from the queue; expansion based on the length of the queue increases both the number of service examples and the cluster capacity. Packagings are the best option because each model will load approximately one gybyte of data into the memory at start-up - in the packaging, this operation will be performed only once throughout the mission life cycle.
Option A: A network load balancer cannot call the Lambda function as the target, and loading data with one gigabyte at each cold start of the function results in a serious deterioration of the delay.
Option B: The load balancer in front of the queue reading service is unnecessary and App Mesh is a service grid for traffic routers - it does not handle cluster expansion.
Option C: The number of vCPUs in the Lambda function cannot be adjusted by automatic extension (set in the in-house configuration) and the model that saves a gjibytes size in the memory does not match the Lambda execution model.

options.text: Direct the requests from the API to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by the NLB.

Direct the requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use AWS App Mesh to scale the instances of the ECS cluster based on the SQS queue size.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by SQS events. Use AWS Auto Scaling to increase the number of vCPUs for the Lambda functions based on the SQS queue size.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from the queue. Enable AWS Auto Scaling on Amazon ECS for both the cluster and copies of the service based on the queue size.

question_text:
A company is running a custom application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. The application has frontend nodes that need to run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and backend nodes that need to run only for a short time based on workload. The number of backend nodes varies during the day.
The company needs to scale out and scale in more instances based on workload.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Two different load configurations require two different modes of purchase. The front end is running on a continuous and predictable basis, and therefore the deepest discount is provided by the retention of examples. The back end is only briefly activated, the number of machines changes in one day and the interruption is acceptable — this points to the use of competitive examples, with discounts of up to 90 per cent.
Option A: The cost of using Fargate at the back end is higher than the use of competitive examples at the same break tolerance.
Option C: The use of competitive examples at the front end of a continuous operation is a risk: AWS can recover the capacity at any time and it is not cost-effective to reserve the capacity for variable loads.
Option D: This combines a higher-risk competitive front end with a more expensive Fargate back end for variable work loads.

options.text: Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.
Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Spot Instances for the backend nodes.
Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Reserved Instances for the backend nodes.
Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.

question_text:
A company uses high block storage capacity to runs its workloads on premises. The company's daily peak input and output transactions per second are not more than 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the workloads to Amazon EC2 and to provision disk performance independent of storage capacity.
Which Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume type will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The key requirement is that the provision of performance must be independent of the storage capacity, with a peak of 15,000 IOPS. This is the configuration of the gp3 volume: the basic performance is 3,000 IOPS already included in the price, and the IOPS can be increased to 16,000 without relying on the volume size. gp3 costs less than gp2 per gy bytes, far less than the volume of the IOPS configuration.
Option A: gp2 functions closely aligned to size - 3 IOPS per Gycete - so to reach 15,000 IOPS, a volume of 5 TB is required.
Option B:io2 meets this requirement, but the cost is significantly higher and is only reasonable when tens of thousands of IOPS or more of the rolls are required.
Option D:io1 is the product of the previous generation that configured the IOPS volume: it is also more expensive than gp3 and lags behind io2 on specifications.

io2 volume type
GP3 volume type
io1 volume type

question_text:
A company needs to store data from its healthcare application. The application’s data frequently changes. A new regulation requires audit access at all levels of the stored data.
The company hosts the application on an on-premises infrastructure that is running out of storage capacity. A solutions architect must securely migrate the existing data to AWS while satisfying the new regulation.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is to move the accumulated data safely and to conduct audit visits at the data level. AWS DataSync encrypts the transmission, validates the data integrity and moves the file to S3, while the data event log of CloudTrail records the reading and writing operations of each object - as required by the statute. Managing the incident log does not provide this level of detail.
Option B: Snowcone's capacity is applied to several bytes of data and one-time transfers, and the managing event log cannot capture access to the object itself.
Option C: The speed of the transmission accelerates the speed of upload, but is not used to transport existing data sets and validate data integrity; the log portion of this option is correct.
Option D:Storage Gateway is a long-term hybrid cloud gateway, not a migration tool, and the managing event log does not cover access to data.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log data events.
Use AWS Snowcone to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log management events.
Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log data events.
Use AWS Storage Gateway to move the existing data to Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to log management events.

question_text:
A solutions architect is implementing a complex Java application with a MySQL database. The Java application must be deployed on Apache Tomcat and must be highly available.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Java applications under Tomcat need to be migrated in their original form and ensure high availability. Elastic Beanstalk provides an off-the-shelf Tomcat platform: it will self-configure load balancers and multi-usable area auto-extension teams and manage updates, and a rolling deployment strategy will enable new releases to be released without interruption of service.
Option A: Move complex Tomcat applications to Lambda means that the entire application needs to be rewritten from scratch.
Option C: ElastiCache is a memory cache service that cannot replace a relationship-type MySQL database.
Option D: Run MySQL on the same example as the application and the example is located in the Auto-extend group, which results in inconsistent copies of the data and does not allow for real high availability.

options.text: Deploy the application in AWS Lambda. Configure an Amazon API Gateway API to connect with the Lambda functions.
Deploy the application by using AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Configure a load-balanced environment and a rolling deployment policy.
Migrate the database to Amazon ElastiCache. Configure the ElastiCache security group to allow access from the application.
Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Install a MySQL server on the EC2 instance. Configure the application on the server. Create an AMI. Use the AMI to create a launch template with an Auto Scaling group.

question_text:
A serverless application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB. The Lambda function needs permissions to read and write to the DynamoDB table.
Which solution will give the Lambda function access to the DynamoDB table MOST securely?
explanation_en:
The safest way to grant any AWS service is to use a role, not a long-term valid key. Roles must be trusted in its trust strategy (principal lmbda.amazonaws.com) and carry strategies that contain the required operations (e.g. dynamodb: GetItem and PutItem), which are limited to specific tables and assigned to function as their executive role. The resulting evidence is temporary and automatically rotates, and the code or environment variable does not contain any key.
Option A: The access key in the environment variable is a long-term key that is visible to any person who can read the function configuration and is entirely your responsibility for the rotation.
Option C: Store the same key in the parameter storage simply hides it: once the key is leaked, it remains valid, while the role provides temporary proof and there is no need to store the key anywhere.
Option D: Role requires trust in Lambda service, not DynamoDB: The trust strategy defines who can assume the role. And the role cannot be added from inside the function code -- it is set in the configuration.

options.text: Create an IAM user with programmatic access to the Lambda function. Attach a policy to the user that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Store the access_key_id and secret_access_key parameters as part of the Lambda environment variables. Ensure that other AWS users do not have read and write access to the Lambda function configuration.

Create an IAM role that includes Lambda as a trusted service. Attach a policy to the role that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Update the configuration of the Lambda function to use the new role as the execution role.

Create an IAM user with programmatic access to the Lambda function. Attach a policy to the user that allows read and write access to the DynamoDB table. Store the access_key_id and secret_access_key parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as secure string parameters. Update the Lambda function code to retrieve the secure string parameters before connecting to the DynamoDB table.

Create an IAM role that includes DynamoDB as a trusted service. Attach a policy to the role that allows read and write access from the Lambda function. Update the code of the Lambda function to attach to the new role as an execution role.

question_text:
A manufacturing company has machine sensors that upload .csv files to an Amazon S3 bucket. These .csv files must be converted into images and must be made available as soon as possible for the automatic generation of graphical reports.
The images become irrelevant after 1 month, but the .csv files must be kept to train machine learning (ML) models twice a year. The ML trainings and audits are planned weeks in advance.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Pictures are needed immediately after uploading - This requires an event-driven Lambda function that triggers a file when it appears, without question-taking or free machine (B). From there, the life-cycle strategy addresses the rest: images become useless and directly obsolete after a month, and source documents are used for pre-planned training only twice a year, so that they can be converted to S3 Glacier after one day to provide the cheapest storage, while still meeting acceptable lead times (C).
Option A: Examples of documents downloaded hourly violate the requirement of "immediate processing" and add unnecessary infrastructure.
Option D: S3 One Zone-IA is more expensive than Glacier and keeps the data in a single available area - an unnecessary risk for the only copy of training data.
Option E: S3 Standard-IA is clearly more expensive than Glacier, and reduced redundancy storage is discarded and no longer recommended.

options.text: Launch an Amazon EC2 Spot Instance that downloads the .csv files every hour, generates the image files, and uploads the images to the S3 bucket.
Design an AWS Lambda function that converts the .csv files into images and stores the images in the S3 bucket. Invoke the Lambda function when a .csv file is uploaded.

Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier 1 day after they are uploaded. Expire the image files after 30 days.

Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) 1 day after they are uploaded. Expire the image files after 30 days.

Create S3 Lifecycle rules for .csv files and image files in the S3 bucket. Transition the .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) 1 day after they are uploaded. Keep the image files in Reduced Redundancy Storage (RRS).

question_text:
A company has developed a new video game as a web application. The application is in a three-tier architecture in a VPC with Amazon RDS for MySQL in the database layer. Several players will compete concurrently online. The game’s developers want to display a top-10 scoreboard in near-real time and offer the ability to stop and restore the game while preserving the current scores.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Demand is the persistence of near real-time rankings and the number of minutes when the game is stopped/restarted. ElastiCache for Redis meets these two requirements: the sorting assembly can calculate the top 10 in submarisecond time, and the redis disk durability and copying function can be restored after restart.
Option A: Memcached does not have a sorting data structure for ranking, nor does it have data sustainability: the score will be lost when the game is restarted.
Option C: ClaudFront Caches at edge position, but the ranking will change and distribution will not be able to calculate the ranking.
Option D: Read a copy to divert traffic, but recalculating the top 10 is still slow by executing thousands of queries per second on the relational database.

options.text: Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster to cache the scores for the web application to display.
Set up an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to compute and cache the scores for the web application to display.
Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the web application to cache the scoreboard in a section of the application.
Create a read replica on Amazon RDS for MySQL to run queries to compute the scoreboard and serve the read traffic to the web application.

question_text:
An ecommerce company wants to use machine learning (ML) algorithms to build and train models. The company will use the models to visualize complex scenarios and to detect trends in customer data. The architecture team wants to integrate its ML models with a reporting platform to analyze the augmented data and use the data directly in its business intelligence dashboards.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Requirements include both model training and dashboards, with minimal operation. Amazon SageMaker is responsible for modelling and hosting, while Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence service that can call the SageMaker model and display enhanced data directly on the dashboard.
Option A: AWS Glue ML transportsform only solves the narrow task of finding duplicate records, whereas OpenSearch Service is the search engine, not the reporting platform.
Option C: Pre-constructed AMI from Marketplace implies the need for self-management, patching and maintenance - contrary to demand.
Option D: QuickSight calculation fields are formulae; they cannot be used to train machine learning models.

options.text: Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
Use a pre-built ML Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.

question_text:
A company is running its production and nonproduction environment workloads in multiple AWS accounts. The accounts are in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company needs to design a solution that will prevent the modification of cost usage tags.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is to prevent changes in cost-allocation labels in each account in the organization, unless they are made by a particular credible entity. Only SCP can enforce this boundary: it applies to all subjects in member accounts, including their root users, and cannot be bypassed by local IAM strategies. Usually, this is done by rejecting the actions of tag:* or ec2: CreateTags and ec2: DeleteTags, and by the conditions of tagkey and the anomalies of the main role of the allowed modification aws:PrincipalArn.
Option A: AWSConfig compares configuration to rules and reports non-compliance after operation. It does not stop this operation when calling.
Option B: CloudTrail records who called what operation. It is just a journal, not an implementation mechanism.
Option D: Cloudwatch Logs for Logs. It does not have any restrictions on operations that can be performed in AWS.

options.text: Create a custom AWS Config rule to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create a custom trail in AWS CloudTrail to prevent tag modification.
Create a service control policy (SCP) to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create custom Amazon CloudWatch logs to prevent tag modification.

question_text:
A company hosts its application in the AWS Cloud. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Elastic Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group and with an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company wants to ensure the application can be made available in anotherAWS Region with minimal downtime.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of downtime?
explanation_en:
The key phrase is "the minimum stop time". This means that infrastructure in disaster recovery areas must have existed before the failure occurred, rather than after the failure: the auto-expansion group and load balancer have been deployed, DynamoDB global tables continue to copy data to two regions, while Route 53 records the switchover through a health screening strategy. The recovery time depends on the TTL recorded in DNS.
Option B: Deployment of the CloudFormation stack after a failure means that a few minutes to ten minutes will have to wait, plus DynamoDB tables still need to be filled with data. The stop time is essentially longer.
Option C: There is no problem here at the data level (global table), but the computing layer is still created from the template at the time of the disaster, so the switch speed is slower than the option of having an automatic extension group deployed.
Option D: The infrastructure exists before the failure occurs, but switching through the claudwatch alert and a Lombda function that updates Route 53 records introduces additional delays and complex logic rather than relying on built-in health check failure switching strategies.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group and a load balancer in the disaster recovery Region. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.

Create an AWS CloudFormation template to create EC2 instances, load balancers, and DynamoDB tables to be launched when needed Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.

Create an AWS CloudFormation template to create EC2 instances and a load balancer to be launched when needed. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Configure DNS failover to point to the new disaster recovery Region's load balancer.

Create an Auto Scaling group and load balancer in the disaster recovery Region. Configure the DynamoDB table as a global table. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to trigger an AWS Lambda function that updates Amazon Route 53 pointing to the disaster recovery load balancer.

question_text:
A company needs to migrate a MySQL database from its on-premises data center to AWS within 2 weeks. The database is 20 TB in size. The company wants to complete the migration with minimal downtime.
Which solution will migrate the database MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Twenty-bytes of data that were migrated within two weeks and stopped very briefly are a classic combination: the complete data load is transmitted via Snowball Edge Service Optimized devices, while the cumulative changes during the transmission are synchronized by the continuous copying function of AWS DMS. When a copy is delayed to zero, the application is switched to the new database - the shut-down window is only in minutes. The selection of Storage Optimized is because the task is purely about data volume.
Option B: Snowmobile is a truck designed for dozens of bytes. For 20 TB data volume, it is too costly and is scheduled over a long period of time.
Option C: GPU Accelerator Equipment applies to local calculations (e.g. machine learning, video processing) at higher cost. No computing tasks are required in this scenario.
Option D: A dedicated connection is suitable for a permanent infrastructure, rather than a one-time migration option: it usually takes more than two weeks to be configured and you will have to pay for several months of port costs.

options.text: Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with replication of ongoing changes. Send the Snowball Edge device to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication.

Order an AWS Snowmobile vehicle. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with ongoing changes. Send the Snowmobile vehicle back to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication.

Order an AWS Snowball Edge Compute Optimized with GPU device. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with ongoing changes. Send the Snowball device to AWS to finish the migration and continue the ongoing replication

Order a 1 GB dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection to establish a connection with the data center. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to migrate the database with replication of ongoing changes.

question_text:
A company moved its on-premises PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company successfully launched a new product. The workload on the database has increased. The company wants to accommodate the larger workload without adding infrastructure.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
This condition clearly excludes the addition of infrastructure, and the only way to increase growth is to expand upwards: to expand the specifications of existing examples. In order to make the expansion cost-effective, examples of pre-set databases for stable work loads were purchased — discounts of over 60 per cent compared to needs-based pricing.
Option B: Multi-usable areas increase availability but do not enhance performance: alternative cases do not process requests, but are subject to double costs.
Option C: The second example of a database is the new infrastructure that this condition explicitly excludes.
Option D: A needs-based pricing is the most expensive option and cannot cope with the increase in the workload.

options.text: Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance larger.
Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance a Multi-AZ DB instance.
