question_text:
A company stores data in Amazon S3. According to regulations, the data must not contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company recently discovered that S3 buckets have some objects that contain PII. The company needs to automatically detect PII in S3 buckets and to notify the company’s security team.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Testing of personal data in S3 is Macie ' s responsibility, while sending notifications to the person concerned is SNS 's responsibility. This is standard mode: Macie posts the discovery results to EventBridge, a rule filters events according to the SensiveData type and sends messages to the SNS theme that the security team subscribes to. Please note the key difference between the options: SQS places the message in the queue and a person still needs to read it manually, and the SNS theme sends the notice immediately, for example by e-mail.
Option B: GuardDutiy is used to find signs of invasion rather than to test personal data inside the object. Selects the type of error found.
Option C: Service selection is correct and filtering conditions are more precise, but the SQS queue does not inform people - it requires consumers. SNS is the tool used to alert the team.
Option D: Both service selection and notification delivery are incorrect.

options.text: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.

question_text:
A company wants to build a logging solution for its multiple AWS accounts. The company currently stores the logs from all accounts in a centralized account. The company has created an Amazon S3 bucket in the centralized account to store the VPC flow logs and AWS CloudTrail logs. All logs must be highly available for 30 days for frequent analysis, retained for an additional 60 days for backup purposes, and deleted 90 days after creation.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Logs require frequent access during the first 30 days, the next 60 days are retained as backup and deleted on the 90th day. This means they can move to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval on the 30th day — the cheapest suitable storage category. Even taking into account the cost of a 90-day minimum storage period, this is cheaper than retaining the data in the total remaining 60 days in the Standard-Infrequent Access.
Option A: Migration to the Standard class, where the current object is already in, will not change anything, nor will it save costs.
Option B: Standard-IA costs higher per GB than the archive category, while removing migration to Glacier at the same time on day 90 is futile - a rule that contradicts itself.
Option D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single available area, which contradicts the high availability requirement and also has the same contradictory rule on day 90.

options.text: Transition objects to the S3 Standard storage class 30 days after creation. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

Transition objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class 30 days after creation. Move all objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class after 90 days. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.
Transition objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class 30 days after creation. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

Transition objects to the S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) storage class 30 days after creation. Move all objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class after 90 days. Write an expiration action that directs Amazon S3 to delete objects after 90 days.

question_text:
A company is building an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster for its workloads. All secrets that are stored in Amazon EKS must be encrypted in the Kubernetes etcd key-value store.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
This requirement is very specific: Kubernetes keys must be encrypted in the EKS cluster's etcd storage. There is a dedicated function for this case - Envelope encryption using KMS keys: this function is enabled by specifying a client-managed key in a cluster, and EKS encrypts key objects before writing them to etcd. Do not confuse this with the key of the storage application: AWS Securitys Manager stores them in its own service and has no effect on the content of etcd.
Option A: Secrets Manager stores the key in its own service and does not encrypt the contents of the cluster etcd. The request is specific to etcd.
Option C: EBS CSI driver to attach the volume to Pod. It has nothing to do with the encryption of the Secret object in the control plane storage.
Option D: The default EBS volume encryption is protected by the node disk instead of the etcd that controls the plane, which is managed by EKS itself.

options.text: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to manage, rotate, and store all secrets in Amazon EKS.
Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Enable Amazon EKS KMS secrets encryption on the Amazon EKS cluster.
Create the Amazon EKS cluster with default options. Use the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver as an add-on.
Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key with the alias/aws/ebs alias. Enable default Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume encryption for the account.

question_text:
A company wants to provide data scientists with near real-time read-only access to the company's production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The database is currently configured as a Single-AZ database. The data scientists use complex queries that will not affect the production database. The company needs a solution that is highly available.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Reference answer: C; dispute option: D.
A multi-usable area database cluster (D) with two repertoire-readable examples achieved high availability and reading endpoints using three examples, while option C used four examples.
RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster provides a writer and two readable standby, and reader endpoint, while meeting the high availability and report-only isolation. Original C requires Multi-AZ integration to add two more read studies, usually with more examples; D is more cost-effective without specifying specifications and prices.
Source answer C's original resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
Three elements must be met simultaneously: high availability, provision of a separate area for re-search, and minimal cost. The key answer is C: The deployment of multi-usable area examples provides usability, with two read-only copies serving analysts — four in total. This is controversial because option D solves the same problem with three examples: one multi-usable area database cluster deployment, with two repertoires of readable cases, providing both automatic failovers and reading endpoints for analysts. According to the current document, D is cheaper and simpler, and most communities choose it. It is important to distinguish between two types of multi-usable area deployment: case deployment with non-readable back-up examples, while cluster deployment with readable back-up examples.
Old Source Option A: Extension of a single case does not provide any high availability at all, and the analyst's re-examination still has direct access to the production database — this is precisely what the title requires to avoid.
Source old option B: In multi-usable area example deployment, the backup example is not readable: it cannot be connected to it for query. This option describes what does not exist in this type of deployment.
Source old option D: A strong alternative, with a better answer: using only three examples instead of four, with high availability and built-in reading endpoints. The description of this option predates the introduction of multi-usable database clusters to support readable alternative examples, so it selects C.

options.text: Scale the existing production database in a maintenance window to provide enough power for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment with a larger secondary standby instance. Provide the data scientists access to the secondary instance.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment. Provide two additional read replicas for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ cluster deployment with two readable standby instances. Provide read endpoints to the data scientists.

question_text:
A company runs a three-tier web application in the AWS Cloud that operates across three Availability Zones. The application architecture has an Application Load Balancer, an Amazon EC2 web server that hosts user session states, and a MySQL database that runs on an EC2 instance. The company expects sudden increases in application traffic. The company wants to be able to scale to meet future application capacity demands and to ensure high availability across all three Availability Zones.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Extension capacity across all three available areas is required, as well as high availability. The migration of the database to the DB cluster deployment of the RDS for MySQL multi-usable area, the migration of the Web layer to the auto-extension group across the three available areas, the migration of the session status from the example to ElastiCache for Redis: Redis supports copying and auto-facing transfer, and therefore the loss of a node does not mean that the session is lost.
Option B: Memcached does not copy data, nor does it have a high-availability mode: a failure of a node means that the session data stored on that node will be lost.
Option C: The migration of MySQL to DynamoDB means that data models and queries need to be redesigned, which is not consistent with the requirements.
Option D: Databases located in a single available area directly violate the high availability requirement.

options.text: Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon DynamoDB Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache reads. Store the session data in DynamoDB. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL in a single Availability Zone. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

question_text:
A global video streaming company uses Amazon CloudFront as a content distribution network (CDN). The company wants to roll out content in a phased manner across multiple countries. The company needs to ensure that viewers who are outside the countries to which the company rolls out content are not able to view the content.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
CloudFront can limit access based on the requesting country: distribution of a list of allowed countries is configured, and users from any other country receive a custom-defined rejection page. The phased roll-out of content to countries simply means that the list is gradually being edited over time.
Option B: Sign URLs and Cookies will limit access by a specific user, but no country can be identified.
Option C: Encrypt to protect the data, but cannot prevent anyone who has access rights through an application from viewing the content - it does not provide geographical limitations.
Option D: Time-bound links control the duration of the access, rather than the location of the viewer.

options.text: Add geographic restrictions to the content in CloudFront by using an allow list. Set up a custom error message.
Set up a new URL tor restricted content. Authorize access by using a signed URL and cookies. Set up a custom error message.
Encrypt the data for the content that the company distributes. Set up a custom error message.
Create a new URL for restricted content. Set up a time-restricted access policy for signed URLs.

question_text:
A company wants to use the AWS Cloud to improve its on-premises disaster recovery (DR) configuration. The company's core production business application uses Microsoft SQL Server Standard, which runs on a virtual machine (VM). The application has a recovery point objective (RPO) of 30 seconds or fewer and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 60 minutes. The DR solution needs to minimize costs wherever possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The 30-second recovery point target excludes night backup, while the one-hour recovery time target means that no active-active setting is required. Continuous change data capture copying through AWS DMS to maintain RDS for SQL Server ' s hot state with a delay in seconds and a failure switch can be completed within minutes. This will also allow you to continue using the standard version and will only have to pay for one small example.
Option A: The consistently available availability group requires an enterprise version — a license change — and active-active configuration is the most costly of all options.
Option C: AWS elastic disaster recovery is a viable method to copy disks, but using small-scale configurations means recovery times are longer, and you still need to purchase SQL Server licences on your own; the key difference is that service-level copying is more reliable to the database than block copying.
Option D: The daily backup recovery point is a full day, four orders of magnitude different than the 30-second requirement.

options.text: Configure a multi-site active/active setup between the on-premises server and AWS by using Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise with Always On availability groups.
Configure a warm standby Amazon RDS for SQL Server database on AWS. Configure AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to use change data capture (CDC).
Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery configured to replicate disk changes to AWS as a pilot light.
Use third-party backup software to capture backups every night. Store a secondary set of backups in Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company has an on-premises server that uses an Oracle database to process and store customer information.
The company wants to use an AWS database service to achieve higher availability and to improve application performance. The company also wants to offload reporting from its primary database system.
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
explanation_en:
Inaccuracy in the presentation of the title: Multi-usable Area Database Cluster deployment in Amazon RDS only supports MySQL and PostgreSQL - there is no such pattern for Oracle. Nevertheless, of the options given, C remains the best option, as it provides the only independent example of high availability and use for reporting.
The RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ DB cluster specified in original option C is not supported. Multi-AZ DB cluster only supports RDS for MySQL and RDS for PostgreSQL; this is not a valid option for Oracle, high-availability and read-only reports. The source reference answer should be retained for identification purposes only, and C should not be considered a deployable option.
There are three requirements: greater availability, better application performance and unloading of reporting tasks from the main database. The deployment of RDS into a multi-usable area cluster can satisfy both: it has two repositories in different available areas and can point to these examples by synchronizing them with readable examples. It should be noted that the title is not presented precisely enough - in Amazon RDS, multi-usable area database cluster deployments apply only to MySQL and PostgreSQL and not to Oracle; details are provided in the audit log. Even so, of the options given, C is the only one that meets both requirements.
Option A: Disaster recovery is addressed in different regions rather than availability within the same region and requires continuous maintenance of the DMS mission.
Option B: A single available area means that there is no high availability and a copy of the same area is not available to help in the event of a malfunction in the area itself.
Option D: Aurora is not compatible with Oracle: Migration requires a mode conversion and code rewrite, and "Aurora's multi-usable area deployment" describes a non-existent deployment pattern.

options.text: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create an Amazon RDS DB instance in multiple AWS Regions. Point the reporting functions toward a separate DB instance from the primary DB instance.
Use Amazon RDS in a Single-AZ deployment to create an Oracle database. Create a read replica in the same zone as the primary DB instance. Direct the reporting functions to the read replica.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ cluster deployment to create an Oracle database. Direct the reporting functions to use the reader instance in the cluster deployment.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ instance deployment to create an Amazon Aurora database. Direct the reporting functions to the reader instances.

question_text:
A company wants to build a web application on AWS. Client access requests to the website are not predictable and can be idle for a long time. Only customers who have paid a subscription fee can have the ability to sign in and use the web application.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose three.)
explanation_en:
Loads are unpredictable and may remain idle for long periods of time, so companies should pay only for actual requests. The back end is a Lambda function, located behind API Gateway, which reads data (A) from DynamoDB. A subscriber needs an Amazon Cognito user pool, which stores the account and issues the token (C). The front end is a static site deployed through AWS Amplify with an built-in CloudFront integration (E).
Option B: The ECS service and the RDS database located behind the load balancer will bill all day, even if there is no flow; the option itself is contradictory, as it still refers to a Lambda function.
Option D: The identification pool will issue a temporary AWS voucher to an accredited user; the authentication itself will be handled by the user pool.
Option F: PHP is a server-end language and S3 static web hosting cannot execute it: the site will not work properly.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function to retrieve user information from Amazon DynamoDB. Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint to accept RESTful APIs. Send the API calls to the Lambda function.

Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service behind an Application Load Balancer to retrieve user information from Amazon RDS. Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint to accept RESTful APIs. Send the API calls to the Lambda function.
Create an Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate users.
Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool to authenticate users.
Use AWS Amplify to serve the frontend web content with HTML, CSS, and JS. Use an integrated Amazon CloudFront configuration.
Use Amazon S3 static web hosting with PHP, CSS, and JS. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the frontend web content.

question_text:
A media company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to deliver content over the internet. The company wants only premium customers to have access to the media streams and file content. The company stores all content in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company also delivers content on demand to customers for a specific purpose, such as movie rentals or music downloads.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The content is distributed through the CloudFront service, so access rights must be restricted on the CloudFront instead of on the S3. There are two mechanisms: a signature URL can be granted access to a single file within a limited time frame, while a signature Cookie can be granted access to a group of documents without the need to change the URL. The scene describes the granting of specific access rights for specific content (e.g. film lease or music download) - i.e. access rights for a specific object for a specified time period - which is the signature URL. Empirical law: Sign URLs should be used for a single document or streaming link to a single resource; signature Cookie should be used for an entire library or website.
Option A: There is no "S3 Signature Cookie": S3 provides a presigned URL, while Cookie is signed by CloudFront. Even using S3 pre-signed URLs, you bypass distribution networks and access S3 directly, thus avoiding CDNs.
Option C: Source access controls prevent access to the S3 buckets by all except the CloudFront distribution network itself. It is unable to distinguish between high-level clients and ordinary users - both of which access content via CloudFront.
Option D: Field-level encryption encrypts specific fields (e.g., credit card numbers) in a user POST request, which prevents intermediate services from seeing this information. This has nothing to do with limiting access to content.

options.text: Generate and provide S3 signed cookies to premium customers.
Generate and provide CloudFront signed URLs to premium customers.
Use origin access control (OAC) to limit the access of non-premium customers.
Generate and activate field-level encryption to block non-premium customers.

question_text:
A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in multiple AWS accounts that are individually bled. The company recently purchased a Savings Pian. Because of changes in the company’s business requirements, the company has decommissioned a large number of EC2 instances. The company wants to use its Savings Plan discounts on its other AWS accounts.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The Savings Plans discount is only shared among the accounts of individual organizations with a uniform bill. Currently, these accounts are charged separately, so the company must first create an organization — specifically, an account (E) that already owns the plan and operates an example, otherwise it undertakes to remain outside the shared border — and invite other accounts. Subsequently, the discount sharing function was opened in the management account (A), and unused commitments began to cover the use of other accounts. Compared to Question 467.
Option B: The discount shared switch is only available in the management account of the organization and not in the account where Savings Plan was purchased.
Option C: Resources such as the AWS RAM shared subnet, prefix list and Transit Gateway. Savings Plans are not shared through it.
Option D: A new fee account can be created, but at this point the account of the purchase plan needs to join the organization as a member account; option E is simpler and the commitment is kept within the shared boundary from the first day.

options.text: From the AWS Account Management Console of the management account, turn on discount sharing from the billing preferences section.
From the AWS Account Management Console of the account that purchased the existing Savings Plan, turn on discount sharing from the billing preferences section. Include all accounts.
From the AWS Organizations management account, use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the Savings Plan with other accounts.
Create an organization in AWS Organizations in a new payer account. Invite the other AWS accounts to join the organization from the management account.

Create an organization in AWS Organizations in the existing AWS account with the existing EC2 instances and Savings Plan. Invite the other AWS accounts to join the organization from the management account.

question_text:
A retail company uses a regional Amazon API Gateway API for its public REST APIs. The API Gateway endpoint is a custom domain name that points to an Amazon Route 53 alias record. A solutions architect needs to create a solution that has minimal effects on customers and minimal data loss to release the new version of APIs.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The task was to publish a new version of the API, which had the least impact on clients and the least loss of data. The API Gateway contains mechanisms to achieve this goal: canary distribution at the same stage, receiving a percentage of traffic, having independent indicators and logs, and upgrading to the production stage after validation. Domain names and Route 53 records remain unchanged and rollback is instantaneous.
Option B: Importing in a combined mode will update the existing API once and for all: there is no incremental traffic switch, and rollback operations are complex.
Option C: Cover mode is more risky - it replaces the entire API definition, so an error immediately affects 100% of the customer.
Option D: DNS cache problems when running through a new endpoint, a new domain name and Route 53 log switching: Some clients will continue to access the old version for some time, the switch process cannot be controlled and a certain percentage of traffic cannot be migrated.

options.text: Create a canary release deployment stage for API Gateway. Deploy the latest API version. Point an appropriate percentage of traffic to the canary stage. After API verification, promote the canary stage to the production stage.

Create a new API Gateway endpoint with a new version of the API in OpenAPI YAML file format. Use the import-to-update operation in merge mode into the API in API Gateway. Deploy the new version of the API to the production stage.

Create a new API Gateway endpoint with a new version of the API in OpenAPI JSON file format. Use the import-to-update operation in overwrite mode into the API in API Gateway. Deploy the new version of the API to the production stage.

Create a new API Gateway endpoint with new versions of the API definitions. Create a custom domain name for the new API Gateway API. Point the Route 53 alias record to the new API Gateway API custom domain name.

question_text:
A company wants to direct its users to a backup static error page if the company's primary website is unavailable.
The primary website's DNS records are hosted in Amazon Route 53. The domain is pointing to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company needs a solution that minimizes changes and infrastructure overhead.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The company will need to provide a backup error page when the main site is not available, with minimal changes and no additional infrastructure required. This is what is achieved by the primary-facility transition of the Route 53 standard: the primary record points to the load balancer and is linked to a health check, while the secondary record points to static sites in the S3 S3 bucket. Once the health check is passed, the master record will respond; once the load balancer is found to be unhealthy, Route 53 returns to the address of the S3 bucket.
Option A: A delay-based path selects the quickest end rather than the normal working endpoint. Even if the site is healthy, some users may still have access to the wrong page.
Option C: The EC2 instance, which is configured separately for static pages, is unnecessary infrastructure maintenance, and the active-active configuration conflicts with the requirement "to switch only when a health check fails".
Option D: Multivalue response returns multiple records at one time and does not give priority to the primary record: even if the site is healthy, the user may randomly access the wrong page.

options.text: Update the Route 53 records to use a latency routing policy. Add a static error page that is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket to the records so that the traffic is sent to the most responsive endpoints.

Set up a Route 53 active-passive failover configuration. Direct traffic to a static error page that is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket when Route 53 health checks determine that the ALB endpoint is unhealthy.

Set up a Route 53 active-active configuration with the ALB and an Amazon EC2 instance that hosts a static error page as endpoints. Configure Route 53 to send requests to the instance only if the health checks fail for the ALB.

Update the Route 53 records to use a multivalue answer routing policy. Create a health check. Direct traffic to the website if the health check passes. Direct traffic to a static error page that is hosted in Amazon S3 if the health check does not pass.

question_text:
A recent analysis of a company's IT expenses highlights the need to reduce backup costs. The company's chief information officer wants to simplify the on-premises backup infrastructure and reduce costs by eliminating the use of physical backup tapes. The company must preserve the existing investment in the on-premises backup applications and workflows.
What should a solutions architect recommend?
explanation_en:
The key requirement is to maintain existing local back-up applications and workflows while eliminating physical tapes. This is the design purpose of Tape Gateway: it presents a virtual tape library to backup software via iSCSI protocols while storing virtual tapes in S3 and further storing them in the archive storage category. Software and processes remain the same; physical tapes disappear.
Option A: NFS access via Storage Gateway is file-based, but the backup application is configured to work with the tape library: the workflow needs to be redesigned.
Option B: EFS through NFS means that the process needs to be re-engineered, and file storage costs are significantly higher than those of S3.
Option C: EFS does not have an iSCSI interface at all: it is a file system using NFS protocols.

options.text: Set up AWS Storage Gateway to connect with the backup applications using the NFS interface.
Set up an Amazon EFS file system that connects with the backup applications using the NFS interface.
Set up an Amazon EFS file system that connects with the backup applications using the iSCSI interface.
Set up AWS Storage Gateway to connect with the backup applications using the iSCSI-virtual tape library (VTL) interface.

question_text:
A company has data collection sensors at different locations. The data collection sensors stream a high volume of data to the company. The company wants to design a platform on AWS to ingest and process high-volume streaming data. The solution must be scalable and support data collection in near real time. The company must store the data in Amazon S3 for future reporting.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
A data stream with high volume throughput needs to be ingestion and deposited in S3 with minimal operating costs. Kinesis Data Firehose was designed for this purpose: a fully hosted delivery stream that can be expanded automatically, buffered by time and size, optionally compressed and converted and data written into S3 buckets. No cluster, no segment, no code.
Option B: AWS Glue is an ETL service for batch processing and directory management, not a receiver for streaming data from sensors.
Option C: The Lambda functions, including buffer and retry mechanisms, must be manually prepared and connected, and Firehose has these functions embedded.
Option D: DMS is used to transport data from a database; it is not used to ingestion data streams from sensors.

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver streaming data to Amazon S3.
Use AWS Glue to deliver streaming data to Amazon S3.
Use AWS Lambda to deliver streaming data and store the data to Amazon S3.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to deliver streaming data to Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company has separate AWS accounts for its finance, data analytics, and development departments. Because of costs and security concerns, the company wants to control which services each AWS account can use.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The requirement is to focus on limiting the services available in each sector ' s accounts without building any additional components. In AWS Organizations, this is achieved through the OU structure and SCP: grouping sector accounts into organizational units and attaching to each module a strategy to include a list of permitted or prohibited services. SCPs are valid for every subject (including root users) in the account and cannot be bypassed through the local IAM policy. Please note that the SCPs limit their privileges and never grant them - the actual privileges are the intersection of SCP and IAM strategies.
Option A: Systems Manager template automating, but unable to prevent the use of services not contained in the template.
Option C: CloudFormation is used to describe and deploy resources. It does not prevent users from creating resources manually outside the template.
Option D: Service Catalog facilitates pre-build configuration, but it needs to maintain a catalogue of products in each account and does not limit direct access to the service API.

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager templates to control which AWS services each department can use.
Create organization units (OUs) for each department in AWS Organizations. Attach service control policies (SCPs) to the OUs.
Use AWS CloudFormation to automatically provision only the AWS services that each department can use.
Set up a list of products in AWS Service Catalog in the AWS accounts to manage and control the usage of specific AWS services.

question_text:
A company has created a multi-tier application for its ecommerce website. The website uses an Application Load Balancer that resides in the public subnets, a web tier in the public subnets, and a MySQL cluster hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in the private subnets. The MySQL database needs to retrieve product catalog and pricing information that is hosted on the internet by a third-party provider. A solutions architect must devise a strategy that maximizes security without increasing operational overhead.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Database clusters in private sub-networks need to be able to access external catalogue service providers externally, while access from outside sources must be blocked and operational costs not increased. The NAT gateway in the public subnets, along with the default route for the private subnets, has just achieved this: a managed service with connections that can only be initiated internally.
Option A: An example of NAT is an ordinary machine that requires patching, extension and redundancy: operating costs will increase.
Option C: A private sub-network to the Internet gateway makes it practically public, requiring a public address — less secure.
Option D: Virtual private gateways are used to connect VPN or DirectConnect to your site, which does not provide Internet access.

options.text: Deploy a NAT instance in the VPC. Route all the internet-based traffic through the NAT instance.
Deploy a NAT gateway in the public subnets. Modify the private subnet route table to direct all internet- bound traffic to the NAT gateway.
Configure an internet gateway and attach it to the VPModify the private subnet route table to direct internet- bound traffic to the internet gateway.
Configure a virtual private gateway and attach it to the VPC. Modify the private subnet route table to direct internet-bound traffic to the virtual private gateway.

question_text:
A company is using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt AWS Lambda environment variables. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the required permissions are in place to decrypt and use the environment variables.
Which steps must the solutions architect take to implement the correct permissions? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Access to KMS keys in AWS is always two-way: the subject needs to have access to its IAM policy, and the subject must be explicitly allowed to use the key's own strategy. For the Lambda environment variable, this means that two settings: the performance role of the function needs to include kms: Decrypt permission (B) and the explicit permission of the role in the key policy (D). The absence of any link leads to an error in access while the function is running. Do not confuse the performance role with the resource-based policy of the function: the former describes the actions that a function can perform, and the latter describes which subjects can call that function.
Option A: The resource policy of the Lambda function defines which services and accounts are allowed to call the function. It does not grant permission to use KMS keys.
Option C: Function policy is just another name for a resource-based policy that controls who can call the function. It has nothing to do with decrypted environmental variables.
Option E: In a key policy, privileges are given to the subject — a role or an account — rather than to a `functional policy '. This structure does not exist in KMS.

options.text: Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda resource policy.
Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda execution role.
Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda function policy.
Allow the Lambda execution role in the AWS KMS key policy.
Allow the Lambda resource policy in the AWS KMS key policy.

question_text:
A company has a financial application that produces reports. The reports average 50 KB in size and are stored in Amazon S3. The reports are frequently accessed during the first week after production and must be stored for several years. The reports must be retrievable within 6 hours.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Note size: 50 KB report. S3 Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval both have a subtotal of 128 KB, so a 50 KB file will be billed at 128 KB, which reduces savings at the "low" level by almost two thirds. Retrieving requirements are more liberal - 6 hours - and data must be kept for several years. So the cheapest option is to use Standard the week before, then switch to Glacier Flexible Retrieval: its standard search time is 3-5 hours, meets the six-hour window requirement, and the storage cost is about one sixth of Standard-IA.
Option B: Standard-IA provides msisecond access, which is not required here and is significantly more expensive than Glacier. For a 50 KB object, its 128 KB subtotal cost size further reduces the savings.
Option C: Intelligent-Tiering is charged a surveillance fee for each object, and it will never move less than 128 KB to a cheaper level. In millions of small reports, this brings costs without any benefit.
Option D: Deep Archive takes 12 hours under standard search and up to 48 hours under bulk search. This doesn't meet the six hours requirement.

options.text: Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Glacier after 7 days.
Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 7 days.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to transition the reports to S3 Standard- Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) and S3 Glacier.
Use S3 Standard. Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the reports to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days.

question_text:
A company needs to optimize the cost of its Amazon EC2 instances. The company also needs to change the type and family of its EC2 instances every 2-3 months.
What should the company do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The type and series of examples change every two to three months, so commitments cannot be tied to them. The calculation of savings plans, regardless of case series, size, region or even service, offers discounts, while the option of one year without advance payment is the most flexible option compatible with this frequent change.
Option A: Set aside examples for a three-year period to lock in a specific series and type: As the discount will change every two to three months, the discount will not be available.
Option C: Payment of the full advance fee for the retention of the example would exacerbate the same problem - funds are tied to a particular type of example.
Option D: EC2 instance savings plans are tied to a series of examples in a given region, where the series is constantly changing.

options.text: Purchase Partial Upfront Reserved Instances for a 3-year term.
Purchase a No Upfront Compute Savings Plan for a 1-year term.
Purchase All Upfront Reserved Instances for a 1-year term.
Purchase an All Upfront EC2 Instance Savings Plan for a 1-year term.

question_text:
A solutions architect needs to review a company's Amazon S3 buckets to discover personally identifiable information (PII). The company stores the PII data in the us-east-1 Region and us-west-2 Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The discovery of personal identity information (PII) in multiple drums is the responsibility of Amazon Macie. The details of the tests here are that Macie is a regional service and must be opened in all the regions where the data are located, and create a discovery operation in each region. Centralized management is possible through the fiduciarys in the organization, but the regions still need to be clearly identified.
Option B: Security Hub aggregates findings from other services, while the AWS Config rules check resource allocation instead of object content.
Option C: Inspectr scan loads to detect loopholes and do not analyse data in S3.
Option D: GuardDuty monitors suspicious activities, including those related to S3 data, but it does not classify personal data within the object.

options.text: Configure Amazon Macie in each Region. Create a job to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure AWS Security Hub for all Regions. Create an AWS Config rule to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Inspector to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company's SAP application has a backend SQL Server database in an on-premises environment. The company wants to migrate its on-premises application and database server to AWS. The company needs an instance type that meets the high demands of its SAP database. On-premises performance data shows that both the SAP application and the database have high memory utilization.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Local performance data indicate high memory utilization for SAP applications and databases. Therefore, both levels should be migrated to memory optimization examples — an option recommended by AWS for SAP.
Option A: Compute optimized examples that provide fewer memory per core and are not suitable for memory-intensive SAP applications.
Option B: Storage optimization examples apply to a large number of local I/Os, but the bottlenecks here are memory.
Option D: An example of HPC optimization is designed for a closely coupled, network-intensive computing load and does not apply to SAP applications.

options.text: Use the compute optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.
Use the storage optimized instance family for both the application and the database.
Use the memory optimized instance family for both the application and the database.
Use the high performance computing (HPC) optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.

question_text:
A company runs an application in a VPC with public and private subnets. The VPC extends across multiple Availability Zones. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application uses an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.
A solutions architect needs to design a secure solution to establish a connection between the EC2 instances and the SQS queue.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
SQS is a public API service, so the example of a private subnet is either accessed via NAT or by private access through the interface VPC terminal (PrivateLink). The right option is to place the terminal in the same private subnet where the example is running and protect it by configuring entry rules for these examples by a security group — this is how interface terminal access controls are used. In addition, an end-point strategy can be added to limit accessible queues.
Option B: There is no point in placing a terminal in a public subnet: the interface must be located at the client's end — that is, in a private subnet.
Option C: Put the terminal in the public subnet equally wrongly and add the queue access policy to the queue instead of the terminal.
Option D: Gateway terminals only apply to S3 and DynamoDB - SQS without gateway terminals. And the NAT gateway will send traffic back to the Internet, and that is precisely what needs to be avoided.

options.text: Implement an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS. Configure the endpoint to use the private subnets. Add to the endpoint a security group that has an inbound access rule that allows traffic from the EC2 instances that are in the private subnets.

Implement an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS. Configure the endpoint to use the public subnets. Attach to the interface endpoint a VPC endpoint policy that allows access from the EC2 instances that are in the private subnets.

Implement an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS. Configure the endpoint to use the public subnets. Attach an Amazon SQS access policy to the interface VPC endpoint that allows requests from only a specified VPC endpoint.
Implement a gateway endpoint for Amazon SQS. Add a NAT gateway to the private subnets. Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instances that allows access to the SQS queue.

question_text:
A solutions architect is using an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy a three-tier web application. The web application consists of a web tier and an application tier that stores and retrieves user data in Amazon DynamoDB tables. The web and application tiers are hosted on Amazon EC2 instances, and the database tier is not publicly accessible. The application EC2 instances need to access the DynamoDB tables without exposing API credentials in the template.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Examples need to be written from and from DynamoDB, and no vouchers can be found in the template. Standard method: An IAM role with the required privileges, an example profile with the role, and a reference to the configuration file on the example. The application then obtains a temporary voucher from the case metadata. Note the difference from the adjacent option where the role is given read-only access, but the application also stores user data and therefore also needs to write access rights.
Option A: Read-only roles do not allow applications to store user data, while demand requires user data to be stored and retrieved.
Option C: Enter the access key as a template parameter, which is the behaviour that the demand expressly requires to avoid: the key will eventually appear in stack parameters and fall into the hands of the deploying personnel.
Option D: The GetAttt function does return to the access key that created the user, but the pass key through the user data makes the key appear explicitly in the metadata of the instance.

options.text: Create an IAM role to read the DynamoDB tables. Associate the role with the application instances by referencing an instance profile.

Create an IAM role that has the required permissions to read and write from the DynamoDB tables. Add the role to the EC2 instance profile, and associate the instance profile with the application instances.

Use the parameter section in the AWS CloudFormation template to have the user input access and secret keys from an already-created IAM user that has the required permissions to read and write from the DynamoDB tables.

Create an IAM user in the AWS CloudFormation template that has the required permissions to read and write from the DynamoDB tables. Use the GetAtt function to retrieve the access and secret keys, and pass them to the application instances through the user data.

question_text:
A solutions architect manages an analytics application. The application stores large amounts of semistructured data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The solutions architect wants to use parallel data processing to process the data more quickly. The solutions architect also wants to use information that is stored in an Amazon Redshift database to enrich the data.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Semi-structured data are stored in S3 and need to be processed in parallel: Amazon Athena performs queries on S3 in a distributed, unserver-free manner. By AWS Glue supplements data information from Redshift, AWS Glue provides a connector to S3 and Redshift, so the data link is completed in a single ETL operation.
Option B: EMR can work, but it is a cluster that needs to be configured, configured and maintained, and both steps here are covered by no server service.
Option C: Kinesis Data Streams is used for current data; it is not consistent with the design use to move files already in S3 to Redshift.
Option D: Lake Formation is responsible for access control and data lake catalogue management - it is not responsible for data enhancement.

options.text: Use Amazon Athena to process the S3 data. Use AWS Glue with the Amazon Redshift data to enrich the S3 data.
Use Amazon EMR to process the S3 data. Use Amazon EMR with the Amazon Redshift data to enrich the S3 data.
Use Amazon EMR to process the S3 data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to move the S3 data into Amazon Redshift so that the data can be enriched.
Use AWS Glue to process the S3 data. Use AWS Lake Formation with the Amazon Redshift data to enrich the S3 data.

question_text:
A company has two VPCs that are located in the us-west-2 Region within the same AWS account. The company needs to allow network traffic between these VPCs. Approximately 500 GB of data transfer will occur between the VPCs each month.
What is the MOST cost-effective solution to connect these VPCs?
explanation_en:
The two networks in the same region and under the same account have a monthly data transfer of about 500 GB – the cheapest way to connect them is through VPC peer-to-peer. The connection itself is free of charge and is charged only for the data transmitted, and is not billed on an hourly basis. The configuration requires only one step, while adding a route to the two circuit tables.
Option A: Transit Gateway is charged an hourly fee for each connection and a GB data-processing fee for each connection. For both VPCs, this is clearly more expensive than reciprocal connections.
Option B: The establishment of a VPN between two VPCs increases the cost of an hourly connection, the cost of encryption and the bandwidth limit of the tunnel – which is unnecessary when private connections are already available in the area.
Option D: Direct Contact is used to connect your local site to AWS. It could not be used to connect the two VPCs within the same region and the cost was much higher than the actual demand.

options.text: Implement AWS Transit Gateway to connect the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the transit gateway for inter-VPC communication.
Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the VPN tunnel for inter-VPC communication.
Set up a VPC peering connection between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the VPC peering connection for inter-VPC communication.
Set up a 1 GB AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the Direct Connect connection for inter-VPC communication.

question_text:
A company hosts multiple applications on AWS for different product lines. The applications use different compute resources, including Amazon EC2 instances and Application Load Balancers. The applications run in different AWS accounts under the same organization in AWS Organizations across multiple AWS Regions. Teams for each product line have tagged each compute resource in the individual accounts.
The company wants more details about the cost for each product line from the consolidated billing feature in Organizations.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The labels applied by the team have an impact on the billing only after the tags are activated to allocate costs. They are activated in the billing console (B – user definition label required for selection), specifically in the organization’s management account (E); once activated, cost explorers and summary billing reports can group costs by this label in all accounts and regions. Note the distinction: AWS-generated labels start with aws: prefix and are created by the platform, while user-defined labels are created by you. Related issues: No. 459.
Option A: The label generated by AWS is the internal label of the platform. The product line here uses the company's custom label - the user-defined label.
Option C: The resource group facilitates the operational grouping of resources, but the activation of the cost allocation label is done in the billing console.
Option D: There is no such activation option in the member accounts: the cost allocation label is centrally opened in the management account.

options.text: Select a specific AWS generated tag in the AWS Billing console.
Select a specific user-defined tag in the AWS Billing console.
Select a specific user-defined tag in the AWS Resource Groups console.
Activate the selected tag from each AWS account.
Activate the selected tag from the Organizations management account.

question_text:
A company's solutions architect is designing an AWS multi-account solution that uses AWS Organizations. The solutions architect has organized the company's accounts into organizational units (OUs).
The solutions architect needs a solution that will identify any changes to the OU hierarchy. The solution also needs to notify the company's operations team of any changes.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Organizational OU structural changes need to be tested and reported to the operational team without the need to build customized systems for this purpose. AWS Control Tower maintains a baseline view and reports on its own — including movement of accounts between OUs, hierarchy changes and modifications to protective rules. Notices are posted to a SNS theme, and the operating team subscribes to the theme. There is no need to prepare any custom codes or rules.
Option B: AWS Config rules will handle the allocation of resources within the account. They do not follow the organizational OU hierarchy.
Option C: An organization-level CloudTrain log will show an API call like MoveAccount, but filters, indicators and notifications will need to be built from the top - with a much larger volume than a ready-made drift notification.
Option D: CloudFormation Float Test compares stack resources with templates. It has nothing to do with the OU structure of the organization.

options.text: Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use account drift notifications to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use AWS Config aggregated rules to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Use AWS Service Catalog to create accounts in Organizations. Use an AWS CloudTrail organization trail to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Use AWS CloudFormation templates to create accounts in Organizations. Use the drift detection operation on a stack to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.

question_text:
A company's website handles millions of requests each day, and the number of requests continues to increase. A solutions architect needs to improve the response time of the web application. The solutions architect determines that the application needs to decrease latency when retrieving product details from the Amazon DynamoDB table.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The goal is to minimize DynamoDB reading delays while keeping the operating costs minimal. DAX is designed for this purpose: a hosting cache directly in front of the table is compatible with the same API and therefore does not need to prepare a load or failure logic - these functions are embedded.
Option B: While Redis provides for low delays, caches, expirys and consistency must be managed manually in the application code.
Option C: Memcached also has the same problem and does not have a data copying function.
Option D: Filling the cache through stream and function is the most complex of the proposed design options and the most costly to maintain.

options.text: Set up a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Route all read requests through DAX.
Set up Amazon ElastiCache for Redis between the DynamoDB table and the web application. Route all read requests through Redis.
Set up Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached between the DynamoDB table and the web application. Route all read requests through Memcached.
Set up Amazon DynamoDB Streams on the table, and have AWS Lambda read from the table and populate Amazon ElastiCache. Route all read requests through ElastiCache.

question_text:
A solutions architect needs to ensure that API calls to Amazon DynamoDB from Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC do not travel across the internet.
Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet this requirement? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
A gateway endpoint for DynamoDB(B) provides private access and adds a routing entry (A) with service prefixes that will drive traffic through this endpoint route. These two steps are sufficient: the call to the table will not leave the Internet.
Option C: An EC2 interface peer provides a private access to the API for example management instead of DynamoDB.
Option D: The interface endpoint will create a flexible network interface; the gateway endpoint will work by route and there is no interface.
Option E: The security group applies to interface endpoints. There is no security team at the end of the gateway — access is restricted by an end-point strategy.

options.text: Create a route table entry for the endpoint.
Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB.
Create an interface endpoint for Amazon EC2.
Create an elastic network interface for the endpoint in each of the subnets of the VPC.
Create a security group entry in the endpoint's security group to provide access.

question_text:
A company runs its applications on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters and on-premises Kubernetes clusters. The company wants to view all clusters and workloads from a central location.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The Kubernetes cluster operates both on AWS and locally, and needs to be viewed from one place. Amazon EKS Contractor can register external clusters in the EKS console, and these clusters and their workloads will then be shown alongside the managed clusters. Only one agent would be installed, and no other infrastructure would be required.
Option A: Container Insights collects indicators and logs, but does not provide a unified cluster and negative listing of its work.
Option C: Systems Manager manages nodes instead of Kubernetes objects: It does not display cluster information in the required form.
Option D: EKS Anywhere is a method of running clusters at local sites, not a tool to observe clusters of others.

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect and group the cluster information.
Use Amazon EKS Connector to register and connect all Kubernetes clusters.
Use AWS Systems Manager to collect and view the cluster information.
Use Amazon EKS Anywhere as the primary cluster to view the other clusters with native Kubernetes commands.

question_text:
A company is building an ecommerce application and needs to store sensitive customer information. The company needs to give customers the ability to complete purchase transactions on the website. The company also needs to ensure that sensitive customer data is protected, even from database administrators.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The sorter is "even if it comes from a database administrator. " Any transparent storage-level encryption (EBS, RDS, S3 SSE) will automatically decrypt the data for anyone with access to the service, so database administrators will see the data content as usual. The only way to prevent privileged operators from accessing data is through client encryption: the application encrypts fields with KMS keys before writing the data. The secret is stored in the table, and the secret is useless without access to the key. The control of the key is separate from that of the database - that is the core of the separation of duties.
Option A: EBS volume encryption is transparent to the operating system and to anyone who has access to the example. It can't prevent the administrators from acting.
Option C: S3 Server-end encryption will decrypt objects for anyone who is allowed access to the S3 buckets and keys. In addition, S3 is not a service storage system for transactional purchases.
Option D: Windows filesystem privileges will be bypassed by the server administrator, where there is no data encryption.

options.text: Store sensitive data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Use EBS encryption to encrypt the data. Use an IAM instance role to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) client-side encryption to encrypt the data.
Store sensitive data in Amazon S3. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) server-side encryption to encrypt the data. Use S3 bucket policies to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon FSx for Windows Server. Mount the file share on application servers. Use Windows file permissions to restrict access.

question_text:
A company has an on-premises MySQL database that handles transactional data. The company is migrating the database to the AWS Cloud. The migrated database must maintain compatibility with the company's applications that use the database. The migrated database also must scale automatically during periods of increased demand.
Which migration solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Applications must run on an ongoing basis without any changes, so the target system needs an engine that is compatible with MySQL and that can be expanded automatically. Aurora MySQL is compatible with MySQL at the protocol and query level, and its storage will grow automatically, while the AutoAurora Extension will add or remove read-only copies according to load dynamics. AWS DMS allows source databases to continue during migration while moving data.
Option A: RDS for MySQL compatible, but storage extension is only spatial, not performance: the computing capacity still needs to be expanded manually.
Option B: Redshift is an analytical data repository; it is not service-type loadable and is incompatible with the application.
Option D: DynamoDB is a non-relative storage system: each SQL query needs to be rewritten.

options.text: Use native MySQL tools to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure elastic storage scaling.
Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift by using the mysqldump utility. Turn on Auto Scaling for the Amazon Redshift cluster.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon Aurora. Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Configure an Auto Scaling policy.

question_text:
A company runs multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances in a VPC across two Availability Zones. The instances host applications that use a hierarchical directory structure. The applications need to read and write rapidly and concurrently to shared storage.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The demand is a hierarchy of directories, as well as the rapid co-writing of examples from two available areas. This is precisely the feature of Amazon EFS: a file system using NFS protocols can be mounted on each instance, each available area has a mounted target and is consistent when sent to write.
Option A:S3 is the object storage: it does not have a real directory hierarchy or file operation, and applications are specially constructed around these features.
Option C: An io2 roll is mounted inside a single available area, so the example in the second available area cannot be accessed, and a normal file system is not designed for simultaneous writing from multiple machines.
Option D: Synchronizing a separate volume between the examples leads to data drift and delay: it cannot be provided and sent for writing.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Allow access from all the EC2 instances in the VPC.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system from each EC2 instance.
Create a file system on a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Attach the EBS volume to all the EC2 instances.
Create file systems on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance. Synchronize the EBS volumes across the different EC2 instances.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a workload that will store hourly energy consumption by business tenants in a building. The sensors will feed a database through HTTP requests that will add up usage for each tenant. The solutions architect must use managed services when possible. The workload will receive more features in the future as the solutions architect adds independent components.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Sensors send readings via HTTP, with small and uneven data, and solutions require hosting services and easy addition of components. API Gateway accepts requests, the Lambda function handles and accumulates readings, DynamoDB storage results. There is no need to manage the server, expand automatically, and simply subscribe to events to easily add new stand-alone components.
Option B: A set of examples needs patches, monitors and extensions after the load balancer, and it is awkward to store frequently updated tenant counters in S3.
Option C: The first half is correct, but running SQL Server Express on the EC2 instance means that a machine and a database need to be managed manually, with a single point failure.
Option D: is again a self-managed set of examples and shared file systems are wrong storage models for consumer counters.

options.text: Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda functions to receive the data from the sensors, process the data, and store the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Use an Elastic Load Balancer that is supported by an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to receive and process the data from the sensors. Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store the processed data.
Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda functions to receive the data from the sensors, process the data, and store the data in a Microsoft SQL Server Express database on an Amazon EC2 instance.

Use an Elastic Load Balancer that is supported by an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to receive and process the data from the sensors. Use an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) shared file system to store the processed data.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing the storage architecture for a new web application used for storing and viewing engineering drawings. All application components will be deployed on the AWS infrastructure.
The application design must support caching to minimize the amount of time that users wait for the engineering drawings to load. The application must be able to store petabytes of data.
Which combination of storage and caching should the solutions architect use?
explanation_en:
The need is for several bytes of storage and caches to ensure rapid loading of drawings. S3 can store unlimited amounts of data without the need for capacity planning, while CloudFront caches data near the edge of the user. This combination is standard and does not require the use of a server or a capacitation.
Option B: Glacier is an archive storage, with search times ranging from minutes to hours, while ElastiCache performs memory caches on a regional scale - which do not apply to large files.
Option C: EBS rolls are limited in capacity, bound to a single available area, and do not extend to byte level.
Option D:Storage Gateway is a hybrid gateway used for local sites, and each component of the application is specified to run on AWS.

options.text: Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront
Amazon S3 Glacier with Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes with Amazon CloudFront
AWS Storage Gateway with Amazon ElastiCache

question_text:
An Amazon EventBridge rule targets a third-party API. The third-party API has not received any incoming traffic. A solutions architect needs to determine whether the rule conditions are being met and if the rule's target is being invoked.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
EventBridge posts its own indicators to Cloudwatch, which belongs to the AWS/Events Naming Space: Triggered Rules Shows whether the rules are triggered, and Investments and FailedInvocations show whether the target is actually called. These are just two issues that need to be distinguished.
Option B: Death queue only saves failed calls, and if the rules never trigger, the queue will be empty.
Option C: Cloudwatch Logs instead of the statistical information to be called by the rule; separate configuration is required for the recording of the EventBridge event logs.
Option D: CloudTrail Records Management API calls, not whether the rules are triggered and whether the target is called.

options.text: Check for metrics in Amazon CloudWatch in the namespace for AWS/Events.
Review events in the Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) dead-letter queue.
Check for the events in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Check the trails in AWS CloudTrail for the EventBridge events.

question_text:
A company has a large workload that runs every Friday evening. The workload runs on Amazon EC2 instances that are in two Availability Zones in the us-east-1 Region. Normally, the company must run no more than two instances at all times. However, the company wants to scale up to six instances each Friday to handle a regularly repeating increased workload.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The peaks are repeated in known cycles -- Friday nights a week. The planned operation of the auto-extension group will change the target and minimum capacity at the set time and then return to the status quo ante. This configuration needs only one setup, which will then run automatically.
Option A: Reminders only mean that the group is expanded manually on a weekly basis.
Option C: Manual expansion is the same thing: weekly manual intervention.
Option D: The indicator-based automatic strategy will only react after the load has arrived and will need to adjust the threshold, when the peak occurs is known well in advance.

options.text: Create a reminder in Amazon EventBridge to scale the instances.
Create an Auto Scaling group that has a scheduled action.
Create an Auto Scaling group that uses manual scaling.
Create an Auto Scaling group that uses automatic scaling.

question_text:
A company is creating a REST API. The company has strict requirements for the use of TLS. The company requires TLSv1.3 on the API endpoints. The company also requires a specific public third-party certificate authority (CA) to sign the TLS certificate.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Original answer: B; source correction answer: A.
ACM will not issue certificates signed by a third party public CA - it only supports import certificates; options B and D are technically impossible. examtopics t1 q571
Obtaining a certificate from a third party CA and importing ACM is feasible; the TLS_1_2 policy for API Gateway HTTP API also accepts TLS 1.3, so A can be established if the title requires only TLS 1.3. However, the strategy accepts TLS 1.2 at the same time; if only TLS 1.3 is allowed, A is not satisfied, and the title does not indicate whether TLS 1.2 has to be excluded.
ACM does not issue certificates signed by a third party public CA: it either issues its own certificates or accepts imported certificates. The only viable path, therefore, is to obtain the required CA external certificate, import it into ACM and attach it to the API Gateway custom domain (A).
Option B: It is technically impossible to create a certificate signed by a third party CA in ACM: ACM can only issue a certificate using its own licensing authority.
