question_text:
A company runs an application on AWS. The application receives inconsistent amounts of usage. The application uses AWS Direct Connect to connect to an on-premises MySQL-compatible database. The on-premises database consistently uses a minimum of 2 GiB of memory.
The company wants to migrate the on-premises database to a managed AWS service. The company wants to use auto scaling capabilities to manage unexpected workload increases.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
explanation_en:
The load is inconsistent, the database is MySQL compatible and the company needs to have automatic expansion and manage minimal costs. Aurora Servers v2 meets these needs: each ACU provides approximately 2 GiB memory, as measured in Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs), so that at least 1 ACU can cover the stated 2 GiB memory needs, while clusters can be smoothed out and services will not be interrupted.
Option A: DynamoDB is a non-relative data storage: applications designed for MySQL must be rewrited and 'default capacity settings' refers to a fixed preset capacity with no automatic extension.
Option B: Standard preset Aurora clusters are configured by example group, not by ACUs: The configuration described in this option does not exist and the preset Aurora does not automatically calculate the extension.
Option D: RDS for MySQL uses a fixed memory size that does not respond to sudden-onset load increases: changing the instance class requires manual operation and brings downtime.

options.text: Provision an Amazon DynamoDB database with default read and write capacity settings.
Provision an Amazon Aurora database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with 2 GiB of memory.

question_text:
A company wants to use an event-driven programming model with AWS Lambda. The company wants to reduce startup latency for Lambda functions that run on Java 11. The company does not have strict latency requirements for the applications. The company wants to reduce cold starts and outlier latencies when a function scales up.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
This relates to the cold start delay of the Java function, which is not strictly required and requires the most economical solution. Lambda SnapStart keeps an initialised implementation environment snapshot and restores it on call, significantly reducing the cold start-up time - and does not charge for the capacity for continuous maintenance.
Option A: Preset and distribute solutions to the same problem, but you need to pay for the entire time to set aside the example: in the absence of a strict delay requirement, this is overpayment.
Option B: Timeout settings limit maximum execution time and have no impact on the start-up process.
Option C: Increasing memory will slightly speed up initialization, but it will also increase the cost of each call and will not address the underlying causes of cold startup.

options.text: Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency.
Increase the timeout of the Lambda functions.
Increase the memory of the Lambda functions.
Configure Lambda SnapStart.

question_text:
A financial services company launched a new application that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The company uses the application to track stock market trends. The company needs to operate the application for only 2 hours at the end of each week. The company needs to optimize the cost of running the database.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Reference answer: B; dispute option: A.
2 hours per week: Aurora Servers v2 will shrink but will not drop to zero; a pre-configured cluster can be suspended for up to 7 days — both options are controversial
The currently supported version of Aurora Serverless v2 MySQL sets the minimum capacity to 0 ACU and automatically suspends it when you are free. Use only two hours per week, which is more appropriate than running continuously the original B; the version that supports the automatic pause needs to be selected and the short delay when the recovery is accepted.
Source answer B's original resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
Only two hours a week are required for the database — it makes no sense to pay for the remaining 166 hours. The answer key selects B: A pre-configured Aurora cluster can be stopped and the stopped cluster will not be charged for costing resources (you only have to pay for storage). There are two details that make this answer controversial: AWS will automatically restart a Aurora cluster seven days after it has been discontinued, while in the version of Aurora Serverless v2, which is reflected in this source's practice material, the cluster will shrink but will not fall to zero, and therefore the minimum capacity will continue to be billed. Today's Serverless v2 can be reduced to zero, making option A a stronger answer in the current examination. Its bottom principle remains unchanged: for scarce and short loads, either only the resources actually used or the cluster is completely discontinued.
Old Source option A: A strong alternative. In the service version reflected in this question, Serverless v2 cannot be reduced below its minimum ACU, meaning that it will be billed 24 hours a day - so the answer key is more in favour of a cluster that can be completely stopped.
Old Source Option C: Prescribe examples that are billed regardless of whether the machine is running or not - the worst option for only two hours per week. It also implies the need to manage MySQL on its own rather than using the hosting database.
Source old option D: Operating MySQL in ECS containers means again that you need to manage the database yourself, while you still need to solve the problem of permanent storage. There are no cost savings compared to the discontinued hosting clusters.

options.text: Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Aurora Serverless v2 MySQL database cluster.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Aurora MySQL database cluster.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs MySQL. Purchase an instance reservation for the EC2 instance.
Migrate the existing RDS for MySQL database to an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that uses MySQL container images to run tasks.

question_text:
A company deploys its applications on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind an Application Load Balancer in an AWS Region. The application needs to store data in a PostgreSQL database engine. The company wants the data in the database to be highly available. The company also needs increased capacity for read workloads.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
There is a need for high availability and additional reading capacity, with minimal operating costs. The deployment of the DB cluster in the RDS multi-usable area meets these needs: one main example plus two alternative examples in two other available areas, which can be serviced by a dedicated reading endpoint. A single configuration can meet both needs.
Option A: DynamoDB is not PostgreSQL: the application needs to be rewrited.
Option B: Standard multi-usable area deployment provides usability, but alternative examples do not provide reading traffic and therefore do not increase reading capacity.
Option D: Cross-regional reading of copies is designed for readers in other parts of the world and for disaster recovery; for the availability of individual regions, they increase unnecessary costs and delays.

options.text: Create an Amazon DynamoDB database table configured with global tables.
Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ deployments.
Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment.
Create an Amazon RDS database configured with cross-Region read replicas.

question_text:
A company is building a RESTful serverless web application on AWS by using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The users of this web application will be geographically distributed, and the company wants to reduce the latency of API requests to these users.
Which type of endpoint should a solutions architect use to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Users are distributed around the world and there is a need to reduce the delay in API requests. An optimised end point on the edge will drive the request to the nearest point on the edge of CloudFront, then transmit it to the area through the AWS core network: TLS connections are established near the user, and the overall request is significantly reduced.
Option A: A private endpoint can only be accessed from within the VPC - it does not apply to public users.
Option B: A regional endpoint will receive requests directly in the area: a remote user will experience all delays in reaching the endpoint.
Option C: An interface VPC endpoint is a means of accessing private API via a network, rather than a means of accelerating for Internet users.

options.text: Private endpoint
Regional endpoint
Interface VPC endpoint
Edge-optimized endpoint

question_text:
A company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to serve content pages for its website. The company needs to ensure that clients use a TLS certificate when accessing the company's website. The company wants to automate the creation and renewal of the TLS certificates.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
The certificate for CloudFront is issued by the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and is free of charge. The key detail is the proof of domain name ownership via DNS: ACM automatically renews the certificate as long as the CNAME record is kept in the hosting area when using DNS. This is precisely the automatic issuance and renewal required by the title.
Option A: Security policy sets minimum TLS versions and password packages; it does not issue certificates.
Option B: Source access controls limit access to sources (e.g. S3 drums), unrelated to the certificate.
Option D: E-mail validation requires manual confirmation at each renewal and therefore cannot provide automation.

options.text: Use a CloudFront security policy to create a certificate.
Use a CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to create a certificate.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a certificate. Use DNS validation for the domain.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a certificate. Use email validation for the domain.

question_text:
A company deployed a serverless application that uses Amazon DynamoDB as a database layer. The application has experienced a large increase in users. The company wants to improve database response time from milliseconds to microseconds and to cache requests to the database.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Description of the requirement as `from milliseconds to microseconds' and `Cache the request to a database', describing almost word for word DynamoDB Accerator (DAX): a trustable, API compatible cache is at the front end of the table, so the application needs to change its endpoint.
Option B: Redshift is an analytical repository for large-scale queries, not a solution that provides fast-track databases for applications.
Option C: Migration to RDS means that the data model needs to be redesigned, and it still does not provide a microsecond response time.
Option D: Redis can provide the required speed, but it needs to build a customized cache and failure logic, which means more operating costs.

options.text: Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift.
Migrate the database to Amazon RDS.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.

question_text:
A company runs an application that uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The application receives traffic only on weekdays during business hours. The company wants to optimize costs and reduce operational overhead based on this usage.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The database is needed only during the business hours of the working day, and the company does not want to devote any effort to building automation. The ready-to-use instance scheduler of the AWS solution is deployed from the template and automatically starts and stops the RDS and EC2 instances according to the plan - no custom code is required.
Option B: Turning off automatic backups saves costs, but at the same time gives up a little time to restore functionality.
Option C: Custom functions mean codes that need to be prepared and maintained; furthermore, CPU utilization as a signal to decide to stop the database is poor.
Option D: All prepaid prepaid pre-pricing cases will yield returns on a full-time basis, but in this scenario the database will be required only for a quarter of a week.

options.text: Use the Instance Scheduler on AWS to configure start and stop schedules.
Turn off automatic backups. Create weekly manual snapshots of the database.
Create a custom AWS Lambda function to start and stop the database based on minimum CPU utilization.
Purchase All Upfront reserved DB instances.

question_text:
A company uses locally attached storage to run a latency-sensitive application on premises. The company is using a lift and shift method to move the application to the AWS Cloud. The company does not want to change the application architecture.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
An unstructured migration (lift-and-ship) means that local additional storage is replaced by a volume on the example. gp3 is the cheapest in a general roll: at the same size, it costs about 20% less than gp2 and provides basic performances of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of the size of the roll, while gp2 performance changes with the size of the roll.
Option A: FSx for Lustre is an expensive file system designed for high performance computing, and the application is designed for local disks rather than shared resources.
Option B: gp2 volts have technically solved the problem, but the cost is higher than gp3 at the same capacity, and the cost is a decisive requirement here.
Option C: FSx for OpenZFS is also a shared file system at a higher cost than a block; it also requires structural changes.

options.text: Configure an Auto Scaling group with an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system to run the application.
Host the application on an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) GP2 volume to run the application.
Configure an Auto Scaling group with an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system to run the application.
Host the application on an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) GP3 volume to run the application.

question_text:
A company runs a stateful production application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application requires at least two EC2 instances to always be running.
A solutions architect needs to design a highly available and fault-tolerant architecture for the application. The solutions architect creates an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances.
Which set of additional steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is that at least two examples be kept in operation and that the structure be able to withstand the failure of a usable area. This means that two examples are required for each available area and that the minimum capacity of the group is set at four: if an entire available area is lost, it happens that two examples are running and meeting the requirements.
Option A: One example for each available area: The failure of any available area will leave only one example running, but at least two are required.
Option C: All four examples will not be able to withstand the failure of the available area in a single area, and the Spot capacity can be recovered at any time - unacceptable for a production application in a state.
Option D: The Spot example in the second available area can be recovered at any time, so it is not possible to guarantee that there are two examples running on an ongoing basis.

options.text: Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to two. Deploy one On-Demand Instance in one Availability Zone and one On-Demand Instance in a second Availability Zone.
Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to four. Deploy two On-Demand Instances in one Availability Zone and two On-Demand Instances in a second Availability Zone.
Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to two. Deploy four Spot Instances in one Availability Zone.
Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to four. Deploy two On-Demand Instances in one Availability Zone and two Spot Instances in a second Availability Zone.

question_text:
An ecommerce company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts its website on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company's on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company uses the eu-central-1 Region to host the website. The company wants to minimize load time for the website as much as possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
There are two locations: the company ' s data centre near us-west-1 and the web site at eu-central-1. Route53 The route-geographic route strategy can be used to send users from North America to the data centre and users from the European region to eu-central-1. Each visitor reaches the nearest location, minimizing loading time. There is also a need to consider geographic proximity routes, which are presented in the presentation of questions 120 and 142.
Option B: A simple route policy does not take into account the location of the client: it simply does not provide the behaviour described in this option.
Option C: A delayed single recording policy associated with us-west-1 directs all traffic to one location. The second position is completely non-participatory.
Option D: A weighted router strategy divides traffic evenly regardless of geography: half of Europe ' s users will be routed to U.S. data centres across the ocean.

options.text: Set up a geolocation routing policy. Send the traffic that is near us-west-1 to the on-premises data center. Send the traffic that is near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1.
Set up a simple routing policy that routes all traffic that is near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1 and routes all traffic that is near the on-premises datacenter to the on-premises data center.
Set up a latency routing policy. Associate the policy with us-west-1.
Set up a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.

question_text:
A company has 5 PB of archived data on physical tapes. The company needs to preserve the data on the tapes for another 10 years for compliance purposes. The company wants to migrate to AWS in the next 6 months. The data center that stores the tapes has a 1 Gbps uplink internet connectivity.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Mathematical calculations: The transfer of data from the 5PB via a 1 Gbps link takes about 10 TB per day, or about 485 days, even if the uplink is fully utilized - with a target deadline of only six months. From a mathematical perspective alone, any online transmission programme is not feasible. Snowball with Tape Gateway is designed for this scenario: physical tapes are read directly on the device into a virtual tape, the equipment is transported to AWS, and then the virtual tape is moved to S3 Glacier Deep Archive through a life-cycle strategy — the cheapest storage category to meet the 10-year compliance reservation requirement.
Option A: DataSync will transmit via the same link and therefore the six-month deadline will not be met. It also requires an intermediate 5 PB NFS phase storage, which the company does not have.
Option B: Write Deep Archive directly will still go through the same uplink: about 485 days, with only six months available.
Option D: Local Tape Gateway will create a virtual tape at the cloud end, but the data will still be transmitted via the Internet link - mathematically calculated and timeline results are the same, and thus still fail.

options.text: Read the data from the tapes on premises. Stage the data in a local NFS storage. Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
Use an on-premises backup application to read the data from the tapes and to write directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

Order multiple AWS Snowball devices that have Tape Gateway. Copy the physical tapes to virtual tapes in Snowball. Ship the Snowball devices to AWS. Create a lifecycle policy to move the tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Configure an on-premises Tape Gateway. Create virtual tapes in the AWS Cloud. Use backup software to copy the physical tape to the virtual tape.

question_text:
A company is deploying an application that processes large quantities of data in parallel. The company plans to use Amazon EC2 instances for the workload. The network architecture must be configurable to prevent groups of nodes from sharing the same underlying hardware.
Which networking solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is that nodal groups cannot eventually be deployed on the same bottom hardware. This is precisely the role of a decentralized placement group: each example will be placed on a stand-alone hardware with its own power and network, so a single hardware failure will only affect a node.
Option B: Different accounts have no impact on physical deployment: examples may still be deployed on the same host.
Option C: The exclusive tenant only ensures that there are no other examples of customers sharing the mainframe - your node may still be deployed on the same hardware.
Option D: Shared tenants are the default model and do not provide any assurance of deployment.

options.text: Run the EC2 instances in a spread placement group.
Group the EC2 instances in separate accounts.
Configure the EC2 instances with dedicated tenancy.
Configure the EC2 instances with shared tenancy.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a disaster recovery (DR) strategy to provide Amazon EC2 capacity in a failover AWS Region. Business requirements state that the DR strategy must meet capacity in the failover Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
This requirement is expressed as a volume guarantee in the fault switching area. Only Capability Reservation will actually reserve computing capacity in a given available area: at the time of failure, the example can be guaranteed to start.
Option A: No advance presets for example as required: In case of regional failure, the required capacity may not be available at all.
Option B: The Saves Plan is a financial commitment made to obtain a discount; it does not guarantee capacity.
Option C: Regional reserved examples provide discounts and flexibility across available areas, but they do not reserve capacity; this can only be achieved by zonal reserved examples or capacity retention.

options.text: Purchase On-Demand Instances in the failover Region.
Purchase an EC2 Savings Plan in the failover Region.
Purchase regional Reserved Instances in the failover Region.
Purchase a Capacity Reservation in the failover Region.

question_text:
A company has five organizational units (OUs) as part of its organization in AWS Organizations. Each OU correlates to the five businesses that the company owns. The company's research and development (R&D) business is separating from the company and will need its own organization. A solutions architect creates a separate new management account for this purpose.
What should the solutions architect do next in the new management account?
explanation_en:
Key rules: An AWS account may belong to only one organization at the same time. Therefore, the order of operation must be strict — the R & D account must first leave the organization (which requires that the account must have a valid billing and contact information that cannot be recorded) and then the new organization's management account sends an invitation to the account, which accepts the invitation. The resources themselves remain unchanged: only the membership of the organization of the account has changed.
Option A: It is not technically possible to belong to both organizations.
Option C: Creating a new account and moving resources is a project involving shutdown and risk, and simply moving existing accounts is sufficient.
Option D: The management account of the new organization cannot belong to another organization: it is equally subject to the `rules of an organization'.

options.text: Have the R&D AWS account be part of both organizations during the transition.
Invite the R&D AWS account to be part of the new organization after the R&D AWS account has left the prior organization.
Create a new R&D AWS account in the new organization. Migrate resources from the prior R&D AWS account to the new R&D AWS account.
Have the R&D AWS account join the new organization. Make the new management account a member of the prior organization.

question_text:
A company is designing a solution to capture customer activity in different web applications to process analytics and make predictions. Customer activity in the web applications is unpredictable and can increase suddenly. The company requires a solution that integrates with other web applications. The solution must include an authorization step for security purposes.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The flow is unpredictable and may suddenly surge, requiring integration with multiple Web applications and a delegation of authority step. API Gateway provides a single entry point, while Lambda authorizer - the mechanism that the gateway itself contains - handles the authorization. The data then flowed to Kinesis Data Firehose, which buffered the data and transmitted it to S3 for analysis without any management action.
Option A: A Gateway Load Balancer is designed to route traffic to detection equipment, does not perform the requested authorization, and EFS-based packagings require continuous transport.
Option B: Kinesis Data Stream does not write S3 per se - it requires consumers to do this, using an independent authorized function instead of the authorizer embedded in API Gateway.
Option D: This repeats the same error in using Gateway Load Balancer as the entry point for client requests, while introducing unnecessary container infrastructure.

options.text: Configure a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) container instance that stores the information that the company receives in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Authorization is resolved at the GWLB.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of an Amazon Kinesis data stream that stores the information that the company receives in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an AWS Lambda function to resolve authorization.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose that stores the information that the company receives in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to resolve authorization.

Configure a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) container instance that stores the information that the company receives on an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Use an AWS Lambda function to resolve authorization.

question_text:
An ecommerce company wants a disaster recovery solution for its Amazon RDS DB instances that run Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise Edition. The company's current recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) are 24 hours.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Recovery targets are more liberal: data loss and downtime are acceptable for up to 24 hours. This makes it the most economical option to copy automatic snapshots to another region on a daily basis — you simply pay for the cache, not run a copy of the database in the second area.
Option A: A cross-regional reading copy is an example of ongoing operations, with a round-the-clock billing, which provides a much better RPO/RTO than is actually required.
Option B: DMS needs a copy of the example and a database of ongoing targets — again, this is an unnecessary expense.
Option C: Copying the back-up of the primary engine into a S3 bucket with cross-regional reproduction capabilities would add an additional layer of automation and storage for the same result, and the built-in snapshot copy already provides these functions.

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote the read replica to the primary instance.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create RDS cross-Region replication.
Use cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Copy automatic snapshots to another Region every 24 hours.

question_text:
A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer that has sticky sessions enabled. The web server currently hosts the user session state. The company wants to ensure high availability and avoid user session state loss in the event of a web server outage.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The session status is currently stored on the Web server itself, so server failure could result in the loss of the user session. The correct solution is to relocate it to external storage: ElastiCache for Redis supports copying, auto-failure transfers to copy nodes and data durability, so that even if the cache node or Web server fail, the session status is maintained.
Option A: Memcached does not support either copying or data durability: if the node fails, the session will be lost.
Option C:Storage Gateway is a hybrid gateway for local environments; it is not designed to store Web application sessions.
Option D: The relationship database is technically capable of storing a session, but at a slower and more costly pace than the memory cache; the standard option for storage of a session is Redis.

options.text: Use an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached instance to store the session data. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Memcached to store the session state.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state.
Use an AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store session data. Update the application to use AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store the session state.
Use Amazon RDS to store the session state. Update the application to use Amazon RDS to store the session state.

question_text:
A company migrated a MySQL database from the company's on-premises data center to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The company sized the RDS DB instance to meet the company's average daily workload. Once a month, the database performs slowly when the company runs queries for a report. The company wants to have the ability to run reports and maintain the performance of the daily workloads.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Heavy-reporting queries run on a monthly basis, disrupting daily workloads. A read-only copy absorbs these queries, allowing the primary example to focus on the daily load that it was originally designed to handle.
Option B: Restore a snapshot of a point at which the data will be provided from the backup and require manual operation every month.
Option C: Export to S3 and use the Athena query means that an independent export conduit needs to be constructed and that outdated data needs to be processed.
Option D: An expansion of an example that lasts only one day a month means that a higher cost is required for a full 30 days and that it is not possible to separate the load.

options.text: Create a read replica of the database. Direct the queries to the read replica.
Create a backup of the database. Restore the backup to another DB instance. Direct the queries to the new database.
Export the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the S3 bucket.
Resize the DB instance to accommodate the additional workload.

question_text:
A company runs a container application by using Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The application includes microservices that manage customers and place orders. The company needs to route incoming requests to the appropriate microservices.
Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Reference answer: D; disputed option: B.
The standard mode of route-to-microservice in EKS is through AWS Load Balancer Contractors; API Gateway is usually more expensive
AWS Load Balancer Contractor can create ALBs for EKS Industries and route requests to different Kubernetes service according to HTTP path or rules. Only micro-service routers need not be added to API Gateway, so source D is changed to B.
Source answer D's original resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
The task is to route incoming requests to different micro-services within the EKS - i.e. to select the backend based on the path or host. This requires a 7th layer load balancer. The standard practice in EKS is the use of Ingress resources, deployed by AWS Load Balancer Contractor for an Application Load Balancer: a single ALB serves every service in a cluster, charged on an hourly basis and added to the LCU usage. It is controversial that the dry answer key points to D (API Gateway), which is charged on request and adds an independent component to the cluster. Empirical law: API Gateway is selected when the API Gateway function (e.g. API key, restricted flow, authorization, request for conversion) is really needed; otherwise, ACB is the standard option for EKS.
Source old option A: A Network Load Balancer runs on the 4th floor, distinguishing only between ports and protocols. It cannot request micro-services based on URL route.
Source old option B: A powerful and EKS standard solution: the same controller, but deployed in ALB, which supports path- and mainframe-based paths, is usually cheaper for stabilizing traffic than API Gateway.
Source old option C: Place Lambda in front of EKS means building a custom agent: each call charge, additional delay, and the manual writing of route logic instead of the rules embedded in the load equalizer.

options.text: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision a Network Load Balancer.
Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision an Application Load Balancer.
Use an AWS Lambda function to connect the requests to Amazon EKS.
Use Amazon API Gateway to connect the requests to Amazon EKS.

question_text:
A company uses AWS and sells access to copyrighted images. The company’s global customer base needs to be able to access these images quickly. The company must deny access to users from specific countries. The company wants to minimize costs as much as possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
There are three requirements: rapid delivery to a global audience, blocking country-specific visits and reducing costs. CloudFront meets all three of these needs: content is provided from the edge (more quickly and cheaper than the direct transmission of data from S3), geographical limitations prevent requests from listed countries, and signature URLs limit access to specific clients and only for a limited period. The drum itself is restricted to direct access through source access (OAC) and therefore these restrictions cannot be circumvented.
Option A: A public drum provides a picture to everyone without any country restriction and MFA is not related to anonymous access. For the payment element, this means a loss of income.
Option B: Create an IAM user for each client that would become an administrative nightmare in a large global client scenario, and that would neither provide faster delivery nor meet country-level access restrictions.
Option C: Deployment of a set of examples behind each country, through a load balancer, is the most costly and labour-intensive option and a separate link for each country can easily be bypassed.

options.text: Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) and public bucket access. Provide customers with a link to the S3 bucket.
Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Create an IAM user for each customer. Add the users to a group that has permission to access the S3 bucket.

Use Amazon EC2 instances that are behind Application Load Balancers (ALBs) to store the images. Deploy the instances only in the countries the company services. Provide customers with links to the ALBs for their specific country's instances.
Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute the images with geographic restrictions. Provide a signed URL for each customer to access the data in CloudFront.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing a highly available Amazon ElastiCache for Redis based solution. The solutions architect needs to ensure that failures do not result in performance degradation or loss of data locally and within an AWS Region. The solution needs to provide high availability at the node level and at the Region level.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Both the nodal and regional levels need to be fault-tolerant and data cannot be lost. This requires the use of the Redis copying group of the Multi-AZ, each of which consists of a copy of the main node and its distribution in different available areas: when a node fails, it is automatically switched to a copy and the data is kept.
Option B: The addition of a read-only document (AOF) only protects data on a single node, but failure of the node or its available area will result in disruption of access to the cluster.
Option C: This option sounds close to correct, but it describes clusters with read-only copies, without making it clear that the fractions are distributed across multiple nodes; the correct structure is a clear multi-usable copying group, and each fraction contains multiple nodes.
Option D: Automatic expansion adjusts the capacity to the load, not related to error tolerance.

options.text: Use Multi-AZ Redis replication groups with shards that contain multiple nodes.
Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Redis append only files (AOF) turned on.
Use a Multi-AZ Redis cluster with more than one read replica in the replication group.
Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Auto Scaling turned on.

question_text:
A company plans to migrate to AWS and use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances for its application. During the migration testing phase, a technical team observes that the application takes a long time to launch and load memory to become fully productive.
Which solution will reduce the launch time of the application during the next testing phase?
explanation_en:
It is not an example of slow start-up, but of the time that the application takes to reach full production — it requires preheating memory. The hibernation saves memory to disks, while the automatically extended preheat pool keeps the already initialized cases on standby, which can be restored in a few seconds, rather than going through the full application loading process.
Option A: Automatic expansion adds more examples, but each new example still requires the same slow preheating process.
Option B: The seizure example changes prices only; the initialization time remains unchanged.
Option D: Volume presets the availability of the example, but does not speed up the process of loading the application to memory.

options.text: Launch two or more EC2 On-Demand Instances. Turn on auto scaling features and make the EC2 On-Demand Instances available during the next testing phase.
Launch EC2 Spot Instances to support the application and to scale the application so it is available during the next testing phase.
Launch the EC2 On-Demand Instances with hibernation turned on. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools during the next testing phase.
Launch EC2 On-Demand Instances with Capacity Reservations. Start additional EC2 instances during the next testing phase.

question_text:
A company's applications run on Amazon EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups. The company notices that its applications experience sudden traffic increases on random days of the week. The company wants to maintain application performance during sudden traffic increases.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The peaks of traffic occur on random days, and therefore neither fixed schedules nor historical projections can be used. Dynamic expansion responds on the basis of actual indicators, adding examples only when the actual increase in loads is carried — while providing the required performance, avoiding paying for idle capacity.
Option A: Manually resize groups that need to be kept on standby for random traffic peaks.
Option B: Predictive expansion depends on a pattern of recurrence, but the peak here is random.
Option D: Time extension is also not applicable for the same reason: it is not possible to know in advance when the peak occurs.

options.text: Use manual scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
Use predictive scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
Use dynamic scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
Use schedule scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.

question_text:
An ecommerce application uses a PostgreSQL database that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. During a monthly sales event, database usage increases and causes database connection issues for the application. The traffic is unpredictable for subsequent monthly sales events, which impacts the sales forecast. The company needs to maintain performance when there is an unpredictable increase in traffic.
Which solution resolves this issue in the MOST cost-effective way?
explanation_en:
The problem is the depletion of connections during unpredictable monthly peaks. Aurora Servers v2 can adjust the capacity to the load in a few seconds and automatically shrink during the idle period, so that the cost of peak capacity does not have to be covered throughout the year. The engine is PostgreSQL compatible, so the application does not need to be rewritten.
Option B: There is no automatic expansion of the database running on the EC2 instance: only the example itself can be adjusted and can only be manually performed, leading to a downtime.
Option C: A larger RDS example will be billed all day, even if the peak occurs only once a month: it will be more expensive.
Option D: Redshift is an analytical data repository; it is not a service load for e-commerce applications.

options.text: Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2.
Enable auto scaling for the PostgreSQL database on the EC2 instance to accommodate increased usage.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a larger instance type.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Redshift to accommodate increased usage.

question_text:
A company hosts an internal serverless application on AWS by using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The company’s employees report issues with high latency when they begin using the application each day. The company wants to reduce latency.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Delays occurred at the beginning of the working day - a typical cold start-up mode, since staff members arrived approximately at the same time. The pre-positioning and function-maintenance examples are in an initial state and the extension will commence shortly before the commencement of the work, so that the company will not continue to pay for the reserved capacity.
Option A: The API Gateway limit settings prevent overloading, with no effect on the start-up time of the function.
Option C: Regular calls through a timer only preheat individual cases, and employees generate dozens of simultaneous requests.
Option D: Additional memory will speed up calculation, but the delayed peak at the beginning of the working day is caused by the creation of the newly implemented environment.

options.text: Increase the API Gateway throttling limit.
Set up a scheduled scaling to increase Lambda provisioned concurrency before employees begin to use the application each day.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to initiate a Lambda function as a target for the alarm at the beginning of each day.
Increase the Lambda function memory.

question_text:
A research company uses on-premises devices to generate data for analysis. The company wants to use the AWS Cloud to analyze the data. The devices generate .csv files and support writing the data to an SMB file share.
Company analysts must be able to use SQL commands to query the data. The analysts will run queries periodically throughout the day.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose three.)
explanation_en:
These devices can only be written to SMB sharing, so local storage gateways are deployed in Amazon S3 file gateway mode: CSV files are stored directly as objects in S3 buckets (A). From there, the reptiles of AWS Glue determine the data structure and create a table (C) in the data catalogue, where analysts run SQL queries through Amazon Athena, paying only bytes of scans (F). There is no ongoing cluster involvement - this is the most economical route for cyclical queries.
Option B: FSx file gateways will cache access to FSx filesystems and data will not eventually be stored in S3, so Glue and Athena cannot read it.
Option D: EMR clusters are charged for running time by nodes, but queries are run only a few times a day: the cost is for spare capacity.
Option E: Redshift clusters will also be billed on a continuous basis; for cyclical inquiries, the cost is significantly higher than Athena ' s s scanned-paying pricing model.

options.text: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway on premises in Amazon S3 File Gateway mode.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway on premises in Amazon FSx File Gateway made.
Set up an AWS Glue crawler to create a table based on the data that is in Amazon S3.
Set up an Amazon EMR cluster with EMR File System (EMRFS) to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.
Set up an Amazon Redshift cluster to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.
Setup Amazon Athena to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.

question_text:
A company wants to use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) clusters and Amazon RDS DB instances to build and run a payment processing application. The company will run the application in its on-premises data center for compliance purposes.
A solutions architect wants to use AWS Outposts as part of the solution. The solutions architect is working with the company's operational team to build the application.
Which activities are the responsibility of the company's operational team? (Choose three.)
explanation_en:
Original answer: ACE; source correction answer: ACF.
According to the AWS Joint Liability Model, the physical maintenance of the rack components (option E) and the availability of the Outposts infrastructure itself are the responsibility of AWS, while the customer's responsibilities include power and network connectivity, physical security of the facility, and maintenance of spare capacity in case of server failure - namely, A, C and F
Outposts clients are responsible for physical security of electrical power and network on site, rooms and the planning of additional capacity to respond to server failure and maintenance; AWS is responsible for physical maintenance of the inner-frame components. E of the source ACE should read F
AWS Outlooks is located in the client ' s own facility, so the line of responsibility extends along the rack. Clients are required to provide high-availability power and network connections (A) to hangers, physical safety and access control (C) to the facility itself, and to reserve additional capacity in the ECS cluster to ensure that server failure or maintenance events do not cause disruption (F): Outlooks is a fixed-capacity pool and does not automatically expand.
Option B: AWS owns virtual overloaders, storage systems and AWS services running on Outlooks - client cannot access this layer.
Option D: AWS is responsible for the availability of the Outposts infrastructure, including power supply, servers and network equipment on the rack.
Option E: Physical maintenance of the Outposts component is performed on-site by AWS technicians. The answer key assigns this to the customer's responsibility — this is an error recorded in the audit log.

options.text: Providing resilient power and network connectivity to the Outposts racks
Managing the virtualization hypervisor, storage systems, and the AWS services that run on Outposts
Physical security and access controls of the data center environment
Availability of the Outposts infrastructure including the power supplies, servers, and networking equipment within the Outposts racks
Physical maintenance of Outposts components
Providing extra capacity for Amazon ECS clusters to mitigate server failures and maintenance events

question_text:
A company is planning to migrate a TCP-based application into the company's VPC. The application is publicly accessible on a nonstandard TCP port through a hardware appliance in the company's data center. This public endpoint can process up to 3 million requests per second with low latency. The company requires the same level of performance for the new public endpoint in AWS.
What should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?
explanation_en:
The application runs TCP at non-standard ports and must process millions of requests per second while keeping delays low. This is precisely the characteristic of the network load balancer: it operates on the fourth floor, processing millions of connections per second, introducing minimal delays and listening to any port.
Option B: Apply the load balancer to understand only HTTP and HTTPS: It cannot handle any TCP protocol.
Option C: CloudFront only supports HTTP and HTTPS and cannot listen to any TCP port.
Option D: API Gateway only supports HTTP and WebSocket, does not support any TCP, nor does it provide such throughput.

options.text: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Configure the NLB to be publicly accessible over the TCP port that the application requires.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Configure the ALB to be publicly accessible over the TCP port that the application requires.
Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution that listens on the TCP port that the application requires. Use an Application Load Balancer as the origin.
Deploy an Amazon API Gateway API that is configured with the TCP port that the application requires. Configure AWS Lambda functions with provisioned concurrency to process the requests.

question_text:
A company runs its critical database on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime and data loss.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The standard path for PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL is a copy read by Aurora: it is created from running examples, synchronized and consistent, and is subsequently upgraded to a stand-alone cluster. The shutdown time was reduced to the time required to switch without losing data, and the built-in control desk tool was used throughout the process.
Option A: A copy of the time point will be provided from the restoration of the snapshot: changes after the snapshot will be lost and the stoppage will be significantly longer.
Option C: Importing from S3 requires the early export of data and requires a long time to write to the freeze.
Option D: Using pg_dump for export and recovery is the slowest path, with long shut-down windows and manual operation steps.

options.text: Create a DB snapshot of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance to populate a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
Create an Aurora read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Promote the Aurora read replicate to a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
Use data import from Amazon S3 to migrate the database to an Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
Use the pg_dump utility to back up the RDS for PostgreSQL database. Restore the backup to a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.

question_text:
A company's infrastructure consists of hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances that use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage. A solutions architect must ensure that every EC2 instance can be recovered after a disaster.
What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of effort?
explanation_en:
There are hundreds of examples and the work required is minimal. AWS Backup can cover the entire fleet of all instances through a backup plan, the configuration of autoback examples and additional volumes, and can start recovery operations through API or CLI batches. No custom scripts or templates need to be prepared.
Option A: Volume snapshots do not keep the case configuration and will require manual preparation and maintenance of the CloudFormation template for hundreds of machines.
Option B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys the application from the code and does not have the design to restore any instance from the snapshot.
Option D: Two custom Lambda functions for the processing of snapshots and AMI imply the need for code, schedule and error processing - the most time-consuming work, not the least.

options.text: Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to launch new EC2 instances from the EBS storage.
Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to set the environment based on the EC2 template and attach the EBS storage.
Use AWS Backup to set up a backup plan for the entire group of EC2 instances. Use the AWS Backup API or the AWS CLI to speed up the restore process for multiple EC2 instances.

Create an AWS Lambda function to take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance and copy the Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). Create another Lambda function to perform the restores with the copied AMIs and attach the EBS storage.

question_text:
A company recently migrated to the AWS Cloud. The company wants a serverless solution for large-scale parallel on-demand processing of a semistructured dataset. The data consists of logs, media files, sales transactions, and IoT sensor data that is stored in Amazon S3. The company wants the solution to process thousands of items in the dataset in parallel.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
The demand is a server-free solution for the parallel processing of thousands of data in the S3 data set. The Map state in StepFunctions is designed under a distributed mode: it directly reads the list of objects from the drums and activates up to 10,000 parallel sub-executions without clustering and without a custom distribution code.
Option A: The in-link mode of Map status supports up to 40 parallel branches and keeps all data in the performance status - it cannot process thousands of data.
Option C: AWS Glue can do this, but it is based on Space's ETL, with its own operations and configurations - a larger operating cost than the built-in distributed Map.
Option D: Multiple Lambda functions require manual division of loads, tracking of co-production and collection of results - you must build the entire scheduler yourself.

options.text: Use the AWS Step Functions Map state in Inline mode to process the data in parallel.
Use the AWS Step Functions Map state in Distributed mode to process the data in parallel.
Use AWS Glue to process the data in parallel.
Use several AWS Lambda functions to process the data in parallel.

question_text:
A company will migrate 10 PB of data to Amazon S3 in 6 weeks. The current data center has a 500 Mbps uplink to the internet. Other on-premises applications share the uplink. The company can use 80% of the internet bandwidth for this one-time migration task.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
This is again attributable to harsh arithmetic: 80% of 500 Mbps is 400 Mbps, about 4.3 TB per day. At this rate, ten petabytes take thousands of days, but the deadline is only six weeks. Optimization of online transmission is not helpful here — it requires physical shipment: multiple Snowball devices are loaded in parallel. Empirical: Using "1 Gbps ⁇ 10 TB per day" to estimate the amount of data, if this estimate exceeds the allotted time, the answer is offline transmission.
Option A: DataSync accelerates and validates the transmission, but it still uses the same 400 Mbps uplink. Timeline error up to two orders of magnitude.
Option B: rsync cannot be used directly as a file system in conjunction with S3, either way being limited to the same bandwidth.
Option C: Multiple parallel CLI copying processes share the same links: combined throughput will not exceed 400 Mbps.

options.text: Configure AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon S3 and to automatically verify the data.
Use rsync to transfer the data directly to Amazon S3.
Use the AWS CLI and multiple copy processes to send the data directly to Amazon S3.
Order multiple AWS Snowball devices. Copy the data to the devices. Send the devices to AWS to copy the data to Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company has several on-premises Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (ISCSI) network storage servers.
The company wants to reduce the number of these servers by moving to the AWS Cloud. A solutions architect must provide low-latency access to frequently used data and reduce the dependency on on-premises servers with a minimal number of infrastructure changes.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Requirements are lower number of servers, low delayed access to frequently used data and minimal infrastructure changes. The rolls that are configured for the cache are provided through the same iSCSI protocol, so that the client does not detect any difference, while most data are stored in S3 and only active parts are kept in local caches. This is how reliance on local storage servers is reduced.
Option A: S3 file gateway provides sharing through NFS and SMB: protocol changes, but emphasis is required on minimising changes.
Option B: EBS rolls are located inside AWS and are connected to the instance instead of to the local server of the company.
Option C: A stored volume keeps the entire data set on a local disk, so the number and capacity of local storage servers are not reduced.

options.text: Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway.
Deploy Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage with backups to Amazon S3.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is configured with stored volumes.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is configured with cached volumes.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing an application that will allow business users to upload objects to Amazon S3. The solution needs to maximize object durability. Objects also must be readily available at any time and for any length of time. Users will access objects frequently within the first 30 days after the objects are uploaded, but users are much less likely to access objects that are older than 30 days.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
"Maximizing Persistence of Object" and "Able to Access" set standards: Storage classes must keep a copy between the three available areas and be able to return the object immediately. This makes S3 Standard and Standard-IA candidate options. The pattern of access is known and is relevant to the life cycle of the object — the first 30 days of frequent visits, followed by rare visits — so that the visible configuration life cycle rules are more economical than the automatic classification with surveillance costs.
Option A: S3 Glacier takes minutes to hours to retrieve. This is a violation of the requirement of "accessible at any time".
Option C: A Zone-IA keeps only one copy in a single available area. This is directly contrary to the requirement to maximize the persistence of the object.
Option D: This combination makes no sense: Intelligent-Tiering itself moves objects between levels, with superimposed life-cycle rules at the top, pushing objects into IA, and you have paid for surveillance. For known modes of access, the direct and simple transition to Standard-IA is more economical.

options.text: Store all the objects in S3 Standard with an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 Glacier after 30 days.
Store all the objects in S3 Standard with an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 Standard- Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.
Store all the objects in S3 Standard with an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 One Zone- Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.
Store all the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering with an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.

question_text:
A company has migrated a two-tier application from its on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud. The data tier is a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for Oracle with 12 TB of General Purpose SSD Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage. The application is designed to process and store documents in the database as binary large objects (blobs) with an average document size of 6 MB.
The database size has grown over time, reducing the performance and increasing the cost of storage. The company must improve the database performance and needs a solution that is highly available and resilient.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The central problem is that 6MB documents are stored in databases in the form of binary large objects: databases expand, performance decreases and RDS storage costs increase. The right solution is to split the data: store the document itself in S3 and only keep metadata and references in the database. This significantly reduces the size of the database, enhances performance, and the cost of S3 storage is much lower than the database and keeps the Multi-AZ configuration unchanged.
Option A: Disk storage is slower and doubling capacity will only increase costs — performance will change rather than improve.
Option B: The use of larger examples and the retention of IOPS can speed up, but this is the most expensive path and the underlying problem — binary objects in the database — remains unresolved.
Option D: Migration to DynamoDB implies rewrite applications and 400 KB project size limits make it impossible to store six megabytes of documents.

options.text: Reduce the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiB. Change the storage type to Magnetic.
Increase the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiChange the storage type to Provisioned IOPS.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to store documents in the S3 bucket. Store the object metadata in the existing database.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Update the application to use DynamoDB. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate data from the Oracle database to DynamoDB.

question_text:
A company has an application that serves clients that are deployed in more than 20.000 retail storefront locations around the world. The application consists of backend web services that are exposed over HTTPS on port 443. The application is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The retail locations communicate with the web application over the public internet. The company allows each retail location to register the IP address that the retail location has been allocated by its local ISP.
The company's security team recommends to increase the security of the application endpoint by restricting access to only the IP addresses registered by the retail locations.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Only the IP addresses of the registered store need to be allowed to pass, and these are thousands of addresses and the list is constantly changing. The AWS WAF matching IP list is designed for this purpose: address collections are maintained separately from rules, support tens of thousands of entries and can be updated through API without changing Web ACL itself. Web ACL is associated with the load balancer, and any address that is not in the pool is blocked before it reaches the application.
Option B: Firewall Manager centrally distributes the WAF strategy between accounts, but it does not implement filters per se - in any case, WAF is a bottom-up service.
Option C: Application of the load balancer does not have an authorization mechanism based on Lambda: it is responsible for route requests, and the construction of custom validation requires code writing within the application.
Option D: Network ACL The rules for each list are limited to about 20 (maximum only slightly higher) - 200,000 addresses cannot be accommodated.

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the ALB. Use IP rule sets on the ALB to filter traffic. Update the IP addresses in the rule to include the registered IP addresses.
Deploy AWS Firewall Manager to manage the ALConfigure firewall rules to restrict traffic to the ALModify the firewall rules to include the registered IP addresses.
Store the IP addresses in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure an AWS Lambda authorization function on the ALB to validate that incoming requests are from the registered IP addresses.
Configure the network ACL on the subnet that contains the public interface of the ALB. Update the ingress rules on the network ACL with entries for each of the registered IP addresses.

question_text:
A company is building a data analysis platform on AWS by using AWS Lake Formation. The platform will ingest data from different sources such as Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS. The company needs a secure solution to prevent access to portions of the data that contain sensitive information.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
What needs to be hidden is not the entire table, but part of it, and must be done without rewrite the data. LakeFormation provides built-in mechanisms to achieve this - data filters: they define which columns are visible (column security) and which rows are returned on condition (line security) to determine which specific cells a subject can access. Filters are enforced at the service level and therefore have the same behaviour in Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR. The bottom data will remain unchanged and no copy will be created.
Option A: A character with a form permission grants access in either an all-or-all way. The demand is to hide part of the table.
Option C: Stripting sensitive data prior to ingestion means losing information that other teams may need, while building and maintaining a custom treatment conduit.
Option D: Periodically use a function clearing table that both destroys data and leaves windows where sensitive information is exposed before the data is destroyed.

options.text: Create an IAM role that includes permissions to access Lake Formation tables.
Create data filters to implement row-level security and cell-level security.
Create an AWS Lambda function that removes sensitive information before Lake Formation ingests the data.
Create an AWS Lambda function that periodically queries and removes sensitive information from Lake Formation tables.

question_text:
A company deploys Amazon EC2 instances that run in a VPC. The EC2 instances load source data into Amazon S3 buckets so that the data can be processed in the future. According to compliance laws, the data must not be transmitted over the public internet. Servers in the company's on-premises data center will consume the output from an application that runs on the EC2 instances.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
There are two requirements, which are met by two different mechanisms. For example, the flow to S3 must not go through the Internet - this requires creating a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and adding a route to the sub-network route list. The local server of the company must receive the output of the application - this requires a direct connection between local location and VPC to create a private link bypassing the Internet.
Option A: EC2 interface endpoints provide private access for EC2 management API, not S3. The uploading of data to the storage can still go through the Internet.
Option C: Transit Gateway is used to connect a network to a network instead of connecting the network to a S3 service. Cannot attach a S3 bucket to it.
Option D: NAT gateway itself is a path to the public Internet: this is a direct violation of requirements and the proxy example increases additional workload and costs.

options.text: Deploy an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on- premises network and the VPC.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway connection from the VPC to the S3 buckets. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Set up proxy EC2 instances that have routes to NAT gateways. Configure the proxy EC2 instances to fetch S3 data and feed the application instances.

question_text:
A company has an application with a REST-based interface that allows data to be received in near-real time from a third-party vendor. Once received, the application processes and stores the data for further analysis. The application is running on Amazon EC2 instances.
The third-party vendor has received many 503 Service Unavailable Errors when sending data to the application.
When the data volume spikes, the compute capacity reaches its maximum limit and the application is unable to process all requests.
Which design should a solutions architect recommend to provide a more scalable solution?
explanation_en:
503 Errors mean that data intake is limited by the ability to calculate. Kinesis Data Teams capture data independently of processing speed and keep records, while the Lambda function handles data in parallel and expands automatically. As a result of ingestion and processing of decompositions, data surges no longer lead to failure.
Option B: A scheme for the use of quota restrictions would restrict suppliers, meaning that it would discard part of the data rather than accept it.

question_text:
A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. The application needs to process sensitive information from an Amazon S3 bucket. The application must not use the internet to connect to the S3 bucket.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Applications in private subnets need to access S3 without going through the Internet. VPC terminals are the only mechanism that provides such pathways: traffic is transmitted through the AWS network without a public address or NAT. In addition, the storage barrel strategy can be tightened through the aws:sourceVpce condition so that the S3 buckets containing sensitive data do not respond to requests not to pass through this terminal. For S3, a gateway terminal is usually used because it is free of charge; an interface terminal is required when access must be initiated from a local network through DirectConnect.
Option A: An Internet gateway exists to send traffic to the Internet, and the storage barrel strategy itself cannot describe such sources. This is a direct violation of the requirements.
Option B: VPN connects VPC to an external network, not VPC to S3. The request for S3 will still be made through the public endpoint.
Option C: NAT gateway is an Internet export path with address conversion. This is contrary to requirements and additional charges are charged on the basis of the treatment of Gibytes.

options.text: Configure an internet gateway. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from the internet gateway. Update the application to use the new internet gateway.

question_text:
A company uses Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to run a container application. The EKS cluster stores sensitive information in the Kubernetes secrets object. The company wants to ensure that the information is encrypted.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
This relates to an internal function of EKS: key encryption using KMS keys. The cluster needs to be configured only once, after which the Secret object is encrypted by an envelope before writing to etcd - by the control plane, not by the application. No code or extra service is required, so it's called "Minimum Operating Costs". The same mechanism is described in Question 535; do not confuse it with storing application keys in Securitys Manager or Parameter Store.
Option A: Encryption within the application means that each container needs to interact directly with KMS, while the other components of the cluster will still read the keys in explicit form from etcd.
Option C: The use of a separate Lambda function for encryption implies the need for a custom code and additional steps in the chain, while EKS can achieve the same functionality by configuration alone.
Option D: Parameter Store stores parameters outside Kubernetes. The secret objects in etcd will remain unencrypted and the demand is clearly addressed to these objects.

options.text: Use the container application to encrypt the information by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).

question_text:
A company is designing a new multi-tier web application that consists of the following components:
•Web and application servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances as part of Auto Scaling groups
•An Amazon RDS DB instance for data storage A solutions architect needs to limit access to the application servers so that only the web servers can access them.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
An application load balancer is placed between the Web layer and the application layer. The target group consists of an automatic extension group of the application server and limited access through the security group: the load balancer and the entry rules on the application server only allow traffic from the Web server security group. The rule is sustainable regardless of the number of instances or the change of address, as it refers to a security group rather than a specific address.
Option A: PrivateLink is used to publish services to other VPCs or accounts, rather than to separate tiers within the same network. Network Access Control List (Network ACL) functions in subnet and address ranges and does not have reference concepts for dynamic automatic extension groups.
Option B: VPC peer provides access to AWS services or services published through PrivateLink; you cannot place an endpoint in front of your example within the same VPC.
Option C: The configuration of the load balancer is correct per se, but the rule is expressed through the Network ACL - the Web Access Control List is active in the address range and subnet and cannot be quoted in the security group of the Web server, and the rule is no longer accurate once the composition of the fleet changes.

explanation_en:
What is needed is to collect, aggregate and aggregate cluster indicators and logs in one place. Amazon Cloudwatch Container Insights has achieved this for EKS: it collects indicators at cluster, node, Pod and container levels, obtains logs, and constructs a prototype dashboard in the Cloudwatch console.
Option A: Claudwatch Age collects node-level indicators and logs, but does not aggregate with Kubernetes objects, nor does it provide a summary of the type in use.

A company has deployed its newest product on AWS. The product runs in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer. The company stores the product’s objects in an Amazon S3 bucket.

The solution must also report suspicious activity and display the information on a dashboard.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is to continuously monitor suspicious activities in accounts, work loads and access to the drums and to present the findings on the dashboard. This is the GuardDuty: it analyzes CloudTrail, S3 data event logs, DNS logs and VPC flow logs to detect unusual and known malign patterns. The results were found to be sent to AWS Security Hub as a unified dashboard. The difference is that GuardDutiy is in charge of testing and Security Hub is in charge of aggregating and assessing compliance.

explanation_en:
Target storage requires the provision of data to multiple AWS resources through NFS protocols, i.e. Amazon EFS(B). The migration of data without disrupting existing services is the AWS DataSync function: to deploy agents in data centres and to transmit incrementally while verifying data integrity, without affecting operations on the source server (E). 200 gbytes of data are transmitted very quickly through any reasonable connection.

The company has a recovery point objective (RPO) of 5 minutes for planned system maintenance or unplanned service disruptions. The company needs to replicate the file system to the us-west-2 Region. The replicated data must not be deleted by any user for 5 years.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The planned maintenance and accidental interruption of the five-minute RPO (recovery point target) was achieved through the deployment of multi-usable areas (Multi-AZ): FSx synchronized the data to the second available area and automatically achieved a failure switch. Cross-regional replication is generated by the planned AWS backup plan, while five years of non-variability comes from the compliance mode locked in the backup repository, where no person, including the account owner, can shorten or delete the retention period.
