Therefore, the existing portal remains unchanged, but is moved to an automatic extension group containing an example on demand, thereby achieving the required 100 per cent availability. The new text extraction program is running at a low frequency and is therefore designed as a Lambda function, which is triggered by uploading the document: you only have to pay for the number of seconds you actually run.
Option B: Spot instance can be retrieved at any time, which conflicts with the requirement of 100% portal availability.
Option C: Purchase of a savings plan for a rarely running extraction process means payment of almost unused commitment costs.
Option D: This is the option that the source practice material uses as its key. It migrates the portal to the static hosting on S3 and recommends that the current functionality — that is, the re-engineering of the application — be restored through API Gateway and Lambda, which, together with the scene, requires an explicit prohibition twice.

options.text: Run Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Use an AWS Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.

Run Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Run the document extract program on EC2 Spot Instances. Start document extract program instances when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.
Purchase a Savings Plan to run the web portal and the document extract program. Run the web portal and the document extract program in an Auto Scaling group.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket to host the web portal. Use Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function for the existing functionalities. Use the Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when the API that is associated with a new document upload is called.

question_text:
A media company has a multi-account AWS environment in the us-east-1 Region. The company has an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic in a production account that publishes performance metrics. The company has an AWS Lambda function in an administrator account to process and analyze log data.
The Lambda function that is in the administrator account must be invoked by messages from the SNS topic that is in the production account when significant metrics are reported.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Original answer: AB; source correction answer: AC.
Cross-Account SNS Subscribe to Resource Policy (A) in the Lambda function and Theme Policy (C) to allow subscription; SQS buffer in option B has changed the call source and is not compatible with A
Cross-account SNS triggers the target function for Lambda to enable SNS calls and sources topic policy to allow the target account to create subscriptions. The SQS buffer program from AB also lacks a queue access strategy and event source mapping step; change to AC.
Cross-account calls are authorized from both sides. The function requires a resource policy that allows SNS to call it (A) and the theme also needs a policy that allows the function to subscribe to (C). Without any link, subscriptions cannot be created or are not working properly.
Option B: A SQS queue in the administrator account changes the source of the trigger function: the queue becomes the trigger, not the theme. This is incompatible with option A and adds components not required by the task itself.
Option D: An additional service has been introduced using the EventBridge Relay SNS Notification at a location where SNS already has direct access to the Lambda function in another account.
Options E:S3 and Athena replace call functions to change the overall structure: treatment is no longer event-based, analysis becomes needs-based.

options.text: Create an IAM resource policy for the Lambda function that allows Amazon SNS to invoke the function.

Implement an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue in the administrator account to buffer messages from the SNS topic that is in the production account. Configure the SQS queue to invoke the Lambda function.
Create an IAM policy for the SNS topic that allows the Lambda function to subscribe to the topic.

Use an Amazon EventBridge rule in the production account to capture the SNS topic notifications. Configure the EventBridge rule to forward notifications to the Lambda function that is in the administrator account.
Store performance metrics in an Amazon S3 bucket in the production account. Use Amazon Athena to analyze the metrics from the administrator account.

question_text:
A company is migrating an application from an on-premises location to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The company must use a custom subnet for pods that are in the company's VPC to comply with requirements. The company also needs to ensure that the pods can communicate securely within the pods' VPC.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The Amazon VPC CNI plugin is a component of the Pod network that manages the EKS network: it distributes the Pod address directly from the VPC subnet. The custom network mode allows you to specify which subnets these addresses are coming from, which is what the scene requires; because Pod has a real VPC address, the normal security group applies to them -- thus achieving controlled, secure communications within the network.
Option A: A transmission gateway is used for traffic between different networks, not related to the distribution of subnets for Kubernetes Pod.
Option B: Connect the company ' s local site directly to AWS. It has nothing to do with choosing the mode of communication between Pod subnets or Pods.
Option D: Anti-relationship rules control which points Pod is placed on, rather than the subnet that controls Pod's access.

options.text: Configure AWS Transit Gateway to directly manage custom subnet configurations for the pods in Amazon EKS.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection from the company's on-premises IP address ranges to the EKS pods.
Use the Amazon VPC CNI plugin for Kubernetes. Define custom subnets in the VPC cluster for the pods to use.
Implement a Kubernetes network policy that has pod anti-affinity rules to restrict pod placement to specific nodes that are within custom subnets.

question_text:
A company hosts an ecommerce application that stores all data in a single Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that is fully managed by AWS. The company needs to mitigate the risk of a single point of failure.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
explanation_en:
The database was already managed by AWS; the single problem was the lack of alternative examples from another region. The least effort would be to modify the example itself to enable the multi-usable area (Multi-AZ): AWS would create a backup example in another area and set up its own simultaneous copying, with no change in endpoints and no change in the application. The application of the change during the maintenance window also addressed the parking problem.
Option B: Migration to DynamoDB means changes in the data model and rewrite of the application query. That is the best, not the least.
Option C: New examples of recovery from a snapshot mean stoppage, loss of up-to-date data, and end-point changes, and only one setting is required to achieve the same goal.
Option D: RDS is unable to join the EC2 Automatic Extension Group, and spreading the writing request through Route 53 to multiple independent databases will result in data inconsistencies.

options.text: Modify the RDS DB instance to use a Multi-AZ deployment. Apply the changes during the next maintenance window.

Migrate the current database to a new Amazon DynamoDB Multi-AZ deployment. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with a heterogeneous migration strategy to migrate the current RDS DB instance to DynamoDB tables.
Create a new RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. Manually restore the data from the existing RDS DB instance from the most recent snapshot.
Configure the DB instance in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum group size of three. Use Amazon Route 53 simple routing to distribute requests to all DB instances.

question_text:
A company has multiple Microsoft Windows SMB file servers and Linux NFS file servers for file sharing in an on-premises environment. As part of the company's AWS migration plan, the company wants to consolidate the file servers in the AWS Cloud.
The company needs a managed AWS storage service that supports both NFS and SMB access. The solution must be able to share between protocols. The solution must have redundancy at the Availability Zone level.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Demand is fully matched, with only one service meeting: to support the hosting storage of NFS and SMB protocols, to allow both protocols to share access from the same data and to be redundant at the level of available areas. This is the Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP that allows multi protocol access in the multi-usable area configuration.
Option B: Self-managed servers in EC2 cases are not hosting services, data are not shared among them and redundancy must be built manually.
Option C: FSx for Lustre does not provide data services via NFS, and two separate storage systems do not allow shared access to the same file.
Option D: S3 File Gateway supports both protocols, but it is a hybrid gateway that contains local virtual devices, rather than a centralized hosting storage with regional redundancy.

options.text: Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP for storage. Configure multi-protocol access.
Create two Amazon EC2 instances. Use one EC2 instance for Windows SMB file server access and one EC2 instance for Linux NFS file server access.
Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP for SMB access. Use Amazon FSx for Lustre for NFS access.
Use Amazon S3 storage. Access Amazon S3 through an Amazon S3 File Gateway.

question_text:
A software company needs to upgrade a critical web application. The application currently runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance that the company hosts in a public subnet. The EC2 instance runs a MySQL database. The application's DNS records are published in an Amazon Route 53 zone.
A solutions architect must reconfigure the application to be scalable and highly available. The solutions architect must also reduce MySQL read latency.
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The three requirements are achieved through two steps. Widenability and usability of the Web layer: an automatic extension group, where examples are distributed behind private subnets in multiple available areas, through an application load balancer (B). Lower MySQL reading delay: Move to an Aurora MySQL cluster, with main and reading examples in different available areas - reading queries sent to copy and copying delays of millisecond (C). As an additional benefit, the database has also been removed from the public subnet.
Option A: A single example located in the second area, with a fail-over strategy, which neither provides scalability nor reduces the reading delay, is still a machine.
Option D: An automatic extension group and a load balancer target group are located in the same region: examples from other regions cannot be added.
Option E: Cross-regional copies are used for reading operations or disaster recovery in other parts of the globe. The scene was concerned with the delay in reading an application, which would only increase delays and costs.

options.text: Launch a second EC2 instance in a second AWS Region. Use a Route 53 failover routing policy to redirect the traffic to the second EC2 instance.
Create and configure an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. Add the instances to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer.
Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. Create the primary DB instance and reader DB instance in separate Availability Zones.
Create and configure an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions. Add the instances to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer.
Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with cross-Region read replicas.

question_text:
A company runs thousands of AWS Lambda functions. The company needs a solution to securely store sensitive information that all the Lambda functions use. The solution must also manage the automatic rotation of the sensitive information.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Original answer: CD; Source correction answer: BC.
Parameter Store does not support automatic rotations - only Secrets Manager supports; the second step is to use Lambda to get keys
Secrets Manager Native Support Key Auto Rotation; in many Lambda functions, re-use the same player/extension to get the key to reduce duplicates. Parameter Store does not have an automatic primary rotation option that is equivalent to the Secrets Manager, so the source CD is changed to BC.
Of the listed options, only Secrets Manager can automatically rotate the key (C) and, with thousands of functions, you need a way to get the key without copying the paste code — the Lambda Layer (B).
Option A: Lambda@Edge and header information are not related to the storage key: it concerns the processing of HTTP requests on the edge.
Option D: Parameter Store can store parameters at low cost, but it does not have built-in automatic rotations - which is what is needed.
Option E: "Consumers with special throughput" is the term Kinesis, and the environmental variables created in this way will not be rotated.

options.text: Create HTTP security headers by using Lambda@Edge to retrieve and create sensitive information
Create a Lambda layer that retrieves sensitive information
Store sensitive information in AWS Secrets Manager
Store sensitive information in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
Create a Lambda consumer with dedicated throughput to retrieve sensitive information and create environmental variables

question_text:
A company has an internal application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The EC2 instances are compute optimized and use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.
The company wants to identify cost optimizations across the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes the use indicators and also produces recommendations for optimization for the three resource types mentioned in the scenario: EC2 Examples, Automatic Extension Group and EBS Volumes. Just start the service — the report is automatically generated, and no manual export or billing is required.
Option A: Cost and use report is a detailed cost split rather than a proposal to rationalize resource allocation.
Option B: Bill warning warns when the cost threshold is exceeded and does not contain any recommendations.
Option D: There is no need to split tasks into two tools: Compute Optimizer already covers the optimization of automatic extension groups and EBS volumes.

options.text: Create a new AWS Cost and Usage Report. Search the report for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes.
Create new Amazon CloudWatch billing alerts. Check the alert statuses for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes.
Configure AWS Compute Optimizer for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group and the EBS volumes.

Configure AWS Compute Optimizer for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances. Create a new AWS Cost and Usage Report. Search the report for cost recommendations for the Auto Scaling group and the EBS volumes.

question_text:
A company is running a media store across multiple Amazon EC2 instances distributed across multiple Availability Zones in a single VPC. The company wants a high-performing solution to share data between all the EC2 instances, and prefers to keep the data within the VPC only.
What should a solutions architect recommend?
explanation_en:
Examples shared across different available areas, high performance, and required to be kept within VPC - that is, Amazon EFS. The file system is mounted through NFS in each instance and the mounted target is created in the VPC subnet, so the flow is kept inside the network.
Option A: Access to S3 through its API requires rewrite applications and traffic will leave the network without VPC endpoints.
Option B: Cannot use standard tools to mount S3 drums into a volume: no such function exists.
Option C: An EBS volume is located in a single available area and is usually connected to only one instance: it does not meet the requirement for cross-district shared access.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket and call the service APIs from each instance's application
Create an Amazon S3 bucket and configure all instances to access it as a mounted volume
Configure an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and mount it across all instances
Configure an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system and mount it across all instances

question_text:
A company uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. To prepare for end-of-year processing, the company added a read replica to accommodate extra read-only queries from the company's reporting tool. The read replica CPU usage was 60% and the primary instance CPU usage was 60%.
After end-of-year activities are complete, the read replica has a constant 25% CPU usage. The primary instance still has a constant 60% CPU usage. The company wants to rightsize the database and still provide enough performance for future growth.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
After the end of the year-end report, only a quarter of the volume of copies was carried, while the main example remained at 60 per cent. This means that the size of the copy should be reduced, while the main example remains unchanged: the copy load is reasonable and has room for growth.
Option A: Deleting a copy will re-send the report query to the main instance and make it overload again.
Option C: Extending the copy to 25 per cent of the utilization rate would be a waste of money and reducing the main example to 60 per cent would remove its growth margin.
Option D: Delete the copy and expand the master example to the most expensive option and lose the reading and writing separation.

options.text: Delete the read replica Do not make changes to the primary instance
Resize the read replica to a smaller instance size Do not make changes to the primary instance
Resize the read replica to a larger instance size Resize the primary instance to a smaller instance size
Delete the read replica Resize the primary instance to a larger instance

question_text:
A company is migrating its databases to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company is migrating its applications to Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to optimize costs for long-running workloads.
Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The load is long and stable, with the goal of minimizing costs. The largest discount comes from the maximum commitment and full advance: a three-year reservation for RDS and a three-year EC2 case savings plan (full advance) for the example.
Option A: The RDS-based pricing model is the most expensive model for a stable work load.
Option B: A one-year commitment without advance payment provides the least discount in all commitment modalities.
Option C: a one-year, partially up-fronted programme with savings less than three years and full up-front.

options.text: Use On-Demand Instances for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year Compute Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.

Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the No Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.

Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the Partial Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the Partial Upfront option for the EC2 instances.

Purchase Reserved Instances for a 3 year term with the All Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 3 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the All Upfront option for the EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company is using an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The company must ensure that Kubernetes service accounts in the EKS cluster have secure and granular access to specific AWS resources by using IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
IRSA is made up of two parts. Part I: The EKS cluster has an OIDC provider and the IAM role must precisely trust that provider - the trust strategy will designate the provider and a condition (E) for a specific service account. Part II: The Kubernetes service account itself will add the role ARN by annotation, and Pod will then operate under the service account to obtain temporary certificate (D) through Web Service. This is how the authority is precisely delegated to the application, rather than to the entire node.
Option A: The permission to give a node role is available for each Pod on the node - this is the opposite of the fine particle access that IRSA is intended to provide.
Option B: Kubernetes network policy limits traffic between Pods. They neither grant nor revoke AWS API privileges.
Option C: None of the single roles in the cluster can be combined with the privileges of all service accounts: the mapping of privileges is done through separate roles by OIDC and annotation, respectively.

options.text: Create an IAM policy that defines the required permissions Attach the policy directly to the IAM role of the EKS nodes.
Implement network policies within the EKS cluster to prevent Kubernetes service accounts from accessing specific AWS services.
Modify the EKS cluster's IAM role to include permissions for each Kubernetes service account. Ensure a one- to-one mapping between IAM roles and Kubernetes roles.
Define an IAM role that includes the necessary permissions. Annotate the Kubernetes service accounts with the Amazon ResourceName (ARN) of the IAM role.
Set up a trust relationship between the IAM roles for the service accounts and an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider.

question_text:
A company regularly uploads confidential data to Amazon S3 buckets for analysis.
The company's security policies mandate that the objects must be encrypted at rest. The company must automatically rotate the encryption key every year. The company must be able to track key rotation by using AWS CloudTrail. The company also must minimize costs for the encryption key.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Requirements include static data encryption, automatic annual rotation, confirmation of rotation through CloudTrail, and minimum cost keys. If you are able to enable, validate and view log log log rotation, it is provided only by the client-managed KMS key: it has 365 days of automatic rotation switches, historical records of key materials, and the ClaudeTrail log entry for each usage. The cost is $1 per month per key plus the requested cost, which is the minimum price for all three requirements; the only additional savings are from the commissioning of S3 Bucket Key, as described in question 1009.
Option A: When using SSE-C, the client management key: AWS does not store it, rotates it or records its use. There is no automatic rotation, and there is no CloudTrail log.
Option B: SSE-S3 is free, but the key is invisible: the rotation cycle is not specified, and there is no single ClaudTrail entry entry recording key used. The audit requirements could not be met.
Option C: Undefined naming means using the key (ws/s3) administered by AWS: it is free and rotates automatically, but you can neither control its strategy nor its rotation, nor can you configure it. The controls required for this scene are derived from the key managed by the client.

options.text: Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
Use server-side encryption with customer managed AWS KMS keys

question_text:
A company has migrated several applications to AWS in the past 3 months. The company wants to know the breakdown of costs for each of these applications. The company wants to receive a regular report that includes this information.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
To view the expenditure by application, the resource needs to be labeled with the application name and the label is activated in the management account as a cost allocation label - the tab will be ignored in the bill before it is activated. Following activation, the cost explorer will split according to label values and can send periodic reports. There is no need for additional services or storage, which is also the cheapest option.
Option A: AWS Budgets does not export historical expenditure by application: it only monitors thresholds.
Option B: Loading a cost-use report (CUR) into the RDS example means that a database needs to be kept running and preparing its own query - clearly more expensive and complex than a cost explorer.
Option D: The monthly manual download billing is manual and there is no application split in the bill without a activated label.

options.text: Use AWS Budgets to download data for the past 3 months into a .csv file. Look up the desired information.
Load AWS Cost and Usage Reports into an Amazon RDS DB instance. Run SQL queries to get the desired information.
Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Activate cost allocation tags. Use Cost Explorerto get the desired information.

Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application's name. Use the AWS Billing and Cost Management console todownload bills for the past 3 months. Look up the desired information.

question_text:
An ecommerce company is preparing to deploy a web application on AWS to ensure continuous service for customers. The architecture includes a web application that the company hosts on Amazon EC2 instances, a relational database in Amazon RDS, and static assets that the company stores in Amazon S3.
The company wants to design a robust and resilient architecture for the application.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Error tolerance is constructed simultaneously at three levels. Web Layer: Auto-extension groups across multiple available areas, so that failure in a single area does not interrupt the application. Database: RDS has the capability to switch automatically to a backup instance in the multi-usable area configuration. Static content: Unload the load from the example and bring the content closer to the user through the CloudFront service S3.
Option A: Both the examples and the database are located in a single available area: the failure of a sector will completely disrupt the application. Version control prevents deletion, but does not prevent disruption of services.
Option C: The example is still in the same available area and the provision of static content directly from the example will reduce the load of the web layer, but will eventually expire with one of them.
Option D: EFS One Zone-IA type storage is in a single available area - this is the weakest link in the design that should be fault-tolerant.

options.text: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in the same Availability Zone. Use Amazon S3 with versioning enabled to store static assets.
Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy a Multi-AZ RDS DB instance. Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute static assets.
Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in a second Availability Zone for cross-AZ redundancy. Serve static assets directly from the EC2 instances.

Use AWS Lambda functions to serve the web application. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for the database. Store static assets in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone-Infrequent Access (One Zone-IA).

question_text:
An ecommerce company runs several internal applications in multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its AWS accounts.
A security appliance in the company's networking account must inspect interactions between applications across AWS accounts.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The task is to communicate the flow of traffic between accounts transparently through network security devices without the need to change the application. This is precisely the purpose of the design of the gateway load balancer (GWLB): it works on the third floor, encapsulating traffic in GENEVE and transmitting it to a group of inspection devices, while maintaining the original address. Creates a GWLB terminal (a variant of PrivateLink) in the application account and configures the route to send traffic through the terminal to the network account. This is the standard model for centralized inspections.
Option A: An NLB job on the 4th floor is not designed for transparency checks: it terminates traffic and changes address programs, while the security equipment requires original flow.
Option B: An ALB is the HTTP request load balancer located in an application account. It is not able to conduct centralized checks of cross-account flows.
Option D: A common interface peer issues a specific service - it does not encapsulate any traffic for inspection. This clearly requires a GWLB terminal.

options.text: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the NLB by using an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.

Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the GWLB by using an interface GWLB endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.

question_text:
A company runs its production workload on an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that includes six Aurora Replicas. The company wants near-real-time reporting queries from one of its departments to be automatically distributed across three of the Aurora Replicas. Those three replicas have a different compute and memory specification from the rest of the DB cluster.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
Report queries need to be routed to three specific copies with unique configurations. Aurora is providing a self-defined endpoint for this: a set of examples of definitions is added to the endpoint, and only a load balance between these examples is requested. The rest of the cluster will never see the report load.
Option B: The clone cluster will create a separate copy of the data, which will no longer receive a new writing operation: it will not be near real-time.
Option C: The end point of a given instance points to exactly a machine: there is no automatic distribution between three copies.
Option D: The reader peer will disperse the request to each copy of the cluster, including the other three copies, while actually only three selected copies will be required.

options.text: Create and use a custom endpoint for the workload
Create a three-node cluster clone and use the reader endpoint
Use any of the instance endpoints for the selected three nodes
Use the reader endpoint to automatically distribute the read-only workload

question_text:
A company runs a Node js function on a server in its on-premises data center. The data center stores data in a PostgreSQL database. The company stores the credentials in a connection string in an environment variable on the server. The company wants to migrate its application to AWS and to replace the Node.js application server with AWS Lambda. The company also wants to migrate to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and to ensure that the database credentials are securely managed.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Connection strings in environment variables move to Securitys Manager: The key is encrypted with KMS key, the Lambda function takes the key through the GetSecretValue call under its executing role, and the existing AWS rotation function is automatically rotated for RDS PostgreSQL by the 30-day schedule. There is no need to customize the code or to redeploy the function when the password is changed. A practical detail: Keys are usually cached in the global sphere of the function or via Parameters and Securitys Extension, so API is not called on every call.
Option A: Parameter Store store parameters and encrypt them, but it does not have an built-in automatic rotation function - it cannot be configured in Parameter Store. "
Option C: Environmental variables mean that functions must be updated each time a password is changed, and rotations must be written manually. This is the highest operational burden in the given option.
Option D: KMS store encryption keys instead of vouchers: The username and password cannot be retrieved from KMS, and the rotation key does not change the password in the database.

options.text: Store the database credentials as a parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Configure Parameter Store to automatically rotate the secrets every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the parameter.

Store the database credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure Secrets Manager to automatically rotate the credentials every 30 days. Update the Lambda function to retrieve the credentials from the secret.
Store the database credentials as an encrypted Lambda environment variable. Write a custom Lambda function to rotate the credentials. Schedule the Lambda function to run every 30 days.
Store the database credentials as a key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Configure automatic rotation for the key. Update the Lambda function to retneve the credentials from the KMS key.

question_text:
A company wants to replicate existing and ongoing data changes from an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. The amount of data to replicate varies throughout each day. The company wants to use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) for data replication. The solution must allocate only the capacity that the replication instance requires.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The volume of the change shall fluctuate over the course of the day and shall be configured according to actual needs. This is the description of the AWS DMS Servers: the service assesses the load itself and selects the calculation unit, which expands or shrinks according to the dynamic load, so you do not have to pay for idle capacity.
Option A: A multi-usable area (Multi-AZ) configuration increases the tolerance for error in copying the example, but the capacity is fixed.
Option C: DMS Copy Example is a managed resource: it cannot be placed in the EC2 Autoscaling Group.
Option D: DMS cannot run in its own ECS container: it is a managed service with its own configuration capacity.

options.text: Configure the AWS DMS replication instance with a Multi-AZ deployment to provision instances across multiple Availability Zones.
Create an AWS DMS Serverless replication task to analyze and replicate the data while provisioning the required capacity.
Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale the size of the AWS DMS replication instance up or down based on the amount of data toreplicate.

Provision AWS DMS replication capacity by using Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an AWS Fargate launch type to analyze and replicate the data while provisioning the required capacity.

question_text:
A company has a multi-tier web application. The application's internal service components are deployed on Amazon EC2 instances. The internal service components need to access third-party software as a service (SaaS) APIs that are hosted on AWS.
The company needs to provide secure and private connectivity from the application's internal services to the third-party SaaS application. The company needs to ensure that there is minimal public internet exposure.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The SaaS provider deploys its application to AWS and can therefore access it through AWS PrivateLink: the provider deploys a network load balancer behind its service, the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC and initiates a call through a private address. The traffic will never leave the AWS network, there will be no content open to the public network, and the connection will always be launched only by the company side.
Option A: Set-to-Site VPN connects VPC to the company's own network rather than to a third party's SaaS application: There is no customer gateway to connect to their end.
Option B: The transfer gateway is used for traffic between your VPC and the site, but it does not provide access to the services that others have published.
Option C: This description is the same as that of the correct option, but it is cut short and fails to describe a valid configuration: PrivateLink does not have a model `only allowed to flow out of the station and the provider does not publish the service'.

options.text: Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish a secure connection with the third-party SaaS provider.
Deploy AWS Transit Gateway to manage and route traffic between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.
Configure AWS PrivateLink to allow only outbound traffic from the VPC without enabling the third-party SaaS provider to establish.
Use AWS PrivateLink to create a private connection between the application's VPC and the third-party SaaS provider.

question_text:
A solutions architect needs to connect a company's corporate network to its VPC to allow on-premises access to its AWS resources. The solution must provide encryption of all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC at the network layer and the session layer. The solution also must provide security controls to prevent unrestricted access between AWS and the on-premises systems.
Which solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
Encryption requires that "on the Internet and on the session level" describe IPsec, that is, AWS site to site VPN: the tunnel encrypts all traffic between the enterprise network and the VPC. The second requirement, namely, to prevent unrestricted access, is achieved through network controls within the VPC: traffic is sent by route to the virtual gateway, and the security team plus the network ACL allows only the necessary ports and subnets. Remember this key fact: DirectConnect does not provide encryption per se — it must be superimposed with VPN or MACsec in order to be encrypted.
Option A: DirectConnect is a dedicated connection, but not encrypted: encryption requirements are not met. Route lists are also not a access control mechanism.
Option B: IAM strategy controls access to AWS API, which relates to the network connection between the data centre and VPC.
Option D: The transfer gateway is used to connect to different networks, but it does not by itself create an encrypted channel to an enterprise network: this still needs to be achieved by VPN or DirectConect.

options.text: Configure AWS Direct Connect to connect to the VPC. Configure the VPC route tables to allow and deny traffic between AWS and on premises as required.

Create an IAM policy to allow access to the AWS Management Console only from a defined set of corporate IP addresses. Restrict user access based on job responsibility by using an IAM policy and roles.

Configure AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect to the VPConfigure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPConfigure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.

Configure AWS Transit Gateway to connect to the VPC. Configure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPC. Configure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.

question_text:
A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from a database in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB cluster. The company needs to make the application more secure with minimal programming effort. The company has created credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The same task as question 339: remove the hard-coding certificate and start rotation without rewrite the application. Secrets Manager stores usernames-cipher pairs in encrypted form, the application under its role is read by a single call, and rotates by the RDS MySQL template function provided by AWS - just open. The application will never know that the password has been changed: it always takes the current key.
Option A: KMS manages encryption keys, does not store login names and passwords. The rotation key does not change the certificate in the database.
Option B: Local storage and timing tasks mean that a copy of the key is available on each server and that a synchronized logic with the database needs to be prepared manually. This involves more codes and higher risks than hosting services.
Option D: Parameter Store does not have a mechanism to rotate the database: "through Parameter Store configuration rotation scheme" is not possible.

options.text: Store the credentials in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Create keys in AWS KMS. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation
Store the credentials in encrypted local storage. Configure the application to load the database credentials from the local storage. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating a cron job.

Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating an AWS Lambda function for Secrets Manager.

Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule in the RDS for MySQL database by using Parameter Store.

question_text:
A company wants to move its application to a serverless solution. The serverless solution needs to analyze existing data and new data by using SQL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted at rest and replicated to a different AWS Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Question 134 is completely repetitive, and the answer is the same and helps to understand confirmation. The SQL query for data in S3 is Athena, so the RDS option is immediately excluded. Next, select a encryption scheme that is compatible with cross-regional replication: a multi-area KMS key exists in both regions and the key material is the same, so a copy can be read in situ without re-encrypting or managing the second key policy.
Option B: Amazon RDS is a database server that needs to be loaded in, and needs to perform server-free analysis for data already in S3.
Option C: Athena is the right choice, but SSE-S3 means that each region has an independent and invisible key: it is not possible to manage these keys and it is not possible to confirm whether the copy is protected. The combination of `encrypted plus cross-regional copying ' mentioned in the examination was addressed through multi-area KMS keys.
Option D: Encryption selection is correct, but RDS is still not a server-free way to run SQL on an S3 object.

options.text: Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon RDS to query the data.
Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.

question_text:
A company has a web application that has thousands of users. The application uses 8-10 user-uploaded images to generate AI images. Users can download the generated AI images once every 6 hours. The company also has a premium user option that gives users the ability to download the generated AI images anytime.
The company uses the user-uploaded images to run AI model training twice a year. The company needs a storage solution to store the images.
Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
There are three different data sets, with three different modes of access, and the optimal solution would be different in each case. Original uploaded images require training twice a year for modelling and are not urgent - using the cheapest storage category, Glacier Deep Archive. The generated images of the paid users can be downloaded at any time - S3 Standard. The generation of images by ordinary users is provided every six hours, meaning that access is less frequent but still requires an immediate response — Standard-IA. The overall experience is that when multiple different data categories are listed in the scene, not a single storage category is selected for the entire drum.
Option B: All generated images are stored in Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where object recovery takes minutes to hours. Paying users promised to download at any time, and should not wait so long.
Option C: Putting a source image into a Zone-IA is not only more expensive than Deep Archive, but also more risky: saving only one in a single available area for data to be accessed twice a year is a bad trade-off.
Option D: Two errors exist simultaneously: the source image is stored in a more expensive and less sustainable One Zone-IA, while the resulting image is stored in Glacier, where the user cannot be served quickly.

options.text: Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Move premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard. Move non-premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive Move all generated AI images to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA). Move premium user- generated AI images to S3 Standard. Move non-premium user-generated AI images to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Move uploaded images to Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA). Move all generated AI images to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

question_text:
A company is developing machine learning (ML) models on AWS. The company is developing the ML models as independent microservices. The microservices fetch approximately 1 GB of model data from Amazon S3 at startup and load the data into memory. Users access the ML models through an asynchronous API. Users can send a request or a batch of requests.
The company provides the ML models to hundreds of users. The usage patterns for the models are irregular. Some models are not used for days or weeks. Other models receive batches of thousands of requests at a time.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The same scenario as Question 422: Loaded irregularly, from several weeks without requests to the simultaneous processing of thousands of requests, a walk-in interface, and stored one-gji byte model data in memory. A SQS queue receives and saves requests, and ECS services are read from the queue, and automatic extensions driven by the queue length increase both the number of service examples and the capacity of clusters.
Option A: A network load equalizer cannot target the Lambda function, and it is unacceptable that model data of a gigabyte be reloaded for each cold start.
Option B: The load balancer placed in front of the model will make the processing synchronized, while the interface is described as an absconding step, with thousands of requests breaking out leading to failure.
Option C: The number of vCPUs in the Lambda function is not an automatic extension of the adjusted parameter and a gjibytes size model is not suitable for the Lambda implementation model.

options.text: Direct the requests from the API to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy the ML models as AWS Lambda functions that the NLB will invoke. Use auto scaling to scale the Lambda functions based on the traffic that the NLB receives.

Direct the requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Deploy the ML models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that the ALB will invoke. Use auto scaling to scale the ECS cluster instances based on the traffic that the ALB receives.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the ML models as AWS Lambda functions that SQS events will invoke. Use auto scaling to increase the number of vCPUs for the Lambda functions based on the size of the SQS queue.

Direct the requests from the API into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Deploy the ML models as Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) services that read from the queue. Use auto scaling for Amazon ECS to scale both the cluster capacity and number of the services based on the size of the SQS queue.

question_text:
A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application stores data in an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster.
The company needs to create a disaster recovery (DR) solution. The acceptable recovery time for the DR solution is up to 30 minutes. The DR solution does not need to support customer usage when the primary infrastructure is healthy.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The acceptable recovery time is 30 minutes and the back-up site is not required to serve the customer while the main site is healthy. This is the so-called `ignition light' model: pre-positioning a minimum capacity load balancer and automatic expansion group in the second area, converting the Aurora cluster into a global database with continuous replication, and setting up Route 53 based on a health check to make the main switch from failure. In the event of a disruption, the group would automatically expand and the sub-cluster would be upgraded to the main cluster, the entire process being completed within a 30-minute time limit.
Option B: An active-active setup will continue to handle traffic in the second area, which is not consistent with the needs of the scene and is significantly more expensive. The automatic expansion team was also unable to deploy as an example across regions.
Option C: Resume the RPO of the database from the backup in an hour, while the global database controls it in seconds. In addition, the automatic expansion team remains unable to deploy across the region.
Option D: An expected capacity of zero means that the example must be initiated from the beginning at the time of the disaster and accompanied by the application of preheating, and the infrastructure itself is rebuilt from the configuration backup only after the failure. The recovery time of 30 minutes is highly unreliable.

options.text: Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALB and an Auto Scaling group. Set the desired capacity and maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to a minimum value. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database. Configure Amazon Route 53 for an active-passive failover with ALB endpoints.

Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALUpdate the Auto Scaling group to include EC2 instances from the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database.

Back up the Aurora MySQL DB cluster data by using AWS Backup. Deploy the DR infrastructure in a second AWS Region with an ALB. Update the Auto Scaling group to include EC2 instances from the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Create an Aurora MySQL DB cluster in the second Region Restore the data from the backup.

Back up the infrastructure configuration by using AWS Backup. Use the backup to create the required infrastructure in a second AWS Region. Set the Auto Scaling group desired capacity to zero. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-passive failover. Convert the Aurora MySQL DB cluster to an Aurora global database.

question_text:
A company is migrating its data processing application to the AWS Cloud. The application processes several short-lived batch jobs that cannot be disrupted. Data is generated after each batch job is completed. The data is accessed for 30 days and retained for 2 years.
The company wants to keep the cost of running the application in the AWS Cloud as low as possible.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The first requirement excludes half the option: the job "can't be interrupted" and the AWS takes back the Spot example only after two minutes of warning. Therefore, the calculation resource must be On-Demand (for short batch processing, this is cheaper than leaving a preset example because you only have to pay for the actual running time). Second, in terms of data: within 30 days, there were active visits to the Standard category, followed by almost two years of unused Glacier Deep Archive, which is the cheapest category, plus two years after the expiry of the cut-off.
Option A: Spot instance will be interrupted and the scene will explicitly prohibit the interruption of the operation. For two years of unused storage, the price is about four times that of Deep Archive.
Option B: The resource is correctly selected, but the data is automatically read within the first 30 days, and Glacier Instant Retrieval is charged for each search. It also has a minimum storage period of 90 days, so the conversion to Deep Archive on the 30th day will trigger the early removal of the fine.
Option C: Same as Spot 's error, plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more expensive than Deep Archive, and quick access to data over 30 days old is not required in the scene.

options.text: Migrate the data processing application to Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Instant. Retrieval after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.

Migrate the data processing application to Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Move the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.

Deploy Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to run the batch jobs. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.

Deploy Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to run the batch jobs. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Set an expiration to delete the data after 2 years.

question_text:
A company needs to design a hybrid network architecture. The company's workloads are currently stored in the AWS Cloud and in on-premises data centers. The workloads require single-digit latencies to communicate. The company uses an AWS Transit Gateway transit gateway to connect multiple VPCs.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The single-digit millisecond delay rule excludes the Internet and VPN — which require a dedicated connection. A direct connection to the Direct Connect gateway (D) is made through a transmission virtual interface, which is then linked to the existing transfer gateway (B). This pair of objects allows the site to be connected to all VPCs connected to the transfer gateway, and the addition of a new network does not change this configuration.
Option A: Each VPC operates a single VPN that is transmitted via the Internet: delay is unpredictable and does not meet the requirements of single milliseconds.
Option C: VPN is not directly connected to the Direct Contact gateway - this construction does not exist. VPN is terminated on a virtual private gateway or transmission gateway.
Option E: VPN can be linked to the transfer gateway, but it is still an Internet path that delays unforeseeable.

options.text: Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to each VPC.
Associate an AWS Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway that is attached to the VPCs.
Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to an AWS Direct Connect gateway.
Establish an AWS Direct Connect connection. Create a transit virtual interface (VIF) to a Direct Connect gateway.
Associate AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections with the transit gateway that is attached to the VPCs.

question_text:
A global ecommerce company runs its critical workloads on AWS. The workloads use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that is configured for a Multi-AZ deployment.
Customers have reported application timeouts when the company undergoes database failovers. The company needs a resilient solution to reduce failover time.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Timeout occurs in the moment of transition: the application still holds a connection to the old master example and is not immediately informed of the change. RDS Proxy maintains and reorients the connect pool to the new main example, thereby reducing the time of failure actually experienced by the application by more than half.
Option B: Read a copy reduces the load of the main example, but does not affect the duration of the failure switch.
Option C: Performance Insight helps to detect bottlenecks, but does not in itself accelerate any operation.
Option D: Copying snapshots to other regions is a disaster recovery category rather than a problem with the speed of failure switching within the multi-usable area configuration.

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy. Assign the proxy to the DB instance.
Create a read replica for the DB instance. Move the read traffic to the read replica.
Enable Performance Insights. Monitor the CPU load to identify the timeouts.
Take regular automatic snapshots. Copy the automatic snapshots to multiple AWS Regions.

question_text:
A company has multiple Amazon RDS DB instances that run in a development AWS account. All the instances have tags to identify them as development resources. The company needs the development DB instances to run on a schedule only during business hours.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Examples have been labeled and all that is needed is to start and stop them according to the time schedule. This can be achieved directly by the State Management Association in System Management Services: Selecting the target by label, Configure the operation and plan, and completely without any custom code.
Option A: A Cloudwatch alert tracking indicator, rather than time, still requires a custom function.
Option B: A credible consultant (Trustead Advisor) provides recommendations for optimization rather than a list of examples of planned start-up and discontinuation cases.
Option D: A plan with a function is feasible, but that requires the development and maintenance of a custom code, and the State Manager service can solve the task only by configuration.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to identify RDS instances that need to be stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an AWS Trusted Advisor report to identify RDS instances to be started and stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the RDS instances.

question_text:
A consumer survey company has gathered data for several years from a specific geographic region. The company stores this data in an Amazon S3 bucket in an AWS Region.
The company has started to share this data with a marketing firm in a new geographic region. The company has granted the firm's AWS account access to the S3 bucket. The company wants to minimize the data transfer costs when the marketing firm requests data from the S3 bucket.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The same technology as in question 88: S3 exit flow is by default charged to the owner of the S3 bucket, while Requerer Pays flipped the rule. Marketing companies access the barrels through their own accounts and pay for all requests and terminal transfers, while companies continue to pay only for storage costs. The company already has access rights — this need not change, but simply adjusts the billing method. Please note that, in the Requester Pays model, each request must be signed and include confirmation of payment, and anonymous requests will be refused.
Option B: Transregional reproduction means that the company itself pays for the trans-regional transfer of each object and for the storage of copies. This would increase costs rather than reduce them.
Option C: AWS Resource Access Manager is unable to share S3 drums - access to the drums is granted through storage barrel policy or cross-account role. Even if access is granted, the cost of the transmission is borne by the owner.
Option D: Storage categories have no impact on the cost of transmitting out-of-site, and synchronizing data to other S3 buckets is an export act at the company ' s expense.

options.text: Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company’s S3 bucket.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from the company’s S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.
Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share the S3 bucket with the marketing firm AWS account.
Configure the company’s S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.

question_text:
A company uses AWS to host its public ecommerce website. The website uses an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator for traffic from the internet. The Global Accelerator accelerator forwards the traffic to an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is the entry point for an Auto Scaling group.
The company recently identified a DDoS attack on the website. The company needs a solution to mitigate future attacks.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
explanation_en:
Original answer: A; source correction answer: C.
AWS WAF does not support AWS Global Accerator as a protected resource (supported by resources such as CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner and Verified Access), so Web ACL is attached to the ALB behind the accelerator
The WAF web ACL supports direct association with ALB and limits excessive requests with rue-based rule; Global Accerator is not in itself a resource type directly associated with WAF. Source A read C.
The source practice material, key, has been corrected and is under audit. The speed limit is configured through the AWS WAF rules, but it is not possible to attach Web ACL to Global Accerator: this service does not belong to the type of resources supported by WAF (ClaudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access). Therefore, the speed limit rule was created on the Application Load Balancer, located behind the accelerator, which receives its flow. The change was very minor - the structure remained unchanged and only Web ACL was added to the existing load balance.
Option A: Original Source Practice Key. AWS Global Accerator is not an additional resource to the WAF Web ACL, so this configuration is not possible.
Option B: A custom function to read indicators and modify the network ACL implies the need for codes, delayed response and rigid limits for rules in ACL.
Option D: Placing CloudFront in front of Global Accerator is a remarkable restructuring that requires minimal effort.

options.text: Configure an AWS WAF web ACL for the Global Accelerator accelerator to block traffic by using rate-based rules
Configure an AWS Lambda function to read the ALB metrics to block attacks by updating a VPC network ACL
Configure an AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB to block traffic by using rate-based rules
Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the Global Accelerator accelerator

question_text:
A company uses an Amazon DynamoDB table to store data that the company receives from devices. The DynamoDB table supports a customer-facing website to display recent activity on customer devices. The company configured the table with provisioned throughput for writes and reads.
The company wants to calculate performance metrics for customer device data on a daily basis. The solution must have minimal effect on the table's provisioned read and write capacity.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The calculation of the indicator shall not affect the retention capacity of the table. The DynamoDB export connection reading data in AWS Gloe does not come from the table itself, but rather from the S3 export generated by the backup mechanism, and therefore does not consume the reading capacity units at all.
Option A: The Atena connector for DynamoDB directly scans the table itself and consumes its reading capacity.
Option C: The COPY command for Redshift cannot avoid consuming the DynamoDB table - it will perform a scan.
Option D: The live external table in EMR will also read the table data directly, thus taking up the reading capacity and influencing the client-oriented sites.

options.text: Use an Amazon Athena SQL query with the Amazon Athena DynamoDB connector to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.
Use an AWS Glue job with the AWS Glue DynamoDB export connector to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.
Use an Amazon Redshift COPY command to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.
Use an Amazon EMR job with an Apache Hive external table to calculate performance metrics on a recurring schedule.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing the cloud architecture for a new stateless application that will be deployed on AWS. The solutions architect created an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) and launch template for the application.
Based on the number of jobs that need to be processed, the processing must run in parallel while adding and removing application Amazon EC2 instances as needed. The application must be loosely coupled. The job items must be durably stored.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Jobs need to be permanently stored, handled in parallel and kept loosely bound. A SQS queue can sustain storage operations and decouples the sender with the processor, while an automatic extension group increases and reduces according to the number of messages in the queue — that is, depending on the actual workload rather than on indirect signals.
Option A: SNS does not store messages: if there is no ready subscriber, the operation will be lost and the CPU-based extension will not reflect the queue length.
Option B: Queue selection is correct, but network-based extension is an indirect signal that may not be relevant to the number of operations.
Option D: SNS theme once again does not provide a permanent storage of the operation.

options.text: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on CPU usage.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on network usage.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of items in the SQS queue.

Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of messages published to the SNS topic.

question_text:
A global ecommerce company uses a monolithic architecture. The company needs a solution to manage the increasing volume of product data. The solution must be scalable and have a modular service architecture. The company needs to maintain its structured database schemas. The company also needs a storage solution to store product data and product images.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The requirement is to maintain a structured database model, store pictures and operate as simple as possible using modular rather than mono-structures. Run ECS container services on Fargate without managing nodes; RDS configures the relationship pattern and provides error tolerance in multi-usable areas; and images are stored in S3 without caps on storage capacity.
Option A: The EC2 instance requires you to patch and expand yourself, and storing pictures in a relationship database is a bad practice, swelling the database and increasing costs.
Option B: Encapsulating a single-body structure in the Lambda function does not become modular, and the 400 KB project size limit for DynamoDB makes storage of pictures impossible.
Option C: EKS is run on an EC2 instance by managing nodes, and the Glacier deep archive takes hours to retrieve objects - unacceptable for product pictures.

options.text: Use an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group to deploy a containerized application. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute web traffic. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance to store product data and product images.

Use AWS Lambda functions to manage the existing monolithic application. Use Amazon DynamoDB to store product data and product images. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) for event-driven communication between the Lambda functions.

Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with an Amazon EC2 deployment to deploy a containerized application. Use an Amazon Aurora cluster to store the product data. Use AWS Step Functions to manage workflows. Store the product images in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to deploy a containerized application. Use Amazon RDS with a Multi-AZ deployment to store the product data. Store the product images in an Amazon S3 bucket.

question_text:
A company is migrating an application from an on-premises environment to AWS. The application will store sensitive data in Amazon S3. The company must encrypt the data before storing the data in Amazon S3.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
"The company must encrypt the data before storing it to Amazon S3" means that the encryption must be done on the application level before the data is sent. This is a client encryption using company-controlled keys (usually KMS keys managed by the client through envelope encryption, or own keys). All SSE-based options are excluded by definition: these encryption operations are performed by the service after the object is received. Compared to Question 801, the latter also requires that the key be kept entirely outside the AWS.
Option B: SSE-KMS only encrypts objects when they are received by S3. Doesn't meet the "pre-storage" requirement.
Option C: In SSE-C, the client sends the requested key, but S3 encrypts after receiving the specified data. The key will also be transmitted on the network with each request.
Option D: Client encryption using S3-managed keys is impossible: these keys will never leave the service and will not be accessible.

options.text: Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with customer managed keys.
Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C).
Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys.

question_text:
A company wants to create an Amazon EMR cluster that multiple teams will use. The company wants to ensure that each team’s big data workloads can access only the AWS services that each team needs to interact with. The company does not want the workloads to have access to Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) on the cluster’s underlying EC2 instances.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The task is to assign independent authority to each team on the shared EMR clusters, while preventing operations from accessing evidence of role by example metadata. This is the EMR running-time role: assigns a role to which EMRs are used when the job is submitted, and prevents the operation code from accessing the case profile. In this way, the same infrastructure can serve teams with different competencies.
Option A: Interface endpoint traffic control path, rather than permission to operate. They can't distinguish teams by privileges.
Option C: The case profile gives the same authority to each operation in the cluster and can be accessed through the example metadata — this is precisely what needs to be avoided.
Option D: The role of closing the application range is counterproductive: it returns the operation to the shared instance role instead of the running time role.

options.text: Configure interface VPC endpoints for each AWS service that the teams need. Use the required interface VPC endpoints to submit the big data workloads.
Create EMR runtime roles. Configure the cluster to use the runtime roles. Use the runtime roles to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EC2 IAM instance profile that has the required permissions for each team. Use the instance profile to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EMR security configuration that has the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole option set to false. Use the security configuration to submit the big data workloads.

question_text:
A solutions architect is designing an application that helps users fill out and submit registration forms. The solutions architect plans to use a two-tier architecture that includes a web application server tier and a worker tier.
The application needs to process submitted forms quickly. The application needs to process each form exactly once. The solution must ensure that no data is lost.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Forms need to be processed accurately once and no data are lost. A SQS FIFO queue provides this: messages are stored permanently, repeat messages are discarded in the heavy window, and the sequence and precise processing of messages are guaranteed.
Option B: HTTP API forwards the request, but does not store any data: if the processor is not available, the data will be lost.
Option C: The standard queue ensures at least one delivery, so the form may be processed twice.
Option D: Synchronization of workflows closely binds the layers together: data is lost again if the processor is busy or not available.

options.text: Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an AWS Step Functions workflow. Create a synchronous workflow between the web application server tier and the worker tier that stores and forwards form data.

question_text:
A finance company uses an on-premises search application to collect streaming data from various producers. The application provides real-time updates to search and visualization features.
The company is planning to migrate to AWS and wants to use an AWS native solution.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Demand is for ingestion of streamed data, near real-time search and visualization - using AWS native services. Kinesis Data Streams ingestion data streams from producers, OpenSearch Service indexing them and providing real-time updated search functions, while Amazon QuickSight builder dashboards.
Option A: Self-managed examples for ingestion of data streams are unnecessary operations, and Athena is unable to search for data in S3 in real time.
Option B: EMR and Redshift are batch and analytical processes: they cannot provide real-time updates.
Option C: The use of EKS clusters for data streaming implies the need to manage infrastructure, and Cloudwatch is not a search engine for application data.

options.text: Use Amazon EC2 instances to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon S3 buckets tor storage. Use Amazon Athena to search the data. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to create visualizations.
Use Amazon EMR to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon Redshift for storage. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.

Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon DynamoDB for storage. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create graphical dashboards to search and visualize the data.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use OpenSearch Service to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.

question_text:
A company currently runs an on-premises application that usesASP.NET on Linux machines. The application is resource-intensive and serves customers directly.
