The company wants to modernize the application to .NET. The company wants to run the application on containers and to scale based on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. The company also wants to reduce the time spent on operational maintenance activities.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The application needs to be containerized and run in a way that does not require management infrastructure. AWS App2Container analyzes active applications and generates mirrors and deploys work, including the CloudFormation template, and then runs containers by ECS on Fargate without the need to manage nodes and expands on the Cloudwatch indicator.
Option B: The start-up type of EC2 will reintroduce node management: Operations are not reduced.
Option C: App Runner is not a tool for packaging existing applications and does not deploy task loads to ECS: it is an independent running service.
Option D: The same error with respect to the App Runner role and the re-reference to the EC2 node in the EKS implies the need for management infrastructure.

options.text: Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Use an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.
Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Use an AWS CloudFormation template to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 instances.
Use AWS App Runner to containerize the application. Use App Runner to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.
Use AWS App Runner to containerize the application. Use App Runner to deploy the application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) on Amazon EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company is designing a new internal web application in the AWS Cloud. The new application must securely retrieve and store multiple employee usernames and passwords from an AWS managed service.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
What needs to be stored is specific vouchers — usernames — password pairs — using hosting services to minimize efforts. This is Secrets Manager: The key is encrypted using KMS keys, access is granted by character, and a special BatchGetSecretValue call is provided to read multiple keys in a single request. The existence of the API scene is itself a clue: Parameter Store does not have this operation.
Option A: Parameter Store does not have BatchGetSecretValue call: this API is specifically for Secrets Manager. This option describes a combination that does not exist.
Option B: AWS Watch is a service that runs batch processing calculations on containers - it has nothing to do with reading keys. An unnecessary component in the design.
Option C: Two errors exist simultaneously: the storage service selection does not contain the required API and the AWS Watch was added for no reason.

options.text: Store the employee credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use AWS CloudFormation and the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve usernames and passwords from Parameter Store.
Store the employee credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Use AWS CloudFormation and AWS Batch with the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Secrets Manager.

Store the employee credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use AWS CloudFormation and AWS Batch with the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Parameter Store.
Store the employee credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Use AWS CloudFormation and the BatchGetSecretValue API to retrieve the usernames and passwords from Secrets Manager.

question_text:
A company that is in the ap-northeast-1 Region has a fleet of thousands of AWS Outposts servers. The company has deployed the servers at remote locations around the world. All the servers regularly download new software versions that consist of 100 files. There is significant latency before all servers run the new software versions.
The company must reduce the deployment latency for new software versions.
Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Reference answer: C; dispute option: D.
Repeat the same file on servers in different regions, which is the function of the CloudFront cache; Transfer Acceleration mainly accelerates upload to S3 without cache
The same version of the global multi-site download is suitable for the ClaudFront edge cache, reducing cross-continental back-to-back delays; the original C-S3 Transfer Acceleration focuses on accelerating the transmission to S3 and does not repeat downloads as the ClaudFront cache. A Disables cache, B adds copying and dual-source complexity; read D.
Source answer C's original resolution (in conflict with verification results, not accepted):
Thousands of Outlook servers worldwide regularly download the same 100 files from storage barrels in the ap-northead-1 area. The content is identical, the number of remote consumers is numerous, and downloads are repeated — this is the typical CDN problem: CloudFront caches these files at the edge, so that the second and subsequent servers in the region can access them locally. Source Practice Key selects C (S3 Transfer Action), which is its weakness: Transfer Acceleration accelerates transmission through the AWS core network, but it does not cache, so thousands of servers still need to download files directly from Tokyo. From a rational point of view, option D is a more appropriate match.
Source old option A: CachingDisabled policy closed the cache and eliminated the only reason to use CloudFront. Each request will still be transmitted directly to the source server in the ap-northeast-1 area.
Old Source Option B: Copy data to the second S3 bucket and configure the source site failure switch to solve the problem of error rather than delay. In addition, it has tripled storage space and additional configurations, contrary to the requirement to "minimize operating expenses".
Source old option D: This option essentially solves the problem: CloudFront caches 100 files near the server edge and double downloads locally. That's exactly what's at issue with the source's practice material, Key.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in ap-northeast-1 that includes a CachingDisabled cache policy. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Create a second S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region. Configure replication between the buckets. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses ap-northeast-1 as the primary origin and us-east-1 as the secondary origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Configure Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration. Download the software by using the S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.

question_text:
A company currently runs an on-premises stock trading application by using Microsoft Windows Server. The company wants to migrate the application to the AWS Cloud.
The company needs to design a highly available solution that provides low-latency access to block storage across multiple Availability Zones.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
explanation_en:
A Windows Server cluster requires shared storage, which must be accessed by two nodes, both of which must be located in different serviceable areas. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server requires the least volume of work in this regard: it supports the continued availability of shared folders for clustering, enabling simultaneous replication between different regions and bringing self-availability. There is no need to prepare or configure any content manually.
Option B: Reproduction of the application layer between two gp3 volumes requires manual preparation of logic, risks of data inconsistency, and is the most significant of the options.
Option C: Automatic failure transfer cannot be achieved without a cluster master setup, and more configuration is required for the iSCSI access to the ONTAP than is available for shared folders.
Option D: There is no service-level EBS volume reproduction function across available areas - this function does not exist.

options.text: Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as shared storage between the two cluster nodes.

Configure a Windows Server cluster that spans two Availability Zones on Amazon EC2 instances. Install the application on both cluster nodes. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up application-level replication to sync data from one EBS volume in one Availability Zone to another EBS volume in the second Availability Zone.

Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ file system to access the data by using Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) protocol.

Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Configure one EC2 instance as active and the second EC2 instance in standby mode. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes as storage attached to the EC2 instances. Set up Amazon EBS level replication to sync data from one io2 volume in one Availability Zone to another io2 volume in the second Availability Zone.

question_text:
A company is designing a web application with an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB).
The company needs the ALB to receive HTTPS web traffic from the public internet. The ALB must send only HTTPS traffic to the web application servers hosted on the Amazon EC2 instances on port 443. The ALB must perform a health check of the web application servers over HTTPS on port 8443.
Which combination of configurations of the security group that is associated with the ALB will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
explanation_en:
This involves the load balancer ' s own safety group, and therefore requires an entry and two exit rules. The HTTPS entry flow from 0.0.0.0/0 is on port 443 (A) from the public Internet. The HTTPS traffic to the example on the port 443 forwards the request to application (C). The HTTPS flow is a health check (E) at the exit point of the example on the port 8443.
Option B: Allowing the flow of stations to the entire Internet is excessive: the load balancer only needs to connect to its own target example.
Option D: No entry rule from the instance is required: the load balancer will initiate the connection to the target instance on its own initiative and the response is allowed by the connection status.
Option F: Health check also applies: they are out-of-station traffic and therefore do not need to be equipped with entry rules.

options.text: Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.

question_text:
A company hosts an application on AWS. The application gives users the ability to upload photos and store the photos in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to use Amazon CloudFront and a custom domain name to upload the photo files to the S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region.
Which solution will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Original answer: BD; source correction answer: AD.
The certificate of CloudFront must be issued in the us-east-1 area regardless of which area the drum is located
CloudFront customised ACM certificates for domain names must be at us-east-1 instead of at eu-west-1; CloudFront OAC supports a PUT/POST dynamic request for S3 and needs to be configured with a allowed method and a bootet policy. Source BD to AD.
Two separate claims. The certificate issued by CloudFront for a custom domain name always comes from the ACM(A) area of the us-east-1 area - the storage area of the drum is irrelevant. The ability to write through distribution to the drums comes from source access control (D): CloudFront uploads to S3 via source access control (OAC).
Option B: Certificates issued in the eu-west-1 area will not be shown to CloudFront: only from the us-east-1 area will be distributed.
Option C: S3 Transfer Accelerator is a stand-alone endpoint for uploading content directly and more quickly to S3. It does not confer write privileges on Cloud Front, nor does it need to be used with distribution.
Option E: S3 website endpoints are static content via HTTP service, do not support uploading and cannot work with OAC.

options.text: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in the us-east-1 Region. Use the certificate in CloudFront.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in eu-west-1. Use the certificate in CloudFront.
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront origin access control (OAC).
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure an Amazon S3 website endpoint.

question_text:
A weather forecasting company collects temperature readings from various sensors on a continuous basis. An existing data ingestion process collects the readings and aggregates the readings into larger Apache Parquet files. Then the process encrypts the files by using client-side encryption with KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS).
Finally, the process writes the files to an Amazon S3 bucket with separate prefixes for each calendar day.
The company wants to run occasional SQL queries on the data to take sample moving averages for a specific calendar day.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Data is stored in Parquet format in S3 and is encrypted to the client (CSE-KMS) using KMS keys, and query needs only happen occasionally. Amazon Athena can read such documents directly: it supports the encryption of the client using KMS keys, understands Parquet format and prefix-based partitions, and you pay only for scanned bytes - queries for a single calendar day only scan the prefix of that date. There is no need for clusters and no need for sustained infrastructure. Cost tips: The column format and partitions combined with partition filters can significantly reduce Athena ' s billing.
Option B: S3 Select. Each request handles only one object and cannot read the client's encrypted data. It is therefore not possible to calculate the average of movements across multiple documents in this way.
Option C: Redshift Spectrum requires a Redshift cluster, which will be billed on a continuous basis, and the queries here only happen occasionally. For sporadic queries, this is clearly a clear excess of expenditure.
Option D: EMR Serverles is feasible, but it is already a Spak frame with a self-assembly configuration and start-up cost. For a small number of SQL queries, Athena is simpler and cheaper.

options.text: Configure Amazon Athena to read the encrypted files. Run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Redshift to read the encrypted files. Use Redshift Spectrum and Redshift query editor v2 to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to read the encrypted files. Use Apache SparkSQL to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company is implementing a new application on AWS. The company will run the application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones within multiple AWS Regions. The application will be available through the internet. Users will access the application from around the world.
The company wants to ensure that each user who accesses the application is sent to the EC2 instances that are closest to the user’s location.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The requirement is an example of each user being routed to the nearest geographic location. In Route 53, geoproximity is the mechanism for handling distance: it calculates the degree of proximity to the user on the basis of the coordinates of each resource and adjusts the boundaries of the impact range through bias parameters. Within the same area, the load balancer has distributed requests to all available areas.
Option A: The geographical route is based on the country or continent of the person requesting it, not on distance: a user close to the border may easily be sent to a remote area, simply because the rules of the country so provide.
Option C: Multiple-value responses return a random set of health records, with no consideration of the distance between the user and the example.
Option D: The weighted strategy will allocate the flow according to the ratio set, regardless of where the request comes from.

options.text: Implement an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy. Use an internet-facing Application Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.
Implement an Amazon Route 53 geoproximity routing policy. Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.
Implement an Amazon Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy. Use an internet-facing Application Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.
Implement an Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policy. Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer to distribute the traffic across all Availability Zones within the same Region.

question_text:
A financial services company plans to launch a new application on AWS to handle sensitive financial transactions.
The company will deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company will use Amazon RDS for MySQL as the database. The company’s security policies mandate that data must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Both directions need to be covered with minimal expenses. In a static state: The KMS key is used to open the RDS encryption - it covers disks, snapshots, backups and copies, and no changes are required. During the transmission process: TLS is used, while the public network-oriented portion (load balancer, application domain) can be covered by an automatic renewal of a free ACM certificate. A useful detail of the database connection itself: ACM will not issue certificates for it - the client must trust the root certificate from the AWS package, see question 743.
Option B: The IPsec tunnel to the VPC internal database is an over-designed structure that needs to be deployed and maintained, while the RDS itself has been originally supported by TLS.
Option C: Third-party application layer encryption means that a custom development and self-management key is required. This is contrary to the minimum operating cost requirement.
Option D: VPN can provide privacy for inter-network channels, but it cannot be encrypted to apply traffic to a database or replace TLS. It is also an additional component that needs to be transported.

options.text: Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure IPsec tunnels for encryption in transit.
Implement third-party application-level data encryption before storing data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure a VPN connection to enable private connectivity to encrypt data in transit.

question_text:
A company is migrating its on-premises Oracle database to an Amazon RDS for Oracle database. The company needs to retain data for 90 days to meet regulatory requirements. The company must also be able to restore the database to a specific point in time for up to 14 days.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
There are two requirements: to retain the data for 90 days and to be able to return to any point of time in the past 14 days. RDS has a maximum retention period of 35 days for automatic backup, and therefore AWS Backup is required: the scheme sets a 90-day retention period and restores the point of time through continuous backup. All configurations have been completed through a plan.
Option A: RDS has a maximum retention period of 35 days: 90 days cannot be set.
Option B: Daily manual snapshots can be kept indefinitely, but they do not provide a point of recovery and require self-mobilization to remove old snapshots.
Option C: The cloning function belongs to Aurora and does not apply to RDS for Oracle and cannot replace the recovery of time points.

options.text: Create Amazon RDS automated backups. Set the retention period to 90 days.
Create an Amazon RDS manual snapshot every day. Delete manual snapshots that are older than 90 days.
Use the Amazon Aurora Clone feature for Oracle to create a point-in-time restore. Delete clones that are older than 90 days.
Create a backup plan that has a retention period of 90 days by using AWS Backup for Amazon RDS.

question_text:
A company is developing a new application that uses a relational database to store user data and application configurations. The company expects the application to have steady user growth. The company expects the database usage to be variable and read-heavy, with occasional writes.
The company wants to cost-optimize the database solution. The company wants to use an AWS managed database solution that will provide the necessary performance.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Loads are variable, mainly reading operations, with occasional writing operations; databases need to be relationship-type and managed by AWS; and costs are the primary consideration. Aurora Servers will adjust their capacity to actual usage and automatically shrink when the load is low, so you will not continue to pay for peak capacity and the increase in the number of users will be automatically processed.
Option A: Provisioned IOPS storage will continue to be billed at peak values, even if the load is variable.
Option C: DynamoDB is not a relationship database, and the scene explicitly requires the use of a relationship model.
Option D: Disk storage is obsolete and slow, and multiple read-only copies continue to be billed regardless of the actual load.

options.text: Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD storage to ensure consistent performance for read and write operations.
Deploy the database on Amazon Aurora Serverless to automatically scale the database capacity based on actual usage to accommodate the workload.
Deploy the database on Amazon DynamoDB. Use on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale throughput to accommodate the workload.
Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use magnetic storage and use read replicas to accommodate the workload.

question_text:
A company is building a cloud-based application on AWS that will handle sensitive customer data. The application uses Amazon RDS for the database, Amazon S3 for object storage, and S3 Event Notifications that invoke AWS Lambda for serverless processing.
The company uses AWS IAM Identity Center to manage user credentials. The development, testing, and operations teams need secure access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3 while ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive customer data. The solution must comply with the principle of least privilege.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The company has already used IAM Infrastructure Center, so team visits should be granted through its original mechanism — the allocation of a group of privileges to the relevant accounts. Permissions are defined and reused only once, new staff members are granted access through group membership, and vouchers are always temporary. Setting up a separate parallel IAM role or user for each team will repeat access to the model and will require manual maintenance.
Option A: The role of using the fine grain strategy is the right one, but it should be achieved around the configured Identity Center: Access assignments and rotations must be managed separately.
Option C: A separate IAM user is a long-standing document that needs to be maintained manually, which conflicts with the minimization of the workload and the existence of Identity Center.
Option D: The creation of a separate account for each team is a significant re-engineering of the existing structure, simply to separate access to the two services.

options.text: Use IAM roles with least privilege to grant all the teams access. Assign IAM roles to each team with customized IAM policies defining specific permission for Amazon RDS and S3 object access based on team responsibilities.

Enable IAM Identity Center with an Identity Center directory. Create and configure permission sets with granular access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Assign all the teams to groups that have specific access with the permission sets.

Create individual IAM users for each member in all the teams with role-based permissions. Assign the IAM roles with predefined policies for RDS and S3 access to each user based on user needs. Implement IAM Access Analyzer for periodic credential evaluation.

Use AWS Organizations to create separate accounts for each team. Implement cross-account IAM roles with least privilege. Grant specific permission for RDS and S3 access based on team roles and responsibilities.

question_text:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains sensitive data files. The company has an application that runs on virtual machines in an on-premises data center. The company currently uses AWS IAM Identity Center.
The application requires temporary access to files in the S3 bucket. The company wants to grant the application secure access to the files in the S3 bucket.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The application operates outside AWS, so it does not have an example role or task role and should not issue a long-term key. This is the purpose of the design of IAM Rolls Anywhere: the Virtual Machine requests and displays an X.509 certificate to a trusted certification authority, exchanges temporary role vouchers and uses them to interact with S3. There is no key stored anywhere, access life cycle is limited and revocation is effected by withdrawing a certificate or trust.
Option A: Allows a set of public IP addresses not to constitute authentication: access is granted to all devices located behind the same NAT. It is not acceptable for sensitive data.
Option C: The use of IAM user keys on virtual machines is a long-term key that must be manually distributed and rotated. That's exactly what the "temporary visit" would have wanted to avoid.
Option D: Secrets Manager simply more accurately stores the same long-term key: once the key is leaked, it will remain valid until it is manually revoked.

options.text: Create an S3 bucket policy that permits access to the bucket from the public IP address range of the company’s on-premises data center.
Use IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain security credentials in IAM Identity Center that grant access to the S3 bucket. Configure the virtual machines to assume the role by using the AWS CLI.
Install the AWS CLI on the virtual machine. Configure the AWS CLI with access keys from an IAM user that has access to the bucket.

Create an IAM user and policy that grants access to the bucket. Store the access key and secret key for the IAM user in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to retrieve the access key and secret key at startup.

question_text:
A company hosts its core network services, including directory services and DNS, in its on-premises data center.
The data center is connected to the AWS Cloud using AWS Direct Connect (DX). Additional AWS accounts are planned that will require quick, cost-effective, and consistent access to these network services.
What should a solutions architect implement to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
explanation_en:
It is planned to create many new accounts, each requiring access to directories and DNS services in data centres. By setting up a transfer gateway, sharing the gateway with various accounts using AWS RAM, its VPC connects to the gateway and connects the DirectConnect link to the gateway through the DirectConnect gateway. Each new account is added through a single connection, providing quick, affordable and consistent access to all accounts.
Option A: Each account needs a separate DirectConnect link, which means a multiplication of the number of months of configuration time and port costs.
Option B: VPC endpoints provide private access to AWS services, rather than access to the company ' s directories and DNS servers in the data centre.
Option C: Each account needs a VPN connection, which means that traffic passes through the Internet, has unpredictable delays, and many configurations need to be maintained.

options.text: Create a DX connection in each new account. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.
Configure VPC endpoints in the DX VPC for all required services. Route the network traffic to the on-premises servers.
Create a VPN connection between each new account and the DX VPRoute the network traffic to the on- premises servers.
Configure AWS Transit Gateway between the accounts. Assign DX to the transit gateway and route network traffic to the on-premises servers.

question_text:
A company hosts its main public web application in one AWS Region across multiple Availability Zones. The application uses an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer (ALB).
A web development team needs a cost-optimized compute solution to improve the company’s ability to serve dynamic content globally to millions of customers.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The content is dynamic, the audience is global and the costs need to be particularly optimized. Using the existing load balancer as a source server for CloudFront, both problems can be addressed: TLS terminates at the nearest edge, requests to transfer to the area via the AWS backbone network, and the flow of outbound stations from CloudFront is cheaper than the flow of outbound stations directly from the area. Dynamic content does not even need to be cached — the advantage comes from the network itself and the re-use of the connection.
Option B: Geographic route is reasonable when multiple sites are deployed. There's only one area, and the route does not bring the user closer.
Option C: S3 provides static files only: dynamic applications cannot be moved there. Open reading visits are also a bad practice.
Option D: DirectConnect is a dedicated link to a particular company site, rather than a means of distributing content to millions of users worldwide.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the existing ALB as the origin.
Use Amazon Route 53 to serve traffic to the ALB and EC2 instances based on the geographic location of each customer.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket with public read access enabled. Migrate the web application to the S3 bucket. Configure the S3 bucket for website hosting.
Use AWS Direct Connect to directly serve content from the web application to the location of each customer.

question_text:
A company stores user data in AWS. The data is used continuously with peak usage during business hours. Access patterns vary, with some data not being used for months at a time. A solutions architect must choose a cost-effective solution that maintains the highest level of durability while maintaining high availability.
Which storage solution meets these requirements?
explanation_en:
Three requirements are met simultaneously: maximum persistence, high availability, and reasonable prices in a model where data parts have been unreached for a long time. All storage categories share the persistence of 1199, except for a single area (with the same value in a single area — lost area is lost data), and the selection is reduced to standard storage, standard archiving and intelligent layers. Because access patterns are not known in advance and change continuously, the smart stratification wins: the stratification occurs automatically, without the cost of searching and with the same availability and durability as standard storage.
Option A: S3 Standard meets the requirements of persistence and usability, but the data lasts for months without access and you have to pay the full cost. The scenario also requires cost-effectiveness.
Option C: It takes up to 12 hours for deep archiving to return to the object, while the data are in continuous use and peaks during peak periods of operations. This constitutes a serious violation of the requirement of usability.
Option D: A single area archive retains a copy in a single available area: it does not meet the "maximum persistence" or high availability.

options.text: Amazon S3 Standard
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

question_text:
A company is testing an application that runs on an Amazon EC2 Linux instance. A single 500 GB Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSO (gp2) volume is attached to the EC2 instance.
The company will deploy the application on multiple EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. All instances require access to the data that is stored in the EBS volume. The company needs a highly available and resilient solution that does not introduce significant changes to the application's code.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The data in the EBS volume need to be available for each example in the automatic extension group, without significant code changes and with failure resilience. Amazon EFS directly addresses this problem: the file system is mounted through NFS in each instance, applications continue to use normal paths and data are stored in multiple available areas. The generic performance model provides the lowest delay and applies to most workloads.
Option A: There is only one volume of a self-managed NFS server running on an example, with a single point failure and a physical machine that needs to be maintained.
Option B: Applications run on the Linux system, while SMB is restricted to a single available area, providing neither original protocol nor resistance to the failure of the available area.
Option C: EBS volumes are always bound to individual examples and individual available areas: no access functions are shared.

options.text: Provision an EC2 instance that uses NFS server software. Attach a single 500 GB gp2 EBS volume to the instance.
Provision an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Configure the file system as an SMB file store within a single Availability Zone.
Provision an EC2 instance with two 250 GB Provisioned IOPS SSD EBS volumes.
Provision an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Configure the file system to use General Purpose performance mode.

question_text:
A company recently launched a new application for its customers. The application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones. End users use TCP to communicate with the application.
The application must be highly available and must automatically scale as the number of users increases.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The client communicates through TCP, thus requiring a network load balancer - the application of the load balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS(A). Automatically expands as the number of users increases from the auto-extension group, which adds examples as needed and removes redundant examples (B).
Option C: Apply a load balancer to work on HTTP level and is not suitable to handle any TCP traffic.
Option D: The manual addition of examples conflicts with the automatic extension requirement.
Option E: The gateway load balancer is designed to transmit traffic through virtual network devices, not for the release of applications.

options.text: Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Configure an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances.
Add an Application Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Manually add more EC2 instances for the application.
Add a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.

question_text:
A company is designing the architecture for a new mobile app that uses the AWS Cloud. The company uses organizational units (OUs) in AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The company wants to tag Amazon EC2 instances with data sensitivity by using values of sensitive and nonsensitive. IAM identities must not be able to delete a tag or create instances without a tag.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The needs are divided into two parts, each of which is met by a different organizational strategy. Allows label values (sensitive and non-sensitive) to be described by a enabled label policy that enforces EC2 resources (A). Prohibits the absence of labels at the time of creation of examples and prohibits the deletion of labels from API operations, which are rejected by SCP: ec2: RunInstances with aws:RequestTag for Null, and by ec2: DeleteTags (D). Key differences: Label policy manages label values, while SCP manages which operations are allowed.
Option B: SCP cannot describe the allowed label values set -- this is the function of the label policy. The condition is that the specified value can be checked, but that is not a substitute for managing the dictionary.
Option C: The label policy does not bar API calls: it does not prevent the instance from starting or delete labels. That's SCP duty.
Option E: The AWS Config rule plus the deletion of resources by function is an ex post facto response with the risk of losing the required resources. What needs to be done is prevention.

options.text: In Organizations, create a new tag policy that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the tag policy to the appropriate OU.

In Organizations, create a new service control policy (SCP) that specifies the data sensitivity tag key and the required tag values. Enforce the tag values for the EC2 instances. Attach the SCP to the appropriate OU.
Create a tag policy to deny running instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another tag policy that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the tag policies to the appropriate OU.

Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny creating instances when a tag key is not specified. Create another SCP that prevents identities from deleting tags. Attach the SCPs to the appropriate OU.
Create an AWS Config rule to check if EC2 instances use the data sensitivity tag and the specified values. Configure an AWS Lambda function to delete the resource if a noncompliant resource is found.

question_text:
A company runs database workloads on AWS that are the backend for the company's customer portals. The company runs a Multi-AZ database cluster on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
The company needs to implement a 30-day backup retention policy. The company currently has both automated RDS backups and manual RDS backups. The company wants to maintain both types of existing RDS backups that are less than 30 days old.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
RDS autobacks are automatically deleted after the retention period expires, so setting the retention period to 30 days is sufficient - no additional cost and no additional service. The manual fast notes were retained until they were manually deleted, so the old snapshots had to be manually removed.
Option A: AWS Backup is an unnecessary level here: the automatic backup retention period is directly configured in the RDS, and the back-up service increases costs.
Option B: Close the autoback and delete all existing content in contravention of the requirement to keep the backup at a minimum age of 30 days.
Option D: CloudFormation deploys infrastructure instead of deleting backups according to age; existing backups will be lost again.

options.text: Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups by using AWS Backup. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.
Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.
Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.

Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days automatically by using AWS CloudFormation. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.

question_text:
A company is planning to migrate a legacy application to AWS. The application currently uses NFS to communicate to an on-premises storage solution to store application data. The application cannot be modified to use any other communication protocols other than NFS for this purpose.
Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend for use after the migration?
explanation_en:
The application can only use NFS protocols and cannot be changed. In AWS, the hosting file system that supports the agreement is Amazon EFS: it is mounted on an example as a general web resource, is automatically extended and data is stored across multiple available areas.
Option A: DataSync is used to move data between storage systems and is not a storage system in itself.
Option B: Volume EBS provides a piece of equipment rather than NFS network resources: applications cannot interact with them as they used to be.
Option D: EMRFS is an EMR cluster access layer to S3 rather than a NFS file system for common applications.

options.text: AWS DataSync
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
Amazon EMR File System (Amazon EMRFS)

question_text:
A company uses GPS trackers to document the migration patterns of thousands of sea turtles. The trackers check every 5 minutes to see if a turtle has moved more than 100 yards (91.4 meters). If a turtle has moved, its tracker sends the new coordinates to a web application running on three Amazon EC2 instances that are in multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region.
Recently, the web application was overwhelmed while processing an unexpected volume of tracker data. Data was lost with no way to replay the events. A solutions architect must prevent this problem from happening again and needs a solution with the least operational overhead.
What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Applications were flooded with surges of traffic and data were completely lost. A SQS queue can solve both problems: it can absorb any sudden flow, store messages on a permanent basis and pass them to the application at a rate that the application can handle, so that unprocessed events will remain in the queue rather than disappear.
Option A: Scan the S3 buckets to find the new target with a delayed round of queries and require a custom logic to track which objects have been processed.
Option B: A gateway with a function absorbs sudden flows, but this is redesigning the data intake process, which does not have buffer zones and re-encumber capabilities.
Option D: Repeat the questionnaire to search for new records, which requires a custom search logic, and does not provide a buffer for sudden flows.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the data. Configure the application to scan for new data in the bucket for processing.
Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint to handle transmitted location coordinates. Use an AWS Lambda function to process each item concurrently.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to store the incoming data. Configure the application to poll for new messages for processing.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store transmitted location coordinates. Configure the application to query the table for new data for processing. Use TTL to remove data that has been processed.

question_text:
A company's software development team needs an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ cluster. The RDS cluster will serve as a backend for a desktop client that is deployed on premises. The desktop client requires direct connectivity to the RDS cluster.
The company must give the development team the ability to connect to the cluster by using the client when the team is in the office.
Which solution provides the required connectivity MOST securely?
explanation_en:
The maximum security means that the database should not be accessible from anywhere on the Internet and that the channel must be encrypted. Clusters are deployed in private sub-networks without a public network address and offices are connected to the client gateway through site to site VPN: access may only come from the office network, traffic is encrypted and no public network endpoints are available.
Option A: A cluster located in a public subnet will have access to an Internet-accessible endpoint, and having VPN will not eliminate this: databases may still be attacked around tunnels.
Option C: The security group is limited to the source of the office address, but traffic is still transmitted via the open Internet, there is no network layer encryption and the office address may be forged under other network conditions.
Option D: Public subnets plus database users provide protection only at the account level, with fully open network access. This is the most insecure option.

options.text: Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.
Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway in the company's office.
Create a VPC and two private subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the private subnets. Use RDS security groups to allow the company's office IP ranges to access the cluster.
Create a VPC and two public subnets. Create the RDS cluster in the public subnets. Create a cluster user for each developer. Use RDS security groups to allow the users to access the cluster.

question_text:
A solutions architect is creating an application that will handle batch processing of large amounts of data. The input data will be held in Amazon S3 and the output data will be stored in a different S3 bucket. For processing, the application will transfer the data over the network between multiple Amazon EC2 instances.
What should the solutions architect do to reduce the overall data transfer costs?
explanation_en:
This relates to the cost of data transmission between examples. Traffic across available areas is charged, while private address traffic within the same area is not charged. Therefore, every example of the need for data exchange must be located in the same available area.
Option A: Automatically expand the group to manage the number of examples, but without affecting the cost of the transfer.
Option B: A region is necessary but not sufficient: intraregional flows across available areas will still be charged.
Option D: Multiple available areas are the reason why transfer costs are incurred.

options.text: Place all the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.
Place all the EC2 instances in the same AWS Region.
Place all the EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone.
Place all the EC2 instances in private subnets in multiple Availability Zones.

question_text:
A company hosts a multi-tier web application that uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster for storage. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The company's IT security guidelines mandate that the database credentials be encrypted and rotated every 14 days.
What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?
explanation_en:
Full repetition of question 336: Encrypted with minimum input and rotated every 14 days. Secrets Manager uses KMS keys attached to Aurora's cluster for encryption by configuration of all operations. The rotation cycle is set at any number of days, and AWS provides a rotation function for the supporting database. The other options achieve the same result through the distribution of custom codes and self-designed passwords.
Option B: Parameter Store encrypts the password, but rotation must be manually written and maintained.
Option C: Sharing files on the file system with a custom rotational function increases the development workload, document privileges management and risks that databases and files are not synchronized.
Option D: Regular downloading of password files leaves the application with an outdated window and also requires a custom rotation function.

options.text: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to create a new secret that uses the KMS key with the appropriate credentials. Associate the secret with the Aurora DB cluster. Configure a custom rotation period of 14 days.

Create two parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: one for the user name as a string parameter and one that uses the SecureString type for the password. Select AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption for the password parameter, and load these parameters in the application tier. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password every 14 days.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system in all EC2 instances of the application tier. Restrict the access to the file on the file system so that the application can read the file and that only super users can modify the file. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the key in Aurora every 14 days and writes new credentials into the file.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon S3 bucket that the application uses to load the credentials. Download the file to the application regularly to ensure that the correct credentials are used. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the Aurora credentials every 14 days and uploads these credentials to the file in the S3 bucket.

question_text:
A streaming media company is rebuilding its infrastructure to accommodate increasing demand for video content that users consume daily.
The company needs to process terabyte-sized videos to block some content in the videos. Video processing can take up to 20 minutes.
The company needs a solution that will scale with demand and remain cost-effective.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Video processing takes up to 20 minutes, exceeding the 15-minute enforcement limit in Lambda. Packagings must be used: ECS on Fargate expands on demand, expenses the actual running time of the mission and does not need to manage nodes. The metadata are stored in Aurora, while the video file itself is stored in S3 and uses Inteligent-Tiering, which automatically reduces the cost of the content that is rarely visited.
Option A: 20 minutes beyond Lambda's limit of 15 minutes: the mission will be interrupted.
Option C: The EC2 instance queue must be maintained and expanded, and no load balancer is required before the video processing task.
Option D: EKS running on an EC2 instance means that it is necessary to manage nodes, that databases in a single available area are prone to problems and that it takes hours for the Glacier Deep Archive file to be restored.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions to process videos. Store video metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) and AWS Fargate to implement microservices to process videos. Store video metadata in Amazon Aurora. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

Use Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to process videos. Store video content in Amazon S3 Standard. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) for queuing and to decouple processing tasks.

Deploy a containerized video processing application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) on Amazon EC2. Store video metadata in Amazon RDS in a single Availability Zone. Store video content in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

question_text:
A company runs an on-premises application on a Kubernetes cluster. The company recently added millions of new customers. The company's existing on-premises infrastructure is unable to handle the large number of new customers. The company needs to migrate the on-premises application to the AWS Cloud.
The company will migrate to an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The company does not want to manage the underlying compute infrastructure for the new architecture on AWS.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
The cluster needs to be maintained in Kubernetes and companies do not want to manage computing infrastructure. AWS Fargate on EKS completely solved the problem: created a Fargate project, and Pod, which meets its rules, will run completely without relying on any nodes - no patches, no nodes extension.
Option A: Self-managed nodes are the most cumbersome: mirrors, updates, extensions, etc. all need to be done manually.
Option B: The managed nodes group has simplified operations, but the EC2 nodes still exist and their life cycle still requires attention.
Option D: Karpenter automates the configuration of nodes, but nodes still exist - the infrastructure is not gone.

options.text: Use a self-managed node to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.
Use managed node groups to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.
Use AWS Fargate to supply compute capacity. Create a Fargate profile. Use the Fargate profile to deploy the application.
Use managed node groups with Karpenter to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.

question_text:
A company is launching a new application that requires a structured database to store user profiles, application settings, and transactional data. The database must be scalable with application traffic and must offer backups.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Databases need to be structured, able to expand with traffic, backed up and inexpensive. Aurora Servers meets all of these needs: it has a relationship model, capacity can be adjusted automatically according to the actual load, and it is built into an automated backup to AWS storage. Costs are rarely incurred in idle situations.
Option A: Databases that are self-managed on breakable cases may lose nodes at any time and all operations are carried out by the company.
Option B: Amazon RDS does not have the required capacity mode: the type of instance is continuously billed after an earlier selection.
Option D: Non-relationship databases conflict with the requirements of the structured mode and directly back up to Glacier means that recovery is slow.

options.text: Deploy a self-managed database on Amazon EC2 instances by using open source software. Use Spot Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
Use Amazon RDS. Use on-demand capacity mode for the database with General Purpose SSD storage. Configure automatic backups with a retention period of 7 days.
Use Amazon Aurora Serverless for the database. Use serverless capacity scaling. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
Deploy a self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

question_text:
A company runs its legacy web application on AWS. The web application server runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in the public subnet of a VPC. The web application server collects images from customers and stores the image files in a locally attached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The image files are uploaded every night to an Amazon S3 bucket for backup.
A solutions architect discovers that the image files are being uploaded to Amazon S3 through the public endpoint.
The solutions architect needs to ensure that traffic to Amazon S3 does not use the public endpoint.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The request is to stop using the public S3 terminal node. The gateway terminal node is added to the service prefix in the sub-networked list, traffic is transmitted through the terminal node within the AWS network, and the terminal node policy gives permission to the required S3 bucket. Night uploads do not require any changes to the code line.
Option B: The drum cannot be moved inside the VPC: S3 is a regional service whose network address is not in your network.
Option C: Access points change the address allocation and access control, but the call still passes through the public terminal node, unless there is a matching VPC terminal node in the network.
Option D: Connect the company 's site directly to AWS. The example is already inside the VPC, so there is no point in creating a dedicated connection to it.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for the S3 bucket that has the necessary permissions for the VPC. Configure the subnet route table to use the gateway VPC endpoint.
Move the S3 bucket inside the VPC. Configure the subnet route table to access the S3 bucket through private IP addresses.
Create an Amazon S3 access point for the Amazon EC2 instance inside the VPConfigure the web application to upload by using the Amazon S3 access point.
Configure an AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPC that has the Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon S3 to provide a dedicated network path.

question_text:
A company is creating a prototype of an ecommerce website on AWS. The website consists of an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances for web servers, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that runs with the Single-AZ configuration.
The website is slow to respond during searches of the product catalog. The product catalog is a group of tables in the MySQL database that the company does not update frequently. A solutions architect has determined that the CPU utilization on the DB instance is high when product catalog searches occur.
What should the solutions architect recommend to improve the performance of the website during searches of the product catalog?
explanation_en:
The product catalogue rarely changes, and the search operation increases the load of the CPU database. Use the ElastiCache for Redis cache with inert loads to keep query results in the memory: the first request is sent to the database and the subsequent request is retrieved from the cache, thus reducing the load of the example.
Option A: Redshift is designed for analysis on large data sets, not for fast-track directory queries in real-time applications.
Option C: Adding a Web server does not help: The bottlenecks are in the database, and more examples will only further increase the pressure on it.
Option D: Multi-AZ can improve availability rather than performance, and limiting queries will make the site worse rather than better.

options.text: Migrate the product catalog to an Amazon Redshift database. Use the COPY command to load the product catalog tables.
Implement an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to cache the product catalog. Use lazy loading to populate the cache.
Add an additional scaling policy to the Auto Scaling group to launch additional EC2 instances when database response is slow.
Turn on the Multi-AZ configuration for the DB instance. Configure the EC2 instances to throttle the product catalog queries that are sent to the database.

question_text:
A company currently stores 5 TB of data in on-premises block storage systems. The company's current storage solution provides limited space for additional data. The company runs applications on premises that must be able to retrieve frequently accessed data with low latency. The company requires a cloud-based storage solution.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
explanation_en:
Existing storage is block-based (iSCSI), space is about to run out and hotspot data need to be read with low delay. Volume Gateway is designed in Cache mode: volumes are presented to applications as iSCSI devices, complete datasets are stored in S3 and local disks keep recently used data block caches. There is no need to expand local capacity or to rewrite applications. Compared to Question 307 — the same logic, it is expressed differently.
Option A: S3 File Gateway provides data via SMB and NFS, the file protocol. Applications use iSCSI-based rolls, and switching will mean that these applications need to be rewritten.
Option C: The repository saves a complete copy of the data locally and only takes a snapshot of AWS. The lack of local space has not been addressed.
Option D: Tape Gateway simulates a tape library for backup and archiving. It is not designed for low daily delays in access.

options.text: Use Amazon S3 File Gateway. Integrate S3 File Gateway with the on-premises applications to store and directly retrieve files by using the SMB file system.
Use an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway with cached volumes as iSCSI targets.
Use an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway with stored volumes as iSCSI targets.
Use an AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway. Integrate Tape Gateway with the on-premises applications to store virtual tapes in Amazon S3.

question_text:
A company operates a food delivery service. Because of recent growth, the company's order processing system is experiencing scaling problems during peak traffic hours. The current architecture includes Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that collect orders from an application. A second group of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group fulfills the orders.
The order collection process occurs quickly, but the order fulfillment process can take longer. Data must not be lost because of a scaling event.
A solutions architect must ensure that the order collection process and the order fulfillment process can both scale adequately during peak traffic hours.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
The speed with which orders are collected and compliance is slower requires decoupling and setting up buffer zones at all levels: one SQS queue at each stage to ensure that no data is lost in sudden flows. The expansion of the clusters should be based on the corresponding number of messages in the queue, which is a direct measure of the accumulated workload.
Option A: Maintaining a minimum capacity at peak means that all-weather expenses for the number of cases of peaks will still not prevent data loss.
Option B: Launching a new automatic extension group on the basis of a signal is an unfeasible, unmanageable option and does not provide a buffer for the order.
Option C: Queue selection is correct, but SQS does not send a notification about its status: Extension must be driven by the message number indicator.

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure each Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to meet its peak workload value.

Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to create additional Auto Scaling groups on demand.

Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection. Use the second SQS queue for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on notifications that the queues send.

Provision two Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection. Use the second SQS queue for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on the number of messages in each queue.

question_text:
An online gaming company is transitioning user data storage to Amazon DynamoDB to support the company's growing user base. The current architecture includes DynamoDB tables that contain user profiles, achievements, and in-game transactions.
The company needs to design a robust, continuously available, and resilient DynamoDB architecture to maintain a seamless gaming experience for users.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Continuous multi-regional availability is achieved through a global table: DynamoDB replicates data among regions and allows for writing in any area. The load of game services is predictable and stable, and therefore the cost of using preset capacity to accompany automatic expansion is lower than the amount requested.
Option A: There is a contradiction between tables and global tables within a single area: by definition, the global table must span more than one region.
Option B: Cache can speed up reading, but no one will manually maintain cross-regional copying: this is the purpose for which the global table exists.
Option C: Self-repeated reproduction mechanisms based on change streams need to develop and maintain codes, and the cost of the need-based model is higher under stable loads.

options.text: Create DynamoDB tables in a single AWS Region. Use on-demand capacity mode. Use global tables to replicate data across multiple Regions.
Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache frequently accessed data. Deploy tables in a single AWS Region and enable auto scaling. Configure Cross-Region Replication manually to additional Regions.
Create DynamoDB tables in multiple AWS Regions. Use on-demand capacity mode. Use DynamoDB Streams for Cross-Region Replication between Regions.
Use DynamoDB global tables for automatic multi-Region replication. Deploy tables in multiple AWS Regions. Use provisioned capacity mode. Enable auto scaling.

question_text:
A company runs its media rendering application on premises. The company wants to reduce storage costs and has moved all data to Amazon S3. The on-premises rendering application needs low-latency access to storage.
The company needs to design a storage solution for the application. The storage solution must maintain the desired application performance.
Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
explanation_en:
Data has been moved to S3, but local rendering applications need to read data in a low delay and cannot be rewritten through object API. S3 File Gateway is deployed locally to present S3 buckets as shared folders through NFS or SMB, and to maintain local caches of hotspot files: first reading from S3 and subsequent reading from local disks. You only pay for S3 and a lightweight gateway, not a complete second storage system -- and therefore "most cost-effective."
Option A: The mount point mounts S3 as a file system, but each reading still requires access to S3 through a wide-area network and does not provide real hotspot data with local caches or complete POSIX syntax. The delay in local rendering will remain high.
Option C: Copying data to FSx for Windows File Server means adding a second payment storage system, plus a separate gateway, to the S3 that you have paid. It met the request for delay but suffered cost losses.
Option D: A self-study file server calls S3 API to develop and operate on your own: Cache, consistency and tolerance require manual construction.

options.text: Use Mountpoint for Amazon S3 to access the data in Amazon S3 for the on-premises application.
Configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Copy the data from Amazon S3 to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Configure an on-premises file server. Use the Amazon S3 API to connect to S3 storage. Configure the application to access the storage from the on-premises file server.

question_text:
A company hosts its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system in the us-east-1 Region. The system runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Customers use a public API that is hosted on the EC2 instances to exchange information with the ERP system. International customers report slow API response times from their data centers.
Which solution will improve response times for the international customers MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The API is publicly available, operating through HTTP, and complaints of delays come from overseas clients. The deployment of Cloud Front in front of API will solve two problems: the termination of TLS at its recent edge, the request for subsequent transmission through the AWS backbone network, and the cached response will not touch the regional nodes at all. The key difference here is cost: CloudFront does not have a fixed hourly cost, while Global Accerator always has a fixed cost.
Option A: Providing a dedicated link to each client ' s data centre is the most expensive and slowest option and a public virtual interface cannot even be used in conjunction with the DirectConnect gateway.
Option C: Global Accelerator can also speed up, which is the right answer for non-HTTP flows, but it is more costly: it contains fixed accelerator fees and data transfer premiums, and it has no cache function at all.
Option D: The VPN tunnel to each client network cannot be extended, needs to be configured on each client side and cannot speed up the response of the public API.

options.text: Create an AWS Direct Connect connection that has a public virtual interface (VIF) to provide connectivity from each customer's data center to us-east-1. Route customer API requests by using a Direct Connect gateway to the ERP system API.
Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API. Configure the CachingOptimized managed cache policy to provide improved cache efficiency.
Set up AWS Global Accelerator. Configure listeners for the necessary ports. Configure endpoint groups for the appropriate Regions to distribute traffic. Create an endpoint in the group for the API.
Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish dedicated VPN tunnels between Regions and customer networks. Route traffic to the API over the VPN connections.

question_text:
A company tracks customer satisfaction by using surveys that the company hosts on its website. The surveys sometimes reach thousands of customers every hour. Survey results are currently sent in email messages to the company so company employees can manually review results and assess customer sentiment.
The company wants to automate the customer survey process. Survey results must be available for the previous 12 months.
Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST scalable way?
explanation_en:
Tens of thousands of requests per hour require a buffer, while emotional analysis requires a ready-made service. API Gateway receives the results and puts them in a SQS queue that absorbs sudden flows; a Lambda function reads data from the queue and calls Amazon Comprehend for an emotional rating, which will remain for 12 months.
Option B: API on the EC2 instance is a bottleneck and must be extended and maintained manually.
Option C: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and videos - it is not used to judge text emotions.
Option D: Amazon Lex constructs a dialogue robot; it is not used for emotional analysis in investigations.

options.text: Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create an AWS Lambda function to poll the SQS queue, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

Send the survey results data to an API that is running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure the API to store the survey results as a new record in an Amazon DynamoDB table, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results in a second DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

Write the survey results data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function to read the data and call Amazon Rekognition for sentiment analysis. Store the sentiment analysis results in a second S3 bucket. Use S3 lifecycle policies on each bucket to expire objects after 365 days.

Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Lex for sentiment analysis and saves the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

question_text:
A company uses AWS Systems Manager for routine management and patching of Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an IP address type target group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).
New security protocols require the company to remove EC2 instances from service during a patch. When the company attempts to follow the security protocol during the next patch, the company receives errors during the patching window.
Which combination of solutions will resolve the errors? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
The error occurred because the example was patched while still falling within the target group. Systems Manager has an off-the-shelf automated document AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance, which removes cases from the backend of the load balancer, installs updates and then puts them back (C); this process is triggered by the maintenance window, which is responsible for removing them from the service and for patching them out as planned (D).
Option A: Changing the target type from an IP address to an example does not solve the problem: during patching, the example remains in the target group.
Option B: It is the current document that caused the error, so keeping it unchanged is not a viable option.
Option E: State Manager maintains an expected configuration, but it will not remove the instance from the backend of the load balance during the patch.

options.text: Change the target type of the target group from IP address type to instance type.
Continue to use the existing Systems Manager document without changes because it is already optimized to handle instances that are in an IP address type target group behind an ALB.
Implement the AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalanacerInstance Systems Manager Automation document to manage the patching process.
Use Systems Manager Maintenance Windows to automatically remove the instances from service to patch the instances.
Configure Systems Manager State Manager to remove the instances from service and manage the patching schedule. Use ALB health checks to re-route traffic.

question_text:
A medical company wants to perform transformations on a large amount of clinical trial data that comes from several customers. The company must extract the data from a relational database that contains the customer data.
Then the company will transform the data by using a series of complex rules. The company will load the data to Amazon S3 when the transformations are complete.
All data must be encrypted where it is processed before the company stores the data in Amazon S3. All data must be encrypted by using customer-specific keys.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational effort?
explanation_en:
Two requests determine the answer. Minimum Operating Costs point to AWS Glue: It is a hosting, unservered ETL service that does not need to build and destroy clusters, unlike EMR. "All data generated during processing must be encrypted" with "customer's exclusive key" pointing to a client using KMS keys (CSE-KMS): data is encrypted before writing, each client has its own key and the intermediate result of the operation is protected. This is by attaching security configuration settings to the Glue operation.
Option A: SSE-S3 uses service management keys - they cannot be "client exclusive". Encryption only occurs when the data is written to S3, not during processing.
Option B: Each customer needs an EMR cluster, which means that the cluster needs to be managed rather than without a server, and CSE-self-defined needs to deliver the key provider on its own. This is the most expensive option to operate.
Option D: is again a cluster rather than a Glue, and SSE-KMS only protects objects stored staticly in S3 rather than data during processing.

options.text: Create one AWS Glue job for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each job that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) to encrypt the data.
Create one Amazon EMR cluster for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each cluster that uses client-side encryption with a custom client-side root key (CSE-Custom) to encrypt the data.
Create one AWS Glue job for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each job that uses client-side encryption with AWS KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS) to encrypt the data.
Create one Amazon EMR cluster for each customer. Attach a security configuration to each cluster that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) to encrypt the data.

question_text:
A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics application is highly resilient and is designed to run in stateless mode.
The company notices that the application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The application is non-state and fault-tolerant, and it is therefore appropriate to interrupt the capacity.
