The cheapest configuration: Build an AMI, put it in the startup template, create an automatic extension group based on Spot Fleet, and attach an application layer load balancer. The capacity can be expanded automatically, and the costs of the Spot instance are up to 90 per cent lower than the needs one; recovery of the example is not problematic because there is no state to preserve.
Option A: Two examples, on demand, are fixed capacity: it will remain insufficient during peak periods and the company will pay for idle capacity at low peaks. There is no real capacity for expansion.
Option B: There are also shortcomings in fixed capacity, and Route 53's weighted route does not remove cases of failure as immediately as the load balancer.
Option C: Change the type of instance to stop the instance, i.e., there is a stop time and there is still a single machine as a failure point. This is vertical expansion, not seamless expansion.

options.text: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On- Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.

Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On- Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization is more than 75%.

Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group that includes the launch template. Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.

question_text:
A company runs an environment where data is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The objects are accessed frequently throughout the day. The company has strict da ta encryption requirements for data that is stored in the S3 bucket. The company currently uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) for encryption.
The company wants to optimize costs associated with encrypting S3 objects without making additional calls to AWS KMS.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Object is frequently read, policy requires KMS encryption and the cost driver is KMS to call, not to store: in SSE-KMS mode, every reading or writing triggers a call from Decrypt or GeneralDataKey. S3 Bucket Key addresses the problem: S3 will obtain a barrel-grade key from KMS and use it to produce a key for each object at short notice, thereby reducing KMS calls - and associated costs - by approximately 99%. Encryption is still maintained as SSE-KMS and key privileges and log records are maintained.
Option A: SSE-S3 is indeed cheaper, but it completely abandons KMS, which is already strictly required and key management has been built around KMS.
Option C: Use KMS key for client encryption increases the number of KMS calls and requires the re-engineering of the application - contrary to "no additional calls needing KMS".
Option D: This combination is impossible: in SSE-C mode, the client provides the key in each request and the key will never be stored in KMS. It cannot reduce the number of calls.

options.text: Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3).
Use an S3 Bucket Key for server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) on the new objects.
Use client-side encryption with AWS KMS customer managed keys.
Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) stored in AWS KMS.

question_text:
A company runs multiple workloads on virtual machines (VMs) in an on-premises data center. The company is expanding rapidly. The on-premises data center is not able to scale fast enough to meet business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS.
The migration is time sensitive. The company wants to use a lift-and-shift strategy for non-critical workloads.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
explanation_en:
A movement of promotions within a pressing time line means a block reproduction of the virtual machine. The standard tool is the AWS Application Migration Service: The copying agent is installed on the machine (B), the initial copy is completed and the test is initiated for acceptance testing (C). At the switch, the work on the source machine is stopped and the final instance is started (D). The stop time has been reduced to a few minutes.
Option A: The programme conversion tool converts the database model and does not collect information on virtual machines.
Option E: App2Container wraps applications into containers, which changes their way of running - this is no longer a ascending migration.
Option F: DMS moves the contents of the database instead of the entire virtual machine.

options.text: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to collect data about the VMs.
Use AWS Application Migration Service. Install the AWS Replication Agent on the VMs.
Complete the initial replication of the VMs. Launch test instances to perform acceptance tests on the VMs.
Stop all operations on the VMs. Launch a cutover instance.
Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to collect data about the VMs.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the VMs.

question_text:
A company hosts an application in a private subnet. The company has already integrated the application with Amazon Cognito. The company uses an Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate users.
The company needs to modify the application so the application can securely store user documents in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Which combination of steps will securely integrate Amazon S3 with the application? (Choose two.)
explanation_en:
Two parts of the mandate. Permission: Cognito user pool to identify and issue a token, but the token cannot be used to call S3 - an identity pool is required to exchange it for a temporary IAM role certificate (A) with prefixes to the correct S3 bucket. Path: The application is run in a private subnet, so the call for S3 is done through the VPC terminal node and never touches the Internet (C). In the Cognito question, the distinction between user and identity pools is the most common point of confusion.
Option B: User pool issues identity and access tokens for your application, not AWS vouchers. They can't be used to call S3.
Option D: NAT gateways send traffic to the Internet, which contradicts the concept of private access, and there is no condition in the storage barrel policy for "requests triggered by Cognito".
Option E: Limiting through a user IP address is invalid for mobile or household users and is not an authorization mechanism at all.

options.text: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool to generate secure Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.
Use the existing Amazon Cognito user pool to generate Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.
Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint in the same VPC where the company hosts the application.
Create a NAT gateway in the VPC where the company hosts the application. Assign a policy to the S3 bucket to deny any request that is not initiated from Amazon Cognito.
Attach a policy to the S3 bucket that allows access only from the users' IP addresses.

question_text:
A company has a three-tier web application that processes orders from customers. The web tier consists of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The processing tier consists of EC2 instances. The company decoupled the web tier and processing tier by using Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). The storage layer uses Amazon DynamoDB.
At peak times, some users report order processing delays and halls. The company has noticed that during these delays, the EC2 instances are running at 100% CPU usage, and the SQS queue fills up. The peak times are variable and unpredictable.
The company needs to improve the performance of the application.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
Symptoms are described in a very accurate way: Teams are listed in the case CPUs, which continue to grow at 100 per cent and peaks are unpredictable. This means that the extension must track the length of the queue. An indicator tracking strategy based on the Approximate NonMessages indicator (usually the number of messages per instance) would precisely increase processing capacity at the beginning of the information backlog, regardless of any scheduled timetable.
Option A: A time extension cannot cope with an unpredictable peak, and CPU has reached 100% by the time of the trigger, and the signal has arrived too late.
Option B: Adding a cache before DynamoDB will not help: The bottlenecks are the calculation of messages, not the reading of data from the database.
Option C: CloudFront Cache response on the Web layer, but delay occurs in the order processing layer where messages are read from the queue.

options.text: Use scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out the processing tier instances for the duration of peak usage times. Use the CPU Utilization metric to determine when to scale.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the DynamoDB backend tier. Use target utilization as a metric to determine when to scale.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache the responses for the web tier. Use HTTP latency as a metric to determine when to scale.
Use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy to scale out the processing tier instances. Use the ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute to determine when to scale.

question_text:
A company's production environment consists of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. The instances must run for only 12 hours on Sunday and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company wants to cost-optimize the production environment.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
Obsolete expression: AWS no longer provides new clients with examples of plan pre-encumbrances. In this subject logic, option A is still the only option to ensure uninterrupted repetition of time window; in current practice, the same task is addressed by combining the start/stop with Savings Plan or On-Demand plans
The AWS official API document clearly states that Scheduled Industries can no longer be purchased. The original title is chosen according to historical product logic A, but the programme cannot be newly acquired today; the original option is retained and marked as obsolete.
Interruption cannot be tolerated, so the Spot case is completely excluded. In the case of ongoing operations from Monday to Saturday, examples of standard set-ups were purchased; for 12 hours on Sundays, examples of scheduled set-ups were used — specifically for repeat time windows. It is to be noted that AWS no longer provides this type of reservation to new clients, but in this subject logic it is still the only option to ensure uninterrupted repetition of time.
Option B: An example of a convertible reservation is a continuous charge: 12 hours a week, which means almost total unused commitment.
Option C: Spot example can be recycled, while scenes explicitly prohibit interruption.
Option D: There is also a Spot problem here, and the discount on stabilizer loads is even smaller with the convertible preset example.

options.text: Purchase Scheduled Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.

Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.

question_text:
A digital image processing company wants to migrate its on-premises monolithic application to the AWS Cloud.
The company processes thousands of images and generates large files as part of the processing workflow.
The company needs a solution to manage the growing number of image processing jobs. The solution must also reduce the manual tasks in the image processing workflow. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure of the solution.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Image processing is a batch-processing workflow and the company does not want to manage the infrastructure. AWS Watch itself provides and runs computing resources for the operation queue (including on Fargate), AWS StepFunctions describes the sequence of steps and eliminates manual interfaces, while large outcome documents are stored in S3 and their growth is unlimited and less expensive than the file storage system.
Option A: An ECS cluster based on a breakable example still needs to manage the computing environment, and SQS only provides a queue, not a workflow arrangement.
Option C: The Lambda function is limited to time and memory in the processing of heavy load images, and the breakable example means once again that you need to manage your own infrastructure.
Option D: A set of EC2 instances is the infrastructure that the company does not want to manage, and the EBS rolls cannot be shared between multiple machines and are limited in size.

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Configure Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
Use AWS Batch jobs to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Store the processed files in Amazon FSx.
Deploy a group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume.

question_text:
A company's image-hosting website gives users around the world the ability to up load, view, and download images from their mobile devices. The company currently hosts the static website in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Because of the website's growing popularity, the website's performance has decreased. Users have reported latency issues when they upload and download images.
The company must improve the performance of the website.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
explanation_en:
There are two problems — slow downloads and slow uploads — and they are solved through different tools, and the effort needed is minimal. Deployment of CloudFront in front of the S3 bucket increases the speed of download: the image is cached near the user ' s edge. S3 Transfer Acceleration increases upload speed: the file is received at the nearest edge and then transferred to the S3 bucket via the AWS backbone network. Both are activated by configuration without the need to change the structure.
Option B: An example of moving a website to multiple regions is a rewriting of the structure, accompanied by ongoing costs, with minimal workload to achieve.
Option C: Redirecting copying and downloading in multiple S3 buckets is a complex and expensive construction method that is inefficient to upload through CloudFront.
Option D: Global Accerator cannot be used with S3 as an endpoint: this configuration does not exist.

options.text: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket to improve the download performance. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to improve the upload performance.

Configure Amazon EC2 instances of the right sizes in multiple AWS Regions. Migrate the application to the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the website traffic equally among the EC2 instances. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to address global demand with low latency.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as an origin to improve the download performance. Configure the application to use CloudFront to upload images to improve the upload performance. Create S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. Configure replication rules for the buckets to replicate users' data based on the users' location. Redirect downloads to the S3 bucket that is closest to each user's location.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket to improve network performance. Create an endpoint for the application to use Global Accelerator instead of the S3 bucket.

question_text:
A company runs an application in a private subnet behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a VPC. The VPC has a NAT gateway and an internet gateway. The application calls the Amazon S3 API to store objects.
According to the company's security policy, traffic from the application must not travel across the internet.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
explanation_en:
The flow of S3 must be off the Internet and require the cheapest solutions. A S3 gateway endpoint will add a service prefix to the VPC route chart, and traffic will be kept within the AWS network, and the end point itself will not be charged — whether by hour or by the amount of data processed.
Option A: The interface endpoint is also private, but charges are paid for hours and traffic, while the gateway endpoint is free.
Option C: Allows the IP address of the NAT gateway to change the route: traffic will still pass through the Internet.
Option D: Adding another NAT gateway will only double the cost and traffic will still pass through the Internet.

options.text: Configure an S3 interface endpoint. Create a security group that allows outbound traffic to Amazon S3.
Configure an S3 gateway endpoint. Update the VPC route table to use the endpoint.
Configure an S3 bucket policy to allow traffic from the Elastic IP address that is assigned to the NAT gateway.
Create a second NAT gateway in the same subnet where the legacy application is deployed. Update the VPC route table to use the second NAT gateway.

question_text:
A company has an application that runs on an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster on Amazon EC2 instances. The application has a UI that uses Amazon DynamoDB and data services that use Amazon S3 as part of the application deployment.
The company must ensure that the EKS Pods for the UI can access only Amazon DynamoDB and that the EKS Pods for the data services can access only Amazon S3. The company uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
Which solution meals these requirements?
explanation_en:
Pod needs independent powers, not shared nodes, which require IRSA: create separate Kubernetes service accounts for UI and data services, each of which labels the ARN of its corresponding IAM role, and which is limited to specific service accounts by trusting the ODS provider of the cluster of conditions. Thus, UI Pod can only access its DynamoDB tables, while the data service Pod can only access its storage barrels. Note: The description of this option actually swaps the distribution of services (S3 assigned to UI, DynamoDB allocated to data services) — a clerical error in the source's practice material; the mechanism itself is correct. The same technology is described in detail in Question 941, 2.
Option A: The Example Role Policy grants one-time permission to each Pod at the node, while Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes API instead of access to AWS services.
Option B: An IAM policy cannot be attached directly to Pod: The main subject is the role of Pod through its service account.
Option C: The mechanism is almost correctly named, but the FullAccess management strategy gives full access to the entire service, which conflicts with the restricted access requirements that are required.

options.text: Create separate IAM policies for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB access with the required permissions. Attach both IAM policies to the EC2 instance profile. Use role-based access control (RBAC) to control access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB for the respective EKS Pods.

Create separate IAM policies for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB access with the required permissions. Attach the Amazon S3 IAM policy directly to the EKS Pods for the data services and the DynamoDB policy to the EKS Pods for the UI.

Create separate Kubernetes service accounts for the UI and data services to assume an IAM role. Attach the AmazonS3FullAccess policy to the data services account and the AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess policy to the UI service account.

Create separate Kubernetes service accounts for the UI and data services to assume an IAM role. Use IAM Role for Service Accounts (IRSA) to provide access to the EKS Pods for the UI to Amazon S3 and the EKS Pods for the data services to DynamoDB.

question_text:
A company needs to give a globally distributed development team secure access to the company's AWS resources in a way that complies with security policies.
The company currently uses an on-premises Active Directory for internal authentication. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts that support multiple projects.
The company needs a solution to integrate with the existing infrastructure to provide centralized identity management and access control.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation_en:
Users are kept in local Active Directory and need access to multiple accounts across organizations. The lightweight option is AD Contractor: instead of copying the directory, it connects the authentication request to its own domain controller as an identity source to IAM Infrastructure Center. Then assigns privileges to the AD group of the relevant account. There is no need to build forest confidence or to deploy a second catalogue in the clouds — hence minimal operating costs.
Option A: The use of a trust relationship hosting Microsoft AD is feasible, but it is an additional catalogue that needs to be paid for and maintained in the cloud and that requires forest trust. The workload is greater than that of AD Contractor.
Option B: Creating IAM users for distributed teams means manual administration of privileges and long-term vouchers, which conflict with requirements and minimize costs.
Option D: Cognito is designed for application end users, not for staff access to AWS accounts.

options.text: Set up AWS Directory Service to create an AWS managed Microsoft Active Directory on AWS. Establish a trust relationship with the on-premises Active Directory. Use IAM rotes that are assigned to Active Directory groups to access AWS resources within the company's AWS accounts.

Create an IAM user for each developer. Manually manage permissions for each IAM user based on each user's involvement with each project. Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) as an additional layer of security.

Use AD Connector in AWS Directory Service to connect to the on-premises Active Directory. Integrate AD Connector with AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure permissions sets to give each AD group access to specific AWS accounts and resources.

Use Amazon Cognito to deploy an identity federation solution. Integrate the identity federation solution with the on-premises Active Directory. Use Amazon Cognito to provide access tokens for developers to access AWS accounts and resources.

question_text:
A company is developing an application in the AWS Cloud. The application's HTTP API contains critical information that is published in Amazon API Gateway. The critical information must be accessible from only a limited set of trusted IP addresses that belong to the company's internal network.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
explanation_en:
One of the API gateways has its own access limit mechanism - resource policy. It rejects all unlisted credible addresses, and the check is done by the gateway itself before the back end is called.
Option A: How a private integrated control gateway reaches the back end in an internal network - it does not limit access to clients through an IP address.
Option C: API Gateway is a hosting service; it cannot be deployed to your own subnet and the network access control list does not apply to it.
Option D: Could not attach a security group to the API Gateway: the service does not have your network interface to reach the inbound traffic.

options.text: Set up an API Gateway private integration to restrict access to a predefined set of IP addresses.
Create a resource policy for the API that denies access to any IP address that is not specifically allowed.
Directly deploy the API in a private subnet. Create a network ACL. Set up rules to allow the traffic from specific IP addresses.
Modify the security group that is attached to API Gateway to allow inbound traffic from only the trusted IP addresses.
